HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee - company was managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies and also held majority of their conversion shares - 'D' company made an offer to assessee to purchase conversions share of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency - Assessee accepted said offer - Subsequently, agreement was modified and as per new agreement, assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in favour of 'D' company, resigned from it - Revenue authorities brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act amount of compensation received by assessee-company on account of resigning managing agency agreement - Whether since transaction in its true legal character was relinquishment of managing agency and was neither a sale nor transfer thereof, High Court rightly held that assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court : HELD: The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee held certain shares of company ‘G’ and was also managing agent of said company - During relevant accounting year, one ‘T’ made offer to assessee to purchase of aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ held by assessee also managing agency rights of assessee - Assessee accepted aforesaid offer and thereafter wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting his resignation from office of managing agents and further recommended ‘T’ to be appointed as managing agents in his place - Company ‘G’ accepted said letter - Whether resignation by assessee of managing agency and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, was nothing but mode of performance of agreement to sell managing agency arrived at between assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were attracted - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

FACT: The assessee-company entered into an agreement with a firm. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to manufacture ‘bidies’ as per the specifications, such as shape, size, quality and standard, of the firm. The assessee was also free to manufacture bidies for any person, firm or company. It was also provided that the assessee should purchase its own raw materials at its own discretion but, however, the wrapping paper and printed label bearing firm’s trade-mark were to be supplied by the firm. The price was to be fixed mutually from time to time but in no case it was to exceed the manufacturing cost plus 10 per cent profit thereon. Thereafter, another agreement was entered into between the assessee and the firm by which both the parties agreed to terminate mutually the earlier agreement. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to sell and the firm agreed to purchase running business of the assessee. As a consideration for the purchase of the bidi manufacturing business the firm was to pay to the assessee as ‘slump price’ of Rs. 5 lakhs. The IAC held that the assessee was holding an agency and the aforesaid amount received by the assessee was an amount towards termination of this agency, and, therefore, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held it as capital gain and directed the IAC to work out the taxable capital gains in accordance with the relevant provisions.

On appeal:

HELD: The agreement entered into between the parties clearly was one of the type which was entered into on principal to principal basis. The agreement showed that both the parties tried to protect their commercial interests by incorporating into an agreement provisions for this purpose. In this agreement, there was no provision whatsoever, which could be interpreted as the assessee acting as an agency of the firm for the purpose of manufacturing of bidies. The system of accounting arrived at in which the assessee could get the maximum profit of 10 per cent was for the mutual protection of the business interests of the parties. The IAC was, therefore, wrong in holding it as an agency.

So far as the question of capital gain was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wholly wrong because in a slump transaction no such capital gain could arise because the sale was of a going concern. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals ) was to be reversed. Thus, as Rs. 5 lakhs was a sum received by the assessee in a slump transaction, i.e., as a going concern, no part of this amount was taxable either as revenue receipt or as capital gains.

HELD: There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee, but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract. There was no evidence that the agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations. There was also no evidence that as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the special contract with the Central Government. The duties which the director was bound to perform for earning the remuneration of Rs. 400 per month were not on the record, but even in the opinion of the taxing authorities the duties of 'T' as director did not cover attendance to the contract with the Government. 'T' and 'M' were brothers, but that by itself is not sufficient to justify an inference that unreasonable or excessive remuneration was agreed to be paid. The person who was called upon to attend to a contract of this magnitude was required to have expert knowledge of the business, apply his time exclusively thereto, travel from time to time, maintain supervision and control at the stage of purchase, redrying, packing, transport and loading for shipment. Presumably 'T' was such a person, and that is why he was selected for earning for the assessee a large amount of commission by duly performing the contract.

An analysis of the reasons given by the ITO disclosed no grounds to support the view that remuneration at a rate exceeding 10 per cent of the net profit was excessive or unreasonable. The contract with the Government was for the assessee an important contract requiring constant and vigilant application and supervision by a person well acquainted with the practical details of the business. If the management of the assessee as prudent businessman for advancing the interest of the assessee bona fide regarded 30 per cent of the net profits as reasonable remuneration, the revenue authorities were not justified in reviewing their opinion and reducing the rate of remuneration. It was true that if, on a consideration of the relevant materials, the Tribunal was of the opinion that a particular remuneration stipulated to be paid was not bona fide or is unreasonable, the High Court in exercising its advisory jurisdiction had no power to interfere with that opinion. But the material circumstances relating to the nature of the contract, the services to be performed and the nature of the duties by the employee were not at all taken into account by the Tribunal and the income-tax authorities. Therefore, the disallowance of a sum of out of the remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable ?

The contract under which the assessee was appointed managing agent for the 'N' was to enure till 1960, but it had to be prematurely terminated because the Government of Madras exercising its powers under 1949 Act had compulsorily acquired the electricity undertaking. With the acquisition of that undertaking the right of the assessee as managing agent ceased. Under section 15 of the 1449 Act, the Government was bound to pay compensation which would include compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement. The assessee received sum as compensation for termination of the agency, computed in the manner laid down in section 15 of that Act. Prima facie, such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of the assessee, was a capital receipt.

Turning to the facts of the instant case, it must in the first instance be observed that it was for the revenue to establish that a particular receipt was income liable to tax, and beyond stating that the assessee was the managing agent of the 'N' and of two other companies, there was no other evidence about the nature of the business of the two other companies of which the assessee was the managing agent, about their relative importance qua the managing agency of the 'N' and whether by reason of the extinction of the managing agency of the 'N' any enduring asset was lost to the assessee, or its trading organisation was adversely affected. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore 'the receipt was to be considered as revenue'.

Hence, the compensation received for taking over the 'N' was a capital receipt not liable to be taxed, and on the materials placed the Supreme Court did not disagree with the High Court.

The appeal therefore failed and was to be dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii), read with  section 2(34) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A), read with section 2(11) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1955-56 - Assessee, who was managing agent of certain company and whose accounting year was calendar year, entered into agreement with a third person on 8-1-1955, whereby assessee agreed to sell or to procure for that person 2,500 shares of managed company and also agreed to resign its managing agency from that date for specified consideration to be paid by that third person to assessee - Assessing authority brought compensation amount to tax under section 10(5A) in assessment year in question - Whether sum received at or in connection with termination of managing agency was taxable under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether since previous year for managing agency business itself was calendar year 1955, same previous year had to be adopted for receipt of payment in question - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, payment received on 8-1-1955 was assessable in assessment year 1956-57 and not in assessment year in question - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was appointed as the managing agents of the K Mills Ltd. under a managing agency agreement entered into in 1935. One C entered into an agreement with the assessee on 8-1-1955, whereby the assessee agreed to sell or to procure for C 2,500 shares of K Mills before a specified date. Another term of this agreement was that the assessee should resign its managing agency of the K Mills Ltd. and that a consideration of Rs. 2,24,000 should be paid therefor to the assessee by C. It was common ground that the terms of the agreement were fulfilled and that the resignation of the assessee-firm was also accepted by the board of directors of the K Mills Ltd. In the return of the assessee for the calendar year relevant to the assessment year 1955-56, the above receipt of Rs. 2,24,000 was not returned as part of the income. The ITO applied section 10(5A) and called upon the assessee to show cause why the said amount should not be included in the total income of the relevant year ending on 31-3-1955. The assessee objected contending that there was no termination of the managing agency agreement by the managed company and that the payment having been made by a third party and not by the principals, the amount was not compensation within the meaning of the Act. A further objection advanced was that since the amount was received on 8-1-1955, and since the previous year of the assessee was the calendar year, this amount could not be brought to assessment in the assessment year 1955-56. These objections were overruled. On the first question, the departmental authorities and the Tribunal came to the conclusion that section 10(5A) applied and that the amount was taxable. On the second question, the ITO was of the view that the previous year for a business "which had no books of account which were not made up to profit and loss account for any particular period" should be the financial year. So that, since the amount was received in the financial year ending on the 31-3-1955, it was assessable in the assessment year 1955-56. The appeal to the Tribunal on this point also failed.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee company was managing agents of various companies including one 'G', in which assessee held a large block of shares - In 1951, board of directors of 'G' decided to terminate agency against payment of certain amount to assessee - Whether termination of managing agency in question had resulted in destruction of source of in come of assessee and, thus, amount received by assessee was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - High Court - Reference to - Assessment year 1952-53 - Whether neither High Court nor Supreme Court has jurisdiction to reappreciate material on record to find out whether facts found by Tribunal are correct or not - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee was appointed by Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and agreed to pay to assessee price of tobacco purchased, and commission on all purchases – Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' in 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of net profit as remuneration – Under contract with Government of India, certain amount became due to assessee as commission after providing for expenses, 30 per cent of balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - ITO reduced stipulated rate to 10 per cent. on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of company, bound to attend to all activities of company including contract - Whether since there was no evidence that agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all activities of company including special contract with Central Government, disallowance of a sum out of remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as – Assessment year 1952-53 – Assessee was acting as managing agents for 'N' - Subsequently, agreement was terminated when Government of State of Madras in exercise of powers conferred upon it by Electrical Undertakings Acquisition Act, 1949, compulsorily acquired undertaking of that company, and assessee was paid as compensation for premature termination of its agency - The ITO observed that assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end, assessee still continued as 'managing agents of other companies' and therefore receipt was to be considered as revenue - Whether such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of assessee, was a capital receipt, therefore, same was not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company carried on business in hides and skins, minerals, tobacco and other commodities, and also acted as managing agents for the 'N' and for two other companies. 'T', 'M' and 'C' were directors of the company. The assessee was appointed by the Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and in accordance with the directions issued from time to time and agreed to pay to the assessee price of the tobacco purchased, charge at the rate of one anna per 1b. for tobacco not redried, and at the rate of two annas per 1b. for tobacco redried, and commission on all purchases. Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, inspecting tobacco at Guntur and at Madras Port, and for supervising shipment of tobacco, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of the net profit as remuneration. Under the contract with the Government of India, certain amount became due to the assessee as commission in the account year ending 31-3-1952. After providing for expenses, 30 per cent of the balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed in the assessment year 1952-53 as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act. The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds : that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1956-57 - Assessee was one of two managing directors of private limited company namely 'T' Ltd. - He held nine shares and his son one share in 'T' Ltd whereas remaining ten shares were held by 'P', his wife and cousin - 'T' Ltd. was managing agent of public limited company i.e., 'A' Ltd. - Assessee held 1674 shares in said public limited company - Subsequently, assessee sold his shares in 'T' Ltd. as well as in 'A' Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin - Whether profits earned on sale of aforesaid shares were assessable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, no

FACT: The assessee was one of the two managing directors of a private limited company T. Ltd. The other managing director was one 'P'. Out of the total of 20 shares of Rs. 100 each, the assessee held nine shares and his son one share, the remaining shares being held by 'P', his wife and cousin. This company was the managing agent of a public limited company A Ltd. Both these companies had been incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The public limited company had issued 11,986 shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each, out of which the assessee held, 1,674 shares. The assessee and his son transferred ten shares in T. Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin or their nominees for Rs. 3,50,000 as also 4,165 shares in the A Ltd.

By the transfer two sets of shares the assessee made a profit of Rs. 3,14,100 in respect of nine shares and another sum of Rs. 72,515 in respect of 1,674 shares. These two amounts were brought to tax for the assessment year 1956-57 treating them as income and liable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act. Both the ITO as well as the AAC repelled the assessee's contention that the receipts were in the nature of capital assets by sale of the shares. The AAC accepted the view that the amounts in excess of the book value of the shares transferred by the assesses were in the nature of inducement to him or compensation for giving up the management.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was neither a manager nor a managing agent of an Indian company within the meaning of section 2(9A) of the Indian Companies Act and that the provisions of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act were, therefore, not applicable to the two amounts.

The Tribunal also considered the further question whether the two amounts could be regarded as compensation for loss of management rights in A. Ltd. and came to the conclusion that there was no material to hold that the profit represented such compensation.

On reference:

HELD: Having regard to the definitions of managing agent and manger in section 2(9A) and 2(9) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the assessee by himself could not by any means be regarded as a managing agent. He by himself never entered into an agreement with either of the companies by which he was entitled to be a managing agent. Nor it could be said that as one of the two managing directors he was entitled to the management of the whole affairs of either of the companies. It was only the corporation of which the assessee along with 'P' was the managing director that was entitled to manage the whole affairs of the 'A' Ltd. That was one of the lines of reasoning on which the Tribunal held that clauses (a) and (b) of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act would be inapplicable to the amounts. That view was to be accepted. Thus, the assessee by himself was neither a managing agent nor a manager as the terms were defined in the Indian Companies Act, 1913.

Clause (c) of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act will be inapplicable because, as the Tribunal rightly held, that contemplates a company other than an Indian company.

For clause (d) to apply, the assessee must be holding an agency relating to the business of "any other person". It is impossible to say that the assessee in instant case by himself held such an agency. The managing agency was vested in the corporation and not in any one of the directors.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipts - Assessment year 1944-45 - By an agreement assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent of a company - During relevant accounting year managed company received offer from another company, company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as managing agents - Said offer was accepted by managed company and it asked assessee to retire - Assessee received certain amount by way of compensation towards termination of managing agency - Majority of shareholders of company ‘J’ were members of assessee-firm - Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was not casual receipt and it did arise out of business of assessee and, therefore, was not exempted under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

HELD: The instant case was not one of a change of opinion by the successor as on the findings of the Tribunal the predecessor being unaware of the nature of the receipt had no occasion to form any opinion and the case was simply one of omission or may even be one of negligence and where the successor became aware of the omission or negligence. The case of a change of opinion simpliciter occurs only where without reference to the papers on the record or books or information from any outside source the same person who formed the opinion originally, changes that opinion subsequently by process of contemplation or by mere thinking about it a second time. It followed that action under section 34 of the 1922 Act was validly taken.

The Tribunal was also justified in holding that the receipt was a revenue receipt liable to tax.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.
