The covenants affected or impaired the trading structure itself of the assessee and thus, it was a capital receipt. [Para 21] Section 28(ii) specifically deals with compensation for general termination of agency or modification of terms and conditions relating thereto. These provisions were brought in only in the context of managing agency agreements. The assessee in its own right distributed products bottled by ‘S’ in pursuance of a distribution agreement, which definitely was not an agency agreement. The first appellate authority had observed that invoking of the provisions of section 28 by the Assessing Officer was not relevant as the assessee was not a management agent nor the agreement with ‘S’ was an agency agreement. Thus, the receipt in question would not fall within the net of section 28(ii) and was for restrictive covenant and the agreement had resulted in the entire business structure of the assessee in line of soft drinks distribution being impaired or destroyed. Therefore, what the assessee received was a compensation for loss of its source of business and not compensation for loss of income or profit and, thus, it was a capital receipt not exigible to tax. [Para 26]

The perception of the Assessing Officer that there was no requirement for ‘B’ to pay consideration for goodwill to the assessee-company as it was a mere transporter and not a distributor and dealer in soft drinks was not borne out by record or evidence. On the contrary, the statistics submitted by the assessee showed that it was marketing products of ‘S’ as distributor and there was substantial improvement in the business of the assessee. Further, the agreement of goodwill showed that ‘B’ acknowledged the fact that the assessee-company had goodwill and had agreed to pay for the same. The basis on which such goodwill was to be quantified was given in the agreement itself. The Assessing Officer could not simply state that he disbelieved the agreement, as in his perception there was no goodwill whatsoever, that too without any rhyme or reason. Hence, the observation made by the Assessing Officer that the agreement in question was a make-believe agreement was without an iota of evidence. Thus, the order of the appellate authority to tax amount of goodwill under capital gain was to be upheld. [Paras 27 and 29]

Section 50(2) refers to block of assets ceasing to exist as such by reason of transfer of the entire ‘block of assets’. The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. Even if it was taken as a capital asset, in view of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Ambica Chemical Production v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal No. 238/V/2002, dated 26-5-2005] no tax was leviable in terms of section 45 on the amount received by the assessee. [Para 30]

Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld. [Para 32]

of grant under the notified order was relatable to the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Saurashtra Grants (Resumption) Ordinance, 1949, which empowered the Government of the State of Saurashtra, inter alia, to resume the grant and to provide for incidental and consequential matters. In this background, it could never be said that the assessee had purchased income by surrendering his capital asset, viz., ‘jagir’ under the said grant. Such resumption had the effect of the capital asset of the assessee, which was an income producing estate, being lost to the assessee and in lieu of such capital loss, the reimbursement was being made by providing for payment of a determined amount only during the life-time of the assessee. This payment was clearly intended to compensate for the loss to the assessee, which was caused by virtue of his capital estate being taken over under the resumption order warranted by the said Ordinance. These annual instalments though described as cash annuity, were, when the substance of the transaction was looked at, not income, but were only intended to be payments towards the loss of the income-producing assets of the assessee and, therefore, they were capital receipts. It could be noted that these periodic payments described as cash annuity were required to be debited by the Government under the head ‘76. Other Misc. Compensation and Assignment - A-2 pension in lieu of Resumed Lands’. Thus, even the Government treated it as compensation, which was being paid to the assessee in lieu of the resumption of lands included in the Jagir granted to the assessee under the said grant. Further, it would be reasonable to assume that since the payments were required to be made under the resumption order, simultaneously on resumption of the grant they were in reality intended to compensate the assessee for the loss of his capital asset, i.e., the ‘jagir’. The true quality of the payment clearly showed that the payment though described as cash annuity was not annuity in the sense of purchase of income, but it was annual payment of compensation to the assessee for the loss of his income-producing asset. These payments were, therefore, clearly capital receipts in the hands of the assessee and could never be termed as income. Such capital receipts would not be taxable except as capital gains and any tax on such capital receipts would amount to taxing the capital, which is not the intention of the income-tax law.

Moreover, where a voluntary payment is made entirely without consideration and is not traceable to any source which a practical man may regard as a real source of income, but depends entirely on the whim of the donor, such payment cannot fall in the category of income. Therefore, even if the amount was paid under the resumption order voluntarily and without any consideration, and was not traceable to any real source of income depending entirely on the pleasure of the Government, such payment would not fall in the category of income.

Therefore, the Tribunal committed an error in holding that the cash annuity in the resumption of two villages was an income and not capital receipt in the hands of the assessee.

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation for termination of agency, etc. - Assessment year 1970-71 - Assessee was working as consultant of a company on 10 years contract and receiving annual remuneration - When its services were terminated after 5 years, it received lump sum payment as compensation as per mutual agreement - Revenue contended that amount received was revenue receipt and even if held to be capital, it was assessable under section 28(ii)(c) - Whether since cancellation of contract had impaired profit-making trading structure/asset of assessee which had resulted in loss of source of income to assessee and also considering unexpired period which was quite long, payment made was a capital asset/receipt - Held, yes - Whether pre-requisite for applicability of section 28(ii)(c) is that it must be an agency agreement - Held, yes - In instant case, Tribunal recorded a finding that agreement was purely one of consultancy service and what was contemplated in agreement was between principal and principal and there was no agency agreement - Whether, therefore, compensation received by assessee on termination of agreement was not taxable even under provisions of section 28(ii)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was acting as a managing agent of two companies. As per agreement, the assessee was entitled to claim remuneration at certain percentage on profit calculated for these companies, in addition to certain minimum remuneration receivable every month. The additional remuneration was payable in the event of remuneration payable exceeding the minimum and the same was payable only after the audited balance sheet and profit and loss account of the relevant year were placed and duly approved by the General Body Meeting of the companies. The assessee was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis and the department was also making assessment up to the assessment year 1970-71, on the basis that the additional remuneration was assessable in the hands of the assessee when the relevant balance sheet and profit and loss account were approved in the AGM. But, in the year 1971-72, the Assessing Officer changed the method of taxation of the additional remuneration and according to the Assessing Officer, the additional remuneration became due to the assessee as per the agreement entered into with the companies and it was assessable in the year in which the minimum remuneration was payable and the fact that it was paid subsequently was not a relevant consideration. On appeal, the AAC affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal following the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. [1979] 120 ITR 913 held that the additional remuneration was approved only after the audited balance sheet and the profit and loss account were placed before the General Body Meeting of the managing companies and approved in the said General Body Meeting; therefore, the additional remuneration would be assessable in the year in which it was approved.

HEADNOTE: Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B of the Indian  Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was partner in a firm - Said firm sold shares of a company together with its managing agency rights at an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share though market value of share was Rs. 46 only - Whether full value must be true value and not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset and, hence, for purposes of section 12B of 1922 Act sale price of shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. at 65 per share - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a firm. The said firm by agreement dated 7-9-1946 sold shares in a company together with the managing agency right of said company which it was holding to another firm for an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share, though the market value at the time was Rs. 46 per share. The department held that for purposes of computation of capital gains of assessee partner, the sale price of each share should be taken at Rs. 65 while the assessee contended that the market value of Rs 46 should be taken into account. The Tribunal upheld the decision of the department.

On reference:

HELD: The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee company appointed ‘C’ as its managing agents -It, however, terminated managing agency prior to completion of period as prescribed in managing agency agreement and appointed other company, namely company ‘J’, as its managing agents - Certain amount was paid as compensation to ‘C’ for such termination - Facts revealed that start assessee was not faced with any immediate or present danger to be averted, neither any financial problem confronted board of directors for terminating managing agency agreement nor was any economic difficulty to be surmounted by adopting this course - Whether on facts, it could be said that assessee compounded consolidated claim of managing agents whose services were terminated apparently without any cause and amount paid for this purpose brought into existence advantage of enduring nature from economic paint of view and thus amount paid by it to ‘C’ was not permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act in hands of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company appointed ‘C’ as its managing agents in 1938 for a period of thirty years on a monthly remuneration besides ten per cent commission on net yearly profits of the company. Subsequently, in August 1941, Company ’J’ was appointed as its managing agents of the assessee instead of ‘C’. On 19-11-1952, the board of directors decided to terminate the managing agency agreement of ‘C’ and a resolution was passed to this effect by the extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders. The managing agents wrote back that the resolution constituted a breach of the contract of the managing agency and lodged a claim for compensation. The dispute was settled against certain payment which was approved in the extra ordinary general meeting of the assessee. For the assessment year 1952-53, the assessee claimed deduction of aforesaid amount as business expenditure. The ITO held that whole affairs was so hastily planned as to give an odour "of the pre-planned camouflage" and that the sum paid to the managing agents was a sort of solatium not admissible as a revenue business expenditure. However, on appeal, the AAC allowed the assessee’s claim. The order of AAC was confirmed by the Tribunal.

On reference:

HELD: The concepts of capital and revenue expenditure are not defined anywhere in the statute, but there is no dearth of guidelines indicated by eminent judges in reported decisions both in England and in India.

In the instant case the assessee was not forced with any immediate or present danger to be averted, neither any financial problem confronted the board of directors for terminating the managing agency agreement nor was any economic difficulty to be surmounted by adopting this course. Plainly, the directors compounded a consolidated claim of the managing agents whose services were terminated apparently without any cause and the amount was paid for this purpose which, undoubtedly, resulted in an enduring benefit, from the economic point of view, for the assessee. Considering that the agreement which was being terminated was assignable and no managing agents were appointed to succeed in place of company ‘J’, there was brought into existence a clear advantage of an enduring nature, an advantage indistinguishable from a material or fixed asset for the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the assessee’s contention must fail and it was held that the payment of made to ‘C’ was not a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act, in the hands of the assessee.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipt - Assessment year 1942-43 and 1944-45 - Assessee-company was incorporated with an object of carrying on business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, etc. - Assessee invested certain amount with a newly incorporated sugar company with a condition that assessee was to be given managing agency in a company to be erected in future - That company, however, could not be erected - During relevant accounting years assessee sold shares acquired by it and made certain profit - Whether object of assessee in buying shares in sugar company was purely to obtain managing agency of new mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from inception no intention whatever on part of assessee to re-sell shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them - Held, yes - Whether therefore investment of money in purchase of shares was of a capital nature and profits arising out of sale of shares were of a capital nature and were not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with an object to undertake and carry on the general business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, export and import agents, clearing and forwarding or house or land agents. In 1933 another sugar company was incorporated. Managing director of the assessee entered into an agreement with the sugar company in March 1933, whereby the assessee-company was to invest Rs. 5,00,000 in the sugar company in lieu of which it was to be given the managing agency of the third mill of the sugar company not in existence at the time.

The third mill was, however, not erected and the agreement about acquiring the managing agency fell through. The managing director died in December 1940, and the assessee decided to sell all the shares in 1941. The excess amount realized on sale of these shares was taxed by the ITO, as revenue receipts, the first in the assessment year 1942-43 and the second in 1944-45. The assessee-company's contention that the excess was in the nature of capital appreciation was not accepted. This order was confirmed by the AAC and the Tribunal.

On reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The exact nature of the business which the assessee was doing was admittedly not clear from the record but it was not denied that the memorandum of association of the assessee did not authorise it to purchase and/or sell shares as dealers nor was it denied that beyond this isolated transaction of purchase and sale the assessee did not deal in shares. It seemed that the object of the assessee in buying shares was purely to obtain the managing agency of the third mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from the inception no intention whatever on the part of the assessee to re-sell the shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them. Naturally when the third mill was not erected and the object of securing the managing agency became impossible of fulfilment, the assessee withdrew the shares and sold them at a profit. After conceding that the taking up of the shares by the assessee in the sugar company was an essential part of the arrangement arrived at, the only reasonable conclusion to which the High Court should have come was that the investment of the money in the purchase of shares was of a capital nature and the profits arising out of the sale of the shares in the circumstances of this case were accretions to capital and were not liable to tax.

Accordingly, the decision of the High Court was to be reversed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. [1979] 120 ITR 913 held that the additional remuneration was approved only after the audited balance sheet and the profit and loss account were placed before the General Body Meeting of the managing companies and approved in the said General Body Meeting; therefore, the additional remuneration would be assessable in the year in which it was approved.

On reference : HELD: In identical situation in the case of South Madras Industrial Development (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Madras High Court held that in the absence of inadequacy of the profit, under the agreement, the managing agent was entitled to the minimum remuneration payable at such rate for each year and insofar as the additional remuneration was concerned, there was no provision in the agreement as to when it accrued. The High Court held that in the absence of any provision in the agreement as to when it accrued, it accrued at the time when it became payable to the assessee. Similarly, on the facts of the case, the contract was silent as to when the amount became due and in the absence of any material, it was to be held that it was not possible to treat the amount as being due on the last date of the accounting year. The finding of the Tribunal was that the additional remuneration became due only after the audited balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company were laid before the company’s General Body Meeting and approved by the same. Since the additional remuneration was based on the profit and unless the amount of profit was known, it was not possible to hold that the additional remuneration accrued at the end of the relevant accounting year. The department was not able to show that under provision of the agreement, the additional remuneration became due prior to the approval in the General Body Meeting. Therefore, it was to be held that the view of the Tribunal that the income did not accrue to the assessee on or before 31-03-1970 and the additional remuneration received by the assessee was not liable to be included for the assessment year 1970-71 appeared to be in order.
