It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

On principle also it was difficult to understand why a distinction should be made between the destruction of the whole of the capital asset or a part of the capital asset. In either case, it was clear that the amount received as solatium for that destruction could not be profits arising out of the business of the assessee. The assessee was sought to be taxed under section 10 and the department had to satisfy that the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was profit made by the assessee in the course of its business or profit earned out of its business. Surely when Rs. 25,00,000 had been paid to the assessee for the cessation of its particular business, it could not be urged that this very sum of Rs. 25,00,000 were profits earned by the assessee in the course of its business.

Inasmuch as the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was received by the assessee in consideration of the termination of its managing agency, it was a solatium for the cessation of one of the several activities which the assessee company was entitled to carry on under the agreement, and if it was a solatium then it could not be looked upon as income but must be looked upon as representing the capital asset which had ceased to exist.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

The subject-matter of appeal would get confined to the limits of the grounds specifically raised in the memorandum of appeal, the new grounds raised by the appellant with the previous permission of the Tribunal and the grounds urged by the respondent in support of the decree passed in his favour, even though the decision of the Court, against which the appeal is filed, is against him. It is thus clear that the Tribunal will have no jurisdiction to found its decision on grounds which have not been raised before it by any of the parties at all. In other words, it would not be open to the Tribunal to make out a new case for either the appellant or the respondent. The finding of the AAC was that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital loss and the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. Deducting the capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares, the total figure of the capital gain was arrived at, and from the total gain, the capital gain falling to the share of the assessee was computed at. In this context, it would not be reasonable to assume that by raising this ground the appellant was challenging the finding which was already in his favour, but it would be reasonable to hold that he was challenging the finding which was only against him, and that finding was that the value of the managing agency as on 1-1-1939, was nil. In dealing with this ground, the Tribunal itself observed that the said contention of the assessee related to the capital gains computed by the department.

The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee, but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract. There was no evidence that the agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations. There was also no evidence that as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the special contract with the Central Government. The duties which the director was bound to perform for earning the remuneration of Rs. 400 per month were not on the record, but even in the opinion of the taxing authorities the duties of 'T' as director did not cover attendance to the contract with the Government. 'T' and 'M' were brothers, but that by itself is not sufficient to justify an inference that unreasonable or excessive remuneration was agreed to be paid. The person who was called upon to attend to a contract of this magnitude was required to have expert knowledge of the business, apply his time exclusively thereto, travel from time to time, maintain supervision and control at the stage of purchase, redrying, packing, transport and loading for shipment. Presumably 'T' was such a person, and that is why he was selected for earning for the assessee a large amount of commission by duly performing the contract.

An analysis of the reasons given by the ITO disclosed no grounds to support the view that remuneration at a rate exceeding 10 per cent of the net profit was excessive or unreasonable. The contract with the Government was for the assessee an important contract requiring constant and vigilant application and supervision by a person well acquainted with the practical details of the business. If the management of the assessee as prudent businessman for advancing the interest of the assessee bona fide regarded 30 per cent of the net profits as reasonable remuneration, the revenue authorities were not justified in reviewing their opinion and reducing the rate of remuneration. It was true that if, on a consideration of the relevant materials, the Tribunal was of the opinion that a particular remuneration stipulated to be paid was not bona fide or is unreasonable, the High Court in exercising its advisory jurisdiction had no power to interfere with that opinion. But the material circumstances relating to the nature of the contract, the services to be performed and the nature of the duties by the employee were not at all taken into account by the Tribunal and the income-tax authorities. Therefore, the disallowance of a sum of out of the remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable ?

The contract under which the assessee was appointed managing agent for the 'N' was to enure till 1960, but it had to be prematurely terminated because the Government of Madras exercising its powers under 1949 Act had compulsorily acquired the electricity undertaking. With the acquisition of that undertaking the right of the assessee as managing agent ceased. Under section 15 of the 1449 Act, the Government was bound to pay compensation which would include compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement. The assessee received sum as compensation for termination of the agency, computed in the manner laid down in section 15 of that Act. Prima facie, such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of the assessee, was a capital receipt.

Turning to the facts of the instant case, it must in the first instance be observed that it was for the revenue to establish that a particular receipt was income liable to tax, and beyond stating that the assessee was the managing agent of the 'N' and of two other companies, there was no other evidence about the nature of the business of the two other companies of which the assessee was the managing agent, about their relative importance qua the managing agency of the 'N' and whether by reason of the extinction of the managing agency of the 'N' any enduring asset was lost to the assessee, or its trading organisation was adversely affected. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore 'the receipt was to be considered as revenue'.

Hence, the compensation received for taking over the 'N' was a capital receipt not liable to be taxed, and on the materials placed the Supreme Court did not disagree with the High Court.

The appeal therefore failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There was no dispute that the portion of the compensation which represented past profits was a revenue receipt. The only question was whether the remaining portion was a revenue receipt or capital receipt. The remaining portion purported to be compensation given to the three partners for giving up: (i) the managing agency rights, (ii) the selling agency rights, and (iii) the goodwill. The managing agency rights vested with new firm (BJ). Similar was the case of the goodwill assuming that any goodwill had been built up by that time. 'BJ' continued to be in existence. It had not parted with managing agency rights nor its goodwill taken away. What had happened was that the partners representing the assessee firm in 'BJ' had surrendered their rights in partnership to the remaining partners and obtained certain payments for such surrender. This was not a case of parting with any agency rights. This was really a case of cancellation of a contract which had been entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such contracts are liable, in the ordinary course of business, to be altered or terminated on terms and any payment received in settlement of the rights as a result of the termination of the contract really represents the profits which the assessee would have made had the contract been performed. In the instant case, no deed of partnership had been entered into. Therefore, the same was terminable at will. Any of the partners of the firm could have brought the partnership to an end. Consequently, the possibility of termination of a partnership was inherent in the very course of business. Further the assessee-firm had various business activities; one of which was to join 'BJ' to carry on certain business activities. The assessee's representatives by entering into that agreement were merely carrying on a trading activity. Such being the case, it could not be held that the compensation paid for the termination of the contract was a capital receipt. It was not the case of the assessee that its only trading activity had come to an end. It had several activities. Just one of its trading had been put an end to. Hence, the amount received could not be considered as compensation for stopping its business.

As regards the transfer of the selling agency to 'BJ', this was not a right transferred under agreement as that right had been transferred to 'BJ' even at the time the partnership was formed. Further the trading structure of the assessee-firm was not affected. It merely replaced one trading activity by another with the aid of Rs. 35,01,000. In such circumstances, the amount received from the cancellation of agency did not represent the price paid for the loss of capital; it was of the nature of income. Therefore, the entire sum of Rs. 35,01,000 received by the assessee was a revenue receipt assessable under section 10 of 1922 Act.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Even if it was assumed that the impugued payment was for surrendering of the managing agency, unless there was a finding that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency, this aspect would not support the revenue's stand.

Accordingly, the surplus arising out of the transaction of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains.

There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. The former only is treated as income, but not so with regard to the latter. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the firm itself was formed solely for the purpose of managing the company by entering into the agreement in question with the I.T.F. and there was no other business for it. If that was so, when on account of the loss of the managing agency the assessee-firm lost its business itself, the compensation received by it for that loss would be capital in nature. It is also generally held by the courts that lump sum amounts received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreements are capital in nature.

In the possible case, it was not possible to say that the agreement entered into between the assessee-firm and the I.T.F. under which the assessee-firm acquired the managing agency of the company was a contract, entered into in the ordinary course of business or a trading contract. It followed from the above discussion that the amount of compensation awarded to the assessee-firm was capital receipt and not a revenue receipt liable to tax. Though the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was capital in nature, none the less it was to be treated as "profits and gains of business" as provided under section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act and section 28(ii ) of the 1961 Act.

It was true that the assessee-firm did not enter into any agreement directly with the managed company. It was only the ‘I.T.F.’ which entered into the managing agency agreement with the managed company. But as per the terms of the agreement entered into between the ‘I.T.F.’ and the assessee-firm, the ‘I.T.F.’ assigned its rights under the managing agency agreement to the assessee-firm. The managed company also passed a resolution ratifying the assignment. The umpire awarded damages to the assessee-firm for its loss of managing agency commission, which the assessee-firm would have otherwise been entitled to, but for the breach of the agreement. It was only on the basis of the managing agency commission which the assessee-firm, would have received and estimating it, the umpire awarded the damages to the assessee-firm. What was relevant was whether the amount received was towards compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement or not. It mattered little who paid the amount. Therefore, the amount awarded to the assessee-firm must be deemed as profits and gains of business carried on by it and, therefore, it was income liable to tax.

In the instant case, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum monthly remuneration. Though some quantification was also involved in arriving at the actual damages, the compensation was awarded to the assessee-firm on the basis of the remuneration of so much per year as having accrued to it during the relevant years 1955-56 to 1959-60 (up to 14-8-1960). It was on that basis estimation of the damages was made by the umpire in the arbitration proceedings in awarding the compensation. As the assessee-firm employed the mercantile system of accountancy the relevant amounts as estimated by the umpire in the award must be deemed to have accrued to the assessee-firm during the relevant years.

Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of the revenue.

There could be no doubt that by paying the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 the managed company had secured for itself a release from the obligation to pay a higher remuneration to the assessee for the rest of the period of managing agency covered by the principal agreement. Prima facie, that release from liability to pay a higher remuneration for over 17 years must be an advantage gained by the managed company for the benefit of its business and the immunity thus obtained by the managed company might well be regarded as the acquisition of an asset of enduring value by means of a capital outlay which would be a capital expenditure.

In the resolution adopted by the managed company as well as in the recitals set out in the supplementary agreement that sum had been stated to be a payment "as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous term as to remuneration contained" in the principal agreement. It was true that the language used in the document was not decisive and the question had to be determined by a consideration of all the attending circumstances; nevertheless, the language could not be ignored altogether but must be taken into consideration along with other relevant circumstances.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued.

A managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at the rate of 20 per cent of the profits was not the same thing as a managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at 10 per cent of the profits. There was a distinct deterioration in the character and quality of the managing agency viewed as a profit-making apparatus and this deterioration was of an enduring kind. The reduced remuneration having been separately provided, the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 must be regarded as having been paid as compensation for that injury to or deterioration of the managing agency.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid and received not to make up the difference between the higher remuneration and the reduced remuneration but was in reality paid and received as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous terms as to remuneration as it was in terms expressed to be. In other words, so far as the managed company was concerned, it was paid for securing immunity from the liability to pay higher remuneration to the assessee firm for the rest of the term of the managing agency and, therefore, a capital expenditure and so far as the assessee firm was concerned, it was received as compensation for the deterioration or injury to the managing agency by reason of the release of its rights to get higher remuneration and, therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax.

Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375. As regards the point that compensation was for past service of the firm, from a perusal of paragraph 2 of the agreement, it was clear that the promotion of the company by the partners of the firm was consideration for the appointment of the firm and for its tenure. It was a duly executed consideration. The period of 99 years was a fixed period. The firm was to continue for the whole of that period, unless it resigned the managing agency. It was not removable while the period of 99 years was still running. It could be removed only after the expiry of that period, and then also, only by a 3/4th majority of the shareholders of the company. It is clear that the situation in which the managing agency firm might resign or be removed prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years was not envisaged in the agreement at all. It followed that services rendered by the partners of the managing agency firm in promoting the company could not under the agreement for the basis of any compensation to be awarded to the firm for termination of the agreement either by its resignation or by its removal prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years. The compensation paid could not be consideration for past services.

It was paragraph 3 only of the agreement, which made provision for the premature termination of the managing agency. That paragraph contemplated termination only in one contingency, that of the company being wound up. If the company itself was wound up, the managing agency would be discontinued. In that event only, compensation as provided in paragraph 3(a) was payable. Thus it was clear that the compensation paid on the termination of the managing agency was not compensation for past services and was quite independent of that agreement. At the Tribunal stage this argument stood overruled when the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the payment was not collusive but was genuine and bona fide and further when it held that services were actually rendered by the firm in pursuance of the managing agency agreement after the company came into existence. In the face of the finding that services were actually rendered by the firm, which is a finding of fact, the argument that if any service was at all rendered, it was only the past service for promoting the company, stood overruled.

The result was that the compensation paid was receipt of a capital nature.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The agency agreement entered into by the assessee with ‘HML’ in the year 1955 was a capital asset; the whole of it was not destroyed, lost or parted when the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ in the year 1960. It was merely an exploitation of the commercial assets in a different form. Till then, the recurring amount which the assessee was getting from ‘P’ was income. But by the arrangement arrived at on the basis of the second agreement, the whole of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee was parted with and lost. The question has presented some difficulty when the assessee gets some amount of compensation on termination of agency agreement from the principal itself. Sometimes, in a given case, such compensation, and especially with regard to the managing agency business, has been treated as revenue receipts. But, in the instant case, the type of agreement which the assessee entered into with ‘O’ even if it would have entered into with ‘P’ on payment of Rs. 50,000, would not have clothed the receipt with the chartered of a revenue receipt; still it would have been a capital receipt. This was clearly so, without presenting any difficulty, when the agreement was with another company. After having parted with all its rights of profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960, by a subsequent agreement executed in the year 1962, the assessee was left with no business activity in connection with the agency agreement with ‘HML’. The amount, therefore, received by it was not in lieu of compounded profit but surely in lieu of loss of profit-making apparatus.

What is received by way of price or compensation on disposing of circulating capital or stock-in-trade, namely, the trading asset, is ordinarily and generally revenue receipt. What, however, comes in the hands of the assessee on disposal of the capital assets referable to fixed capital is generally a capital receipt. What is capital asset in the hands of one may be a trading asset in the hands of another.

In the instant case the assessee was not parting with the benefits of a trading contract, rather it parted with its profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960; by utilising that apparatus it was earning profit from the agency business, and the whole of it was lost when he decided to retire on the receipt of Rs. 50,000. It was a sum paid to the assessee, truly a compensation for parting with its business, and the agreement entered into deprived the assessee of the benefit of its agreement entered in 1960, with ‘P’ which constituted the framework or whole structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus. For the reasons stated above, the receipt of Rs. 50,000 by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There was no fact to warrant the conclusion that the rent of Rs. 2.50 per sq. ft. as agreed to was less than the market rate. It was only when the premises were let out at a rate lower than the prevailing market rate, that it could be said that the lump sum amount was in the nature of advance rent. According to the Commissioner (Appeals), the onus to prove that the rent charged was less than the market rate was on the ITO. This onus had not been discharged. This finding remained uncontroverted. The company was occupying the premises through the assessee because the assessee was their managing agent. The previous rent paid by the company was very low and nominal. With the cessation of the managing agency agreement, the right of the company to occupy the premises also ceased, and that was why the aforesaid leave and licence agreement was entered into. The Commissioner also came to a definite finding that the rent of Rs. 2.50 per sq. ft. per month in 1977 could not be said to be low compared to the generally prevailing rates at the material time.

In that view of the matter, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the sum of Rs. 2 lakhs received by the assessee was a capital receipt. But the Tribunal did not consider whether the receipt, although capital in nature, was liable to tax as capital gains or not. Even if if was not taxable as a revenue receipt, the question still remained whether the capital receipt by way of salami or premium would be liable to tax as a capital gain in the hands of the assessee or not. The Tribunal would, therefore, deal with and dispose of the contention as to whether the receipt in question was chargeable to tax as a capital gain or not.

( - Matter remanded.)

It is well settled that the taxing authorities are not entitled to ignore the legal character of the transaction which is the source of the receipt. The legal effect of the transaction cannot be displaced by probing into the substance of the transaction.

The word 'income'' defined in section 2(6)(c ) of the 1922 Act includes also the value of any benefit or perquisite, whether convertible into money or not obtained from a company, either by a director or by any other person, who has a substantial interest in the company. Therefore, any benefit received from the transfer of the office of the managing director can be included in the income of any person.

From a perusal of the agreement between the assessee and the purchaser, it was manifest that the consideration received by the assessee was not only towards the value of the shares but also for the transfer of the office of managing director which was previously held by the assessee. Under the income-tax law, any income, whether accruing legally or illegally, can be taxed in the hands of the assessee. Therefore, whether the assessee had power or not to transfer the office of the managing director was not relevant but the fact remained that the assessee had received some consideration for delegating his power to the purchaser of shares. The income-tax authorities had come to the conclusion that the entire amount of capital gains had accrued from the sale of shares by ignoring the legal character of the agreement. This was not correct in law.

For the foregoing reasons, the impugned amount of difference between the face value of the shares and the amount of consideration could not in its entirety be treated and taxed as capital gains of the assessee. The matter was accordingly remanded to the Tribunal for making apportionment of the capital gains arising out of the sale of shares as well as the price for the delegation of the powers of managing director to the purchaser of the shares, and for computation of the taxable capital gains after allowing deductions admissible under the Act.

Sub-section (5A) of section 10 of the 1922 Act came into force on 1-4-1955; therefore, the amount in question, if received by the assessee during the previous year for the assessment year 1955-56 would be taxable under that sub-section. By a legal fiction introduced by sub-section (5A) any amount received by a managing agent as compensation for the termination of his managing agency agreement which would otherwise have been a capital receipt is to be deemed as profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent.

The fiction introduced by sub-section (5A) regards the capital receipt as income and does not extend to treating the termination of managing agency itself as a business. The amount received by the assessee was a payment for the termination of the managing agency business and, as such, the receipt was obviously related to that business. It was of course true that the amount was not earned in carrying on the business of managing agency, but it was clear that the source of the receipt was the managing agency business itself. It could not, therefore, be said that the receipt was income from a new and independent source. The High Court was right in holding that in enacting sub-section (5A) the legislature was concerned only with providing a head under which the receipt which has been deemed to be income could be brought to tax and was not concerned with creating a new source for that deemed income.

The Bombay High Court, in CIT v. Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Private Ltd. [1967] 65 ITR 50 and the Madras High Court in R.V. Lakshmiah Naidu and Co. v. CIT [1963] 48 ITR 661 have both held that the compensation paid for termination of a managing agency business is a payment in relation to said business and, therefore, the previous year relevant to that receipt would be the same as the previous year for the managing agency business itself. These two decisions state the law on the point correctly.

Thus, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

In the case the assessee, taking up managing agency along with secretary ship to the plantation company and other trading rights was part of the assessee's normal trading activities. The assessee dealt with, among other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other rights from the plantation companies certainly facilitated that trade in tea. The managing agencies, the assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event the assessee received the compensation it was entitled to by agreement. The agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for T. It was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to the assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea. The assessee was in a position to obtain such contracts with plantation companies because of its large experience in handling tea for export and also in managing plantations in India. Even confining to the managing agency the loss of one of several such managing agencies could have little effect on the structure of the assessee's business even in tea or on its profit earning apparatus as a whole. They endured virtually unimpaired by the termination of the managing agency for the T even as the business of the assessee remained unimpaired when other managing agencies were terminated in the past. The assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding the termination of such agreements. The termination of the agreement with the T could well be said to have been brought about in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and the money paid to the assessee as a result of or in connection with the termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and that therefore, it was a trading receipt.

Firstly, in the instant case, it was certainly not the assessee's case before the Tribunal that the amount received towards goodwill was his income, nor did it appear to have been the case for taxing authority. The Tribunal apparently on its own motion came to that conclusion on the facts before it.

Following the decision in New India Life Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1957] 31 ITR 844 it could be said that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to do so.

As regards question whether capital gain arose in instant case, one has merely to read the definition of 'capital gain' to realise that transfer in question could not conceivably be a capital gain, because there was no transfer, sale or exchange of a capital asset. All that was done was to give the management of that asset to someone else. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

In this background, it could never be said that the assessee had purchased income by surrendering his capital asset, viz., ‘jagir’ under the said grant. Such resumption had the effect of the capital asset of the assessee, which was an income producing estate, being lost to the assessee and in lieu of such capital loss, the reimbursement was being made by providing for payment of a determined amount only during the life-time of the assessee. This payment was clearly intended to compensate for the loss to the assessee, which was caused by virtue of his capital estate being taken over under the resumption order warranted by the said Ordinance. These annual instalments though described as cash annuity, were, when the substance of the transaction was looked at, not income, but were only intended to be payments towards the loss of the income-producing assets of the assessee and, therefore, they were capital receipts. It could be noted that these periodic payments described as cash annuity were required to be debited by the Government under the head ‘76. Other Misc. Compensation and Assignment - A-2 pension in lieu of Resumed Lands’. Thus, even the Government treated it as compensation, which was being paid to the assessee in lieu of the resumption of lands included in the Jagir granted to the assessee under the said grant. Further, it would be reasonable to assume that since the payments were required to be made under the resumption order, simultaneously on resumption of the grant they were in reality intended to compensate the assessee for the loss of his capital asset, i.e., the ‘jagir’. The true quality of the payment clearly showed that the payment though described as cash annuity was not annuity in the sense of purchase of income, but it was annual payment of compensation to the assessee for the loss of his income-producing asset. These payments were, therefore, clearly capital receipts in the hands of the assessee and could never be termed as income. Such capital receipts would not be taxable except as capital gains and any tax on such capital receipts would amount to taxing the capital, which is not the intention of the income-tax law.

Moreover, where a voluntary payment is made entirely without consideration and is not traceable to any source which a practical man may regard as a real source of income, but depends entirely on the whim of the donor, such payment cannot fall in the category of income. Therefore, even if the amount was paid under the resumption order voluntarily and without any consideration, and was not traceable to any real source of income depending entirely on the pleasure of the Government, such payment would not fall in the category of income.

Therefore, the Tribunal committed an error in holding that the cash annuity in the resumption of two villages was an income and not capital receipt in the hands of the assessee.

It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

The primary significance of the word "compensation" is "equivalence" and the secondary or more common meaning is "something given or obtained as an equivalent". The large number of ways in which this expression "compensation" has been interpreted has one common factor running through them all, that is, that compensation is regarded as an equivalent or recompense, that which makes good the lack of variation of something else. Flowing from this concept, the enlargement of the meaning of this expression takes in that which compensates for loss or privation, amends, remunerates or recompenses. Therefore the contention of the assessee that, unless and until the amount received by the assessee could be regarded as compensation, in the light of a recompense for a right which the managed company wilfully deprived the assessee of, it could not come within the scope of section 10(5A) , could not be accepted. Even apart from this argument raised upon the precise significance of the expression "compensation", the relevant section takes in both compensation or other payments. While it may be true that compensation in the special sense will certainly come within the scope of the provision, any other payment which was received by the managing agent "at or in connection with the termination" of his managing agency agreement is also within the mischief of the section. It is not necessary that the agency agreement should have been terminated by the managed company. If the payment is received at or in connection with the termination, that would be sufficient for the purpose of bringing it to tax under the Act. It could not be denied that it was so received. Therefore, the sum of Rs. 2,24,000 was rightly held taxable.

As to the question whether the receipt could be brought to tax in the assessment for the assessment year 1955-56, from the statement of the case of the Tribunal, it was clear that originally the previous year adopted by the assessee was the period ending on the 15th of March and from 1938-39 assessment till 1940-41, a change was allowed in the accounting year which ended on the 31st of July. Once again in 1941-42, there was a change in the previous year and this time it was the year ending with the 31st of December. It was clear that the previous year of the assessee was the calendar year. The disputed receipt was on 8-1-1955, that is, the calendar year 1955, relevant to the assessment year 1956-57.

The main part of section 10(5A) refers to any compensation or other payment received by a managing agent at or in connection with the termination of the managing agency agreement. If the managing agency was the business carried on by the assessee and its termination resulted in this receipt, it was not clear why this receipt should not be related to that source, viz., the managing agency itself. It was true that it could not be stated to be income, profits or gains of a business carried on, because it was not the carrying on of the business of the managing agency that gave rise to this receipt. But, undoubtedly, the source of this receipt was the managing agency business.

By the fiction embodied in section 10(5A) it is brought to tax as a revenue receipt and in addition is impressed with the character of the profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent, there was no obstacle to holding that this receipt must necessarily be correlated to the source from which it was deprived, which was the managing agency business; and if that was so, the previous year relevant to this receipt could not be a previous year different from the one relevant to the managing agency business itself. The source of this receipt was the managing agency itself, though it arose on the termination of the managing agency agreement, and it is the source that is important for determining the previous year. That during the calendar year 1955 the assessee was carrying on the business of managing agency up to 8-1-1955, was beyond question. During part of the year the managing agency itself was carried on and the profits and gains of that business would be assessable to tax in the assessment year 1956-57; and since this sum of Rs. 2,24,000, was derived from that very source, the same previous year as for the business must be adopted for this receipt as well.

In view of the above, the sum of Rs. 2,24,000 was rightly, includible in the taxable income of the assessee, but that it could not be brought to assessment in the assessment year 1955-56.

Note : The case was decided partly against assessee and partly in his favour.

It was in connection with the business activities of the assessee that the assessee received the sum. That it was a capital receipt in its hand did not make it any the less income from business, and it certainly could not be treated as something of a casual receipt or windfall.

Therefore, the amount in question was assessable to tax as capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act.

The reasoning of the authorities below the Tribunal that the compensation had been quantified on three counts, i.e., the cost of trained manpower, compensation for cost of dealers and compensation for loss of profits and, thus, the payment received by the assessee was only reimbursement of such cost factors, was not correct. The divesting of its management was really divesting the company of its property represented by its opportunity to carry on an activity for profit. The compensation paid was, therefore, for the loss of a capital asset and constitutes a capital receipt.

The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

It was not the case of the Department and it had never been their case that the capital asset in respect of which capital gain was made by the assessee and which was sought to be taxed was the shares and the managing agency. The whole of the reference was based upon the fact that the only capital asset concerned with was the shares and not the managing agency. Therefore, one must separate the managing agency from the shares in considering what was the value to be put upon the shares. The parties had put upon the shares a value which was much higher than the market value. Admittedly, it was an artificial value and it was artificial because the value put upon the shares was not the value of the shares alone but it was the composite consideration paid by the purchasers for obtaining the shares and also acquiring the managing agency. Under the circumstances, for the purposes of section 12B(2) the sale price of the shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. 65 per share.

Note : The case was decided in favour of assessee.

So far as the question of capital gain was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wholly wrong because in a slump transaction no such capital gain could arise because the sale was of a going concern. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals ) was to be reversed. Thus, as Rs. 5 lakhs was a sum received by the assessee in a slump transaction, i.e., as a going concern, no part of this amount was taxable either as revenue receipt or as capital gains.

Section 10 of the 1922 Act, indicates that tax is payable under the head of "business" in respect of the profits or gains of any business carried on by the assessee; and section 12 of the 1922 Act which deals with the residuary heading "other sources" expressed that the tax shall be payable in respect of "income, profits and gains of every kind and from every source to which the Act applies (if not included under any of the preceding heads)". If therefore, a payment comes under clause (vii) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, it is not covered by section 12 at all.

In the instant case, the assessee-company had several – managing agencies. The assessee was given the said sum of money because, without notice the them, in the middle of the year, one of their managing agencies was being brought to a close. In the circumstances, it was thought right to give the assessee this amount by way of compensation for their sudden dismissal. It was impossible to say that the receipt was not a receipt arising from business and that was the statutory test which had to be applied. It was not contended before the Commissioner that the instant case, if it did not come under section 10 of the 1922 Act, would not, apart from this exemption clause, be hit by section 12 of the 1922 Act. There was no doubt that the payment in the instant case was income within the meaning of section 12of the 1922 Act unless it was saved by section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act. In these circumstances, the Commissioner was right in deciding that the exemption relied on was of no use to the assessee and that income-tax was rightly assessed.

The provision of section 28(ii )(a) is meant for termination of managing agency or modification of terms or modes of appointment of employees or persons managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the Indian company. Once the person has already resigned from the managing directorship, the agreement entered into after a month of the event cannot be viewed as modification of the terms of appointment. [Para 6.1]

It is true that an item which is treated as capital in nature in the hands of the payer need not be capital but can be treated as revenue in the hands of the recipient. But in the instant case the very same payment under the same non-competition agreement entered into between the two parties had been treated as non-compete fee in the hands of the payer, but treated as payment received for modification of terms of appointment in the hands of the assessee (recipient). This was a peculiar stand that the very same department had taken while interpreting the very same document between the very same two parties in a different way while dealing with the assessments of the parties. In other words, the revenue could not blow hot and cold on the same situation. [Para 6.2]

The minutes of the meeting of the directors and the terms of the subsequent agreement for non-competition were all to be considered in the light of the above. If done so, it was to be treated as fees received for non-competition only and it could by no stretch of imagination be treated as payment received for modification of the terms and conditions of employment. Moreover, competition need not always be from outside only. On the other hand it could also be from within. The managing director of one company is not generally prohibited from being a director in some other company and render services as director of that other company. In the instant case, the assessee, was contemplating such association and only to restrict him from that this agreement was entered into by the company. So, there was no harm in the assessee continuing in the company without being a managing director. So, for that reason it need not be treated as taxable under section 28(ii)(a ). [Para 6.3]

Clause (va ) of section 28 along with proviso and Explanation was introduced only prospectively and not retrospectively. Hence, upto 1-4-2003 the amounts referred to in the clause (va) received by any assessee were not taxable under section 28(va). Thus, non-compete fee received by him was capital in nature not subject to income-tax. [Para 6.4]

Therefore, the amount received by the assessee was the outcome of the non-competition agreement in view of the restrictive covenant put on him for a period of five years and such amount received by the assessee for restrictive covenant was not to be subjected to income tax. In the result, the assessee’s appeal was to be allowed. [Para 6.5]

From the finding of the Tribunal, the following inferences seemed to be derivable : (1) That the receipt was compensation. (2) The compensation was for loss of anticipated profits. (3) The profits were to accrue by the operation of the Hind Roadways Corporation. (4) The loss was suffered by the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation at the instance of the Government.

On this premises which was clearly implied in the finding of the Tribunal, it appeared to be plain that the compensation was not for loss of profit of any business of the assessee but was to accrue out of a profit-making structure, viz., the corporation, of which the assessee was to be appointed the managing agent. With the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation, the prospect of the assessee becoming the managing agent of the corporation also vanished. Compensation was paid to him in lieu of the benefit which he might have derived by becoming the managing agent of the corporation. The corporation or the profit-making structure or the managing agency were only an asset of a capital nature. Compensation paid for the loss of a capital asset is not and cannot be taxable income. It followed that on the finding recorded by the Tribunal, the conclusion in law which it arrived at, namely, that "the amount was clearly taxable" was entirely erroneous.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.
