2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows : “An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

2.2-11 Transferor can claim exemption from capital gains -The tax treatment of the transferor is not at all relevant in the grant of depreciation to the transferee in respect of cost of intangible asset. Thus, the transferee will be eligible to claim depreciation even if the transferor is not subject to tax on account of, say,

◆ applicability of section 47(xii)/(xiii)/(xiv) of the Act, exempting the transferor from capital gains tax.

◆ the transferor claiming exemption by applying the ‘No cost’ principle as laid down in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294 (SC) and in Voltas Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [1998] 64 ITD 232 (Mum.) (in respect of trademark).

◆ applicability of double taxation avoidance agreement.

2.2-12 Sale and lease back - It may be noted that if an intangible asset is sold and then taken for use from the transferee, Explanation 4A to section 43(1) may apply if the transferor has already obtained depreciation on the asset. Under this Explanation, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on the written down value of the transferor at time of transfer of the intangible asset, although he may have acquired the intangible asset for a higher sum. To illustrate, if the written down value of an intangible asset is Rs. 20 lakhs in the hands of the transferor and if he sells the asset for Rs. 50 lakhs, the transferee will continue to get depreciation on Rs. 20 lakhs by virtue of the provisions of Explanation 4A.

It may be noted that the aforesaid Explanation does not apply if the transferor has not claimed any depreciation on the intangible asset. In such an event, the actual cost for the transferee shall not be restricted to the written down value of the transferor and he will get depreciation on his cost of acquisition.

RIGHTS UNDER A CONTRACT

In CIT v. Anglo India Jute Mills Co. Ltd. [1981] 6 Taxman 54/129 ITR 352 (Cal.) the assessee wanted to purchase certain machinery from abroad. For this purpose, the assessee did all that was necessary for obtaining the permission and getting the import licence. In order to protect itself from fluctuations in the exchange rate, the assessee entered into a forward contract with a bank entitling it to obtain the requisite amount of sterling at the time when the contract came to an end or was required to be performed. The assessee could not get this machinery because the licence expired and, therefore the question of enforcing payment in dollars did not arise. Therefore, the State Bank, pursuant to their commitment, credited the assessee minus the necessary costs, charges and expenses, with the difference between the exchange rate and the assessee got a credit of Rs. 3,13,651. The Court held that the amount was obtained not because the assessee surrendered any licence and not because the assessee gave up its own right under a contract but because the assessee realised its dues or, in other words, the assessee transformed its rights under the contract into money. Therefore, neither was there any transfer nor was there any profit arising therefrom. In that background of facts there was no cost of acquisition and, therefore, there could not be any capital gains in respect of such an asset. Accordingly, the sum of Rs. 3,13,651 could not be considered to be capital gains in terms of section 45. However, it appears that the chargeability to tax under the head 'business' could not be disputed.

Non-applicability - The definition of income given in section 2(24)(vi) cannot be applied in the context of section 115E as its application would render a part of the statute otiose [CIT v. Sham L. Chellaram [2015] 54 taxmann.com 348 (Bom.)].

WINNINGS FROM LOTTERIES, ETC. [SECTION 2(24)(ix)]

Lotteries - Winnings of an Indian resident from lotteries conducted outside India (i.e., in a foreign country) is also an 'income' [CIT v. Chaman Lal [1986] 26 Taxman 634 (P&H)].

MISCELLANEOUS

Agricultural income - Where land owned by assessee was not sufficient to generate agricultural income shown by assessee, such income was rightly assessed as income from other sources [P. P. Bhaskaran v. CIT [2017] 88 taxmann.com 456 (Ker.)].

Compensation – Where assessee, promoter of a housing society, had received compensation, in addition to refund of entire booking amount along with interest, from developer on failing to honour commitment of development and construction of flats as per agreement, said amount of compensation received by assessee was not a capital receipt and same was to be assessed as "Income from other sources" [Manoj B. Joshi v. 8th ITO [2009] 179 Taxman 30 (Bom.), affirmed inManoj B. Joshi v. 8th ITO [2022] 144 taxmann.com 14/289 Taxman 623 (SC)].

Where Government of Goa had allotted plot to assessee on leasehold basis and the allotment was cancelled by state law passed due to change of policy and assessee was refunded the lease premium and was paid an amount over and above the lease premium refunded calculated as simple interest @ 10% per annum on the lease premium and from a reading of the state law it was clear that it was compensation for cancellation of lease, the compensation was a capital receipt and not revenue receipt even though it was calculated by way of simple interest on lease premium and could not be taxed as interest under the head income from other sources [PCIT v. Pawa Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2022] 145 taxmann.com 518 (Delhi)].

Gratuity by non-employee - Gratuity received by a director who, under the relevant contract, is not an employee or servant of the company, is assessable as income from other sources [CIT v. Lady Navajbai R. J. Tata [1947] 15 ITR 8 (Bom.)].

Hoardings - Income derived by the assessee on account of display of hoardings of various concerns on top of the assessee's building for advertisement purposes is not assessable as income from house property, since hoardings cannot be treated as part of the building. The said income is assessable as income from other sources only [Mukherjee Estate (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 113 Taxman 313 (Cal.)].

Letting out of business as a whole - The letting out of business as a whole is distinct from letting out commercial assets of the business. If business is as a whole let out, the rental income is assessable as income from other sources and not as income from business [CIT v. Kuya & Khas Kuya Colliery Co. [1985] 23 Taxman 229 (Pat.)].

The Bombay High Court in the case of Prashant S. Joshi v. ITO [2010] 189 Taxman 1/324 ITR 154 (Bom.) relying upon the observations of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CIT v. Mohanbhai Pamabhai [1973] 91 ITR 393 (Guj.) has held that an amount paid to a partner upon retirement, after taking accounts and upon deduction of liabilities, does not involve an element of transfer within the meaning of section 2(47) of the Act and, therefore, there is no transfer of capital asset by way of a distribution of the capital assets, on the dissolution of a firm or otherwise. The appeal against the judgment of the Gujarat High Court in the case of Mohanbhai Pamabhai (supra) was dismissed by a Bench of three learned judges of the Supreme Court in Addl. CIT v. Mohanbhai Pamabhai [1987] 165 ITR 166 (SC) relying upon its judgment in Sunil Siddharthbhai v.CIT [1985] 23 Taxman 14W/156 ITR 509 (SC). The Supreme Court in Sunil Siddharthbhai (supra) reiterated the same principle by relying upon the judgment in Addanki Narayanappa v. Bhaskara Krishtappa AIR 1966 SC 1300 wherein it was held that "what is envisaged on the retirement of a partner is merely his right to realise his interest and to receive its value. What is realised is the interest which the partner enjoys in the assets during the subsistence of the partnership by virtue of his status as a partner and in terms of the partnership agreement. Consequently, what the partner gets upon dissolution or upon retirement is the realisation of a pre-existing right or interest." The Supreme Court in Sunil Siddharthbhai (supra) also held that there was nothing strange in the law that a right or interest should exist in praesenti but its realisation or exercise should be postponed. The Supreme Court, inter alia, in this case cited with approval the judgment of the Gujarat High Court in Mohanbhai Pamabhai (supra) and held that there was no transfer upon the retirement of a partner upon the distribution of his share in the net assets of the firm.

The conclusions arrived at para 15 of the judgment by the Bombay High Court in Prashant S. Joshi (supra) are worth noticing-

"Ex facie sub-section (4) of section 45 deals with a situation where there is a transfer of a capital asset by way of a distribution of capital assets on the dissolution of a firm or otherwise. Evidently, on the admitted position before the court, there is no transfer of a capital asset by way of a distribution of the capital assets, on a dissolution of the firm or otherwise in the facts of this case."

This decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of Prashant S. Joshi (supra) was followed by a subsequent Bench in the case of CIT v. Riyaz A. Sheikh [2014] 41 taxmann.com 455/221 Taxman 118 (Mag.) (Bom.) wherein through a brief judgment it has been held that amounts received on retirement by a partner are exempt from tax. It was noted in this decision that "the earlier decision of this court in the case of Prashant S. Joshi (supra) placed reliance upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. R. Lingmallu Raghukumar [2002] 124 Taxman 127/[2001] 247 ITR 801 (SC), wherein it has been held that amounts received on retirement by a partner are not subject to capital gains tax."

The Chennai Bench of the ITAT in the case of Asstt. CIT v. P. Sivakumar (HUF)[2014] 43 taxmann.com 211/63 SOT 91 (URO) (Chennai - Trib.) following the decision of the Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court in the case of Dynamic Enterprises (supra) has held that additional amounts paid to retiring partners in excess of the capital account are not in nature of any profit or income; and, therefore, not taxable. The Tribunal in this case held that additional amounts paid to retiring partners represented share of retiring partners in worth and value of business in which they were partners and, therefore, such additional payments made to retiring partners were not in nature of any profit or income within meaning of section 28(va) of the Act, being non-taxable capital receipts.

GENERAL

Transfer of part asset - The words 'the transfer of a capital asset' occurring in section 45 cannot be interpreted as a transfer of the entire capital asset and not a part of the same [National Products v. CIT [1986] 26 Taxman 755 (Kar.)].

Capital asset on the date of transfer - It is necessary that property transferred must be a capital asset on date of transfer and not that such property should have been capital asset also on date of its acquisition by the assessee [Arun Sunny v. DCIT [2009] 184 Taxman 498 (Ker.)]. Also see, A. R. Dahiya v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 141 Taxman 449 (P&H).

CAPITAL GAINS OR NOT

Gift for tax avoidance - Where assessee transferred its shareholding, as a gift, in a company to step-down company created in a tax haven country and the said step-down company transferred stake in favour of a third-party investor for a consideration, sole intention of assessee being escape rigour of Indian tax laws, therefore, assessee was liable to tax u/s 45 [PCIT v. Redington (India) Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 136 (Mad.)].

Inherited property - Where assessee inherited certain land, leased out same on payment of ground rent and ultimately sold it after decades, profit arising from sale of land was to be taxed as 'capital gains' [CIT v. Administrator of the Estate of Shri E. F. Dinshaw [2012] 22 taxmann.com 57/208 Taxman 193 (Mag.) (Bom.)].

Intangible assets - Sale of brand names, trademark, copyright and goodwill in journals sold/transferred would clearly be a case of sale of capital asset and exigible to capital gains [CIT v. Mediworld Publications (P.) Ltd. [2011] 11 taxmann.com 374/200 Taxman 1 (Delhi); CIT v. ABB Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 338/[2022] 284 Taxman 350 (Kar.)].

Where collection of assets of undertaking transferred in slump sale included intangible assets like goodwill and intellectual property whose cost of acquisition could not be determined, said sale could not be assessable to capital gains [CIT v. AKZO Noble India Ltd. [2020] 121 taxmann.com 216/[2021] 276 Taxman 259 (Cal.)].

Malba - Proceeds of malba, i.e., material left over after demolition of a structure, would be taxable under the head 'Capital gains' and not under the head 'Income from other sources' [CIT v. Ribu Saggi [2014] 45 taxmann.com 371/223 Taxman 150 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Owelty - Amount of owelty (i.e., compensation deposited to settle inequalities in partition) represents immovable property and would not attract capital gain tax [CIT v. Ashwani Chopra [2013] 30 taxmann.com 299/213 Taxman 490 (P&H)].

Pledge of shares - No capital gains arise where there was no transfer of shares but shares have been pledged for the purposes of obtaining loan [CIT v. Reliance Communication Infrastructure Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 302/[2013] 212 Taxman 177 (Bom.)].

Sale of business as a going concern - Where business is sold as a going concern valuing plant and machinery, etc., surplus arising over and above the difference between WDV and actual cost has to be taxed u/s 45 [CIT v. Artex Mfg. Co. [1997] 93 Taxman 357 (SC)].

Shares - Where assessee-company purchased shares of a private limited company from funds received from its holding company and after some time it had sold said shares to its holding company, profit arising from sale of shares had to be taxed under head 'Capital gains' [CIT v. Renato Finance & Investment Ltd. [2013] 33 taxmann.com 262/218 Taxman 312 (Bom.)].

Where assessee-director received huge amount as non-compete fee but real and true nature of transaction was sale of shares and transfer of control and management of company, amount in question was to be taxed as capital gains in hands of assessee [CIT v. Shiv Raj Gupta [2014] 52 taxmann.com 425 (Del.), SLP granted inShiv Raj Gupta v. CIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 3/244 Taxman 191 (SC)].

.

(3) Gratuitous payment of annuity received by widow of ex-employee is not 'income' since the same is not contractual but only discretionary [CIT v. Rajalakshmi Venkatakrishnan [1996] 86 Taxman 8 (Mad.)].

(4) Amount of rubber replanting subsidy received from Rubber Board [CIT v. M. Shajahan [1996] 221 ITR 594 (Ker.)]. (5) Interest awarded on compensation in motor accident claim cases from date of claim petition till passing of award (or in case of appeal, till the judgment of the High Court in such appeal), is not 'income' [Rupesh Rashmikant Shah v. UOI [2019] 108 taxmann.com 181/266 Taxman 474 (Bom.); Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. CCIT [2022] 138 taxmann.com 88/287 Taxman 522 (Guj.), SLP granted in Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Chief CIT (TDS) [2023] 154 taxmann.com 465 (SC)].

(6) Carbon credit not an offshoot of business but an offshoot of environmental concern. Thus, any receipt from sale of carbon credit is capital receipt, and not business income [CIT v. My Home Power Ltd. [2014] 46 taxmann.com 314 (AP); CIT v. Subhash Kabini Power Corporation Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 394 (Kar.)].

do not constitute 'transfer'

The transfer of the property to an existing partner by mere adjustment of book entries otherwise than in connection with dissolution of the partnership or retirement of the partner from the partnership not accompanied by a duly registered deed of conveyance, does not constitute a transfer- CIT v. Kedarnath Poddar & Co. [1993] 201 ITR 639 (Cal.).

4.20-6 Mutual relinquishment of rights by partners amounts to sale by firm to partners Where, through an instrument executed by the two partners of the assessee-firm, one of them released and relinquished in favour of the other, for specified consideration adjusted in the firm's books, his rights and interest in a building and some land owned by the firm, it was held to be a case of sale by the firm in favour of a partner resulting in transfer of capital assets and thus attracting the provisions of section 45 - CIT v. Bharani Pictures [1980] 3 Taxman 478/[1981] 129 ITR 244 (Mad.).

4.20-7 Payment to retiring partners does not involve 'transfer'

Where on the retirement of a partner from a firm, he was paid his share in the partnership which was worked out by taking the proportionate value of his share in the net partnership assets after deduction of liabilities and prior charges, and including therein the proportionate share in the value of goodwill, it was held that no part of the amount received was assessable as capital gains - Addl. CIT v. Mohanbhai Pamabhai [1987] 165 ITR 166 (SC)/CIT v. Bhupinder Singh Atwal [1981] 5 Taxman 292/128 ITR 67 (Cal.)/CIT v. P.H. Patel [1988] 171 ITR 128 (AP)/CIT v. Legal Representatives of N. Paliniappa Gonndar (Decd.) [1983] 12 Taxman 295/143 ITR 343 (Mad.)/CIT v. Madan Lal Bhargava [1980] 3 Taxman 324/122 ITR 545 (All.)/CIT v. P.N. Sreenivasa Rao [1988] 39 Taxman 234/171 ITR 562 (Ker.)/Addl. CIT v. Smt. Mahinderpal Bhasin [1979] 117 ITR 26 (All.).

But the law has undergone a change after sub-section (4) of section 45 has been substituted by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from assessment year 2021-22 and this issue has been discussed in detail earlier.

4.20-8 Firm or LLP treated as company under provisions of Part IX of Companies Act [now Chapter XXI of the Companies Act, 2013]

In the case of a partnership firm or LLP being treated as company under the statutory provisions of Chapter XXI of the Companies Act, the company succeeds the firm. Generally, in the case of a transfer of a capital asset, two important ingredients are: existence of a party and a counter-party and, secondly, incoming consideration qua the transferor. When a firm or LLP is treated as a company, the said two conditions are not attracted. It is a statutory vesting of properties in the company as the firm is treated as a limited company. On vesting of all the properties statutorily in the company, the cloak given to the firm is replaced by a different cloak and the same firm is now treated as a company after a given date. In the circumstances, there is no transfer of a capital asset as contemplated by section 45(1) - CIT v. Texspin Engg. & Mfg. Works [2003] 129 Taxman 1 (Bom.).

In Commissioner of Income-tax v. Chetak Enterprises (P.) Ltd. [2020] 115 taxmann.com 108/272 Taxman 509 (SC), the Supreme Court explained the effects of Part IX [now Chapter XXI of Companies Act, 2013] conversion of firm into a company as follows:

"7. The question is: what is the effect of conversion of partnership firm into a company under Part IX of the Companies Act? That can be discerned from Section 575 of the Companies Act, which reads thus: —

"575. Vesting of property on registration. - All property, movable and immovable (including actionable claims), belonging to or vested in a company at the date of its registration in pursuance of this Part, shall, on such registration, pass to and vest in the company as incorporated under this Act for all the estate and interest of the company therein."

It is manifest that all properties, movable and immovable (including actionable claims) belonging to or vested in a company at the date of its registration would vest in the company as incorporated under the Act. In other words, the property acquired by a promoter can be claimed by the company after its incorporation without any need for conveyance on account of statutory vesting. On such statutory vesting, all the properties of the firm, in law, vest in the company and the firm is succeeded by the company. The firm ceases to exist and assumes the status of a company after its registration as a company…."

See also Para 5.21-1

India Ltd. [2023] 149 taxmann.com 247/292 Taxman 465 (SC)].

Incomplete transactions - Where assessee received certain amount as fee for implementation of a project which was, in fact, not carried out by such assessee held to be benefit received [Samurai Techno Trading Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 260/[2011] 197 Taxman 144 (Ker.)]. Where assessee received certain advance on assigning development rights of a land but if transaction did not complete for some reason, no income would arise u/s 28(iv) particularly when relevant MOU was not yet cancelled [CIT v. Arvind Securities (P.) Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 166/[2015] 228 Taxman 301 (Mag.) (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. Ashish P. Deora [2016] 73 taxmann.com 259/242 Taxman 214 (Bom.), SLP dismissed inCIT v. Ashish P. Deora [2016] 73 taxmann.com 260/242 Taxman 172 (SC).

Remission or cessation of liability not taxable u/s 28(iv) - Remission of unsecured loans could not be subjected to tax by invoking provisions of section 28(iv) where assessee was not carrying on business of obtaining loans [CIT v. Chetan Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2004] 139 Taxman 301 (Guj.)].

Benefit which one obtains by way of remission or cessation of a trading liability in a later year, in respect of which he has obtained a deduction in an earlier year in computing business income, has to be governed by section 41(1) and not by section 28(iv) [CIT v. Shri Vardhman Overseas Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 350/[2012] 204 Taxman 524 (Delhi)].

Waiver of loan cannot be brought to tax u/s 28(iv) [Essar Shipping Ltd. v. CIT [2020] 117 taxmann.com 389/273 Taxman 49 (Bom.)]. Also see, I. G. Petrochemicals Ltd. v. ITAT [2023] 155 taxmann.com 45/295 Taxman 569 (Kar.).

Excess consideration paid in amalgamation - Where assessee-company amalgamated with three companies, net book value of entities taken over by assessee over and above consideration paid for acquiring such three companies would not fall within ambit of provisions of section 28(iv) [CIT v. Areva T & D India Ltd. [2021] 129 taxmann.com 55 (Mad.)].

Amalgamation reserve - Amalgamation reserve, being the difference in value of share capital of amalgamated companies prior and post amalgamation, coming into existence consequent to the merger could not be regarded as profit and gains from business profession u/s 28(iv) [CIT v. STADS Ltd. [2015] 61 taxmann.com 33 (Mad.)].

EMOLUMENTS TO PARTNER OF A FIRM FROM SUCH FIRM [SECTION 28(v)]

Retirement benefits - Payment made to partner in realization of his share in net value of assets upon his retirement from a firm do not fall u/s 28(v) [Prashant S. Joshi v. ITO [2010] 189 Taxman 1 (Bom.)].

NON-COMPETE FEES [SECTION 28(va)]

Section is amendatory and not clarificatory - Compensation received under non-competition agreement became taxable as a capital receipt and not as a revenue receipt by specific legislative mandate vide section 28(va) and that too w.e.f. 1-4-2003. Hence, the section is amendatory and not clarificatory [CIT v. Bisleri Sales Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 364 (Bom.)].

Illustrations - (1) Transfer of shares with all pervasive control over business being entrusted to purchaser and to complete exclusion of assessee with a non-compete clause fell within the realm of section 28(va) [Sumeet Taneja v. CIT [2013] 38 taxmann.com 149 (P&H)].

(2) Where C Ltd., pursuant to sale of one division to its director, received certain amount by entering into a non-compete agreement whereby it could not engage in any business activity similar to that of division sold to such director, amount so received was taxable as business income u/s 28(va) [Arun Toshniwal v. DCIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 274 (Bom.)].

terms of the agreement he can be removed for not discharging the work diligently or if he is found not to be acting in the interest of the Company as Managing Director, then it can hardly be said that he is an agent of the Company and not a servant' (In this case, it was held that payment made to MD is 'salary') - quoted and followed in Sajid Mowjee v. ITO (2005) 148 Taxman 502 (Cal HC DB). In ESIC v. Apex Engineering Ltd. 1997 LLR 1097 = (1998) 1 Comp LJ 10 = 1998(1) SCC 86, it was held that a MD can be employee and liable to pay ESIC dues if his salary is within the ESIC limits. He is not owner of the factory. Company is the 'Principal Employer' for purpose of ESIC. MD cannot be termed as 'Principal Employer'. Even if he is declared as 'Principal Employer' for ESIC purposes, he still can be an employee - followed in ESIC v. Haryana Biological 2010 LLR 38 (P&H HC).

In ESIC v. Sarathi Lines (1996) 26 CLA 67 (Ker HC DB), it was held that a Managing Director can be employee for purpose of ESIC, if he actually functions as an employee, if there is contract of employment.

If a managing director is drawing salary, he is 'employee' and has to be covered under PF provisions. - Tin Printers v. RPFC 2000 LLR 1175 (Cal HC).

If Managing Director of a company is looking after work of the establishment, he will be 'employee', if his wages are lower than the prescribed limit for applicability of ESI Act - ESIC v. Apex Engineering Ltd. 1997 LLR 1097 = (1998) 1 Comp LJ 10 = 1998(1) SCC 86 * ESIC v. Sarathi Lines (1996) 26 CLA 67 (Ker HC DB) * ESIC v. Haryana Biological 2010 LLR 38 (P&H HC) * ESIC v. Padma Bhawan Engineers 2011 LLR 433 (P&H HC).

However, if he does not draw any remuneration over and above as a director on Board, he will not be 'employee' - ESIC v. Navchetan Press P Ltd. 2004 LLR 1047 (Del HC).

As per section 2(94) of the Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding Explanation to section 269 of the 1956 Act], 'wholetime director' includes a director in wholetime employment of the company. Thus, if a wholetime employee is appointed as director of the company, he will be 'wholetime director'.

Executive Director - Executive Director means a wholetime director as defined in section 2(94) of the 2013 Act - Rule 2(1)(k) of Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014.

4.5-1 Services provided on contract basis

Services provided on contract basis i.e. principal-to-principal basis are not services provided in the course of employment - Para 2.9.2 of CBE&C's Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

4.5-2 Commission to salesmen

This is not 'service' since employer is not his 'client'. 'Commission' is only a way of calculating his remuneration. Usually, it is sort of a 'incentive bonus' over and above the salary.

CBE&C, vide letter No. 324/Comm(ST)/2008 dated 1-12-2008 [20 STT 20 (St)], has clarified that so long as activities performed are duties within the framework of terms of employment, amount paid by employer to employee, even if termed as commission, would not be treated as commission under definition of Business Auxiliary Service and service tax would not be leviable.

This view has been reiterated and confirmed vide CBE&C circular No. 115/09/2009-ST dated 31-7-2009.

4.5-3 Amount payable on premature termination of employee not taxable

Amounts received by an employee from the employer on premature termination of contract of employment will not be chargeable to service tax. Such amounts paid by the employer to the employee for premature termination of a contract of employment are treatable as amounts paid in relation to services provided by the employee to the employer in the course of employment. Hence, amounts so paid would not be chargeable to service tax. However any amount paid for not joining a competing business would be liable to be taxed being paid for providing the service of forbearance to act - Para 2.9.3 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Further, if employee is required to pay some amount to employer for not giving required notice before leaving job (notice pay), the employer will be liable to pay service tax on that amount, as it will fall within the meaning of 'tolerating an act or situation', which is a 'declared service'.

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee - company was managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies and also held majority of their conversion shares - 'D' company made an offer to assessee to purchase conversions share of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency - Assessee accepted said offer - Subsequently, agreement was modified and as per new agreement, assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in favour of 'D' company, resigned from it - Revenue authorities brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act amount of compensation received by assessee-company on account of resigning managing agency agreement - Whether since transaction in its true legal character was relinquishment of managing agency and was neither a sale nor transfer thereof, High Court rightly held that assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court : HELD: The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee held certain shares of company ‘G’ and was also managing agent of said company - During relevant accounting year, one ‘T’ made offer to assessee to purchase of aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ held by assessee also managing agency rights of assessee - Assessee accepted aforesaid offer and thereafter wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting his resignation from office of managing agents and further recommended ‘T’ to be appointed as managing agents in his place - Company ‘G’ accepted said letter - Whether resignation by assessee of managing agency and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, was nothing but mode of performance of agreement to sell managing agency arrived at between assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were attracted - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee was managing agent of company F - It entered into agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company - 'M' also agreed to compensate assessee for loss of office - Subsequently, assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of company - Accordingly, assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation received by assessee to relinquish managing agency could not be regarded as revenue receipt and, thus, it was not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a managing agent of a company F. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company and to procure that principal company 'M' also agreed to compensate the assessee for loss of office after it submitted its resignation.

Subsequently, the assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of the company. Accordingly, the assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office. In the proceedings for the relevant assessment year the ITO, included this amount in the assessee's taxable income. On appeal the AAC modified the assessment holding that the sum received by the assessee as compensation for surrendering the managing agency, which was to enure for five years more, and which in normal course might have continued for another term of twenty years, was a capital receipt. On further appeals Tribunal confirmed the order of the AAC. On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee, who was one of partners of managing agency firm and was director of managed company, received his share of compensation from managed company in terms of arbitration award for premature termination of managing agency agreement - Assessee claimed amount so received to be capital receipt and hence not liable to tax - Whether amount in question was capital receipt and not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes

AS-WHETHER ON FACTS GIVEN UNDER HEADING ‘COMPENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF MANAGING AGENCY’ SALE CONSIDERATION RECEIVED BY ASSESSEE- COMPANY FROM FIRM WAS LIABLE FOR CAPITAL GAINS TAX-HELD, NO

FACT: The assessee-company entered into an agreement with a firm. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to manufacture ‘bidies’ as per the specifications, such as shape, size, quality and standard, of the firm. The assessee was also free to manufacture bidies for any person, firm or company. It was also provided that the assessee should purchase its own raw materials at its own discretion but, however, the wrapping paper and printed label bearing firm’s trade-mark were to be supplied by the firm. The price was to be fixed mutually from time to time but in no case it was to exceed the manufacturing cost plus 10 per cent profit thereon. Thereafter, another agreement was entered into between the assessee and the firm by which both the parties agreed to terminate mutually the earlier agreement. Under this agreement the assessee agreed to sell and the firm agreed to purchase running business of the assessee. As a consideration for the purchase of the bidi manufacturing business the firm was to pay to the assessee as ‘slump price’ of Rs. 5 lakhs. The IAC held that the assessee was holding an agency and the aforesaid amount received by the assessee was an amount towards termination of this agency, and, therefore, it was taxable under section 28(ii)( c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held it as capital gain and directed the IAC to work out the taxable capital gains in accordance with the relevant provisions.

On appeal:

HELD: The agreement entered into between the parties clearly was one of the type which was entered into on principal to principal basis. The agreement showed that both the parties tried to protect their commercial interests by incorporating into an agreement provisions for this purpose. In this agreement, there was no provision whatsoever, which could be interpreted as the assessee acting as an agency of the firm for the purpose of manufacturing of bidies. The system of accounting arrived at in which the assessee could get the maximum profit of 10 per cent was for the mutual protection of the business interests of the parties. The IAC was, therefore, wrong in holding it as an agency.

So far as the question of capital gain was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) was wholly wrong because in a slump transaction no such capital gain could arise because the sale was of a going concern. Accordingly, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals ) was to be reversed. Thus, as Rs. 5 lakhs was a sum received by the assessee in a slump transaction, i.e., as a going concern, no part of this amount was taxable either as revenue receipt or as capital gains.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the income-tax Act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessee, holder of two-third shares of a company and also managing agent of said company, sold its entire shareholding in one block to a third company gaining some profit and  surrendering said managing agency-No finding on record that assessee was a dealer in managing agency and transaction was a colourable one-Whether surplus realised out of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains-Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee-company had held two-third shares of company A and was also its managing agent. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold all these shares to company B at a profit of Rs. 3,14,519 and claimed that the surplus realised was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains. The ITO took the view that the assessee had acquired these shares to procure the managing agency and it had, in fact, carried on multifarious activities in various lines including banking, financing of various companies as well as managing agency. He, accordingly, held that the entire profit from the sale of these shares represented business profit. On appeal, the AAC held that a major portion of the sale proceeds was relatable to the assessee's right to the managing agency which passed along with the shares. He further held that in view of the numerous agencies which the assessee carried on, this transaction involving the giving up of the managing agency was of a revenue nature. Consequently, the AAC upheld the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the assessee had parted with an asset of enduring nature and observed that nothing had been received by the assessee as price for its foregoing managing agency rights. What it had legally received was the value of the shares though it could not be denied that it received a higher value because the shares carried with it the managing agency rights. Further, the Tribunal was of the view that it was concerned with the true and legal realisation resulting from the transaction which appeared to be that of the sale of shares and that the shares were not the assessee's stock-in- trade It, accordingly, held that the impugned profit was liable to be taxed as capital gains and not as revenue gains.

On reference:

HELD: Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Even if it was assumed that the impugued payment was for surrendering of the managing agency, unless there was a finding that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency, this aspect would not support the revenue's stand.

Accordingly, the surplus arising out of the transaction of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains.

The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction. It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

The subject-matter of appeal would get confined to the limits of the grounds specifically raised in the memorandum of appeal, the new grounds raised by the appellant with the previous permission of the Tribunal and the grounds urged by the respondent in support of the decree passed in his favour, even though the decision of the Court, against which the appeal is filed, is against him. It is thus clear that the Tribunal will have no jurisdiction to found its decision on grounds which have not been raised before it by any of the parties at all. In other words, it would not be open to the Tribunal to make out a new case for either the appellant or the respondent. The finding of the AAC was that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital loss and the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. Deducting the capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares, the total figure of the capital gain was arrived at, and from the total gain, the capital gain falling to the share of the assessee was computed at. In this context, it would not be reasonable to assume that by raising this ground the appellant was challenging the finding which was already in his favour, but it would be reasonable to hold that he was challenging the finding which was only against him, and that finding was that the value of the managing agency as on 1-1-1939, was nil. In dealing with this ground, the Tribunal itself observed that the said contention of the assessee related to the capital gains computed by the department.

It was thus clear that this was the only contention of the assessee, and this was the only ground of attack as regards the computation of the capital gains made by the AAC. It was indeed true that the Tribunal had gone into the question of determining the capital gains on the transaction of sale of shares. But nowhere from the order it appeared that the departmental representative had raised any contention before the Tribunal or tried to support the order of the AAC on the ground that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gain. From the order of the AAC also, it did not appear that at any time it was the case of the ITO that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gains. These being the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was neither competent nor justified in interfering with the finding of the AAC as regards the transaction of sale and holding that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gains. The assessee's contention that the managing agency had value as on 1-1-1939, had been accepted by the Tribunal, and in view of this finding of the Tribunal, and in the light of the observations herein made, the amount of capital gains would have to be computed afresh.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued. A managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at the rate of 20 per cent of the profits was not the same thing as a managing agency yielding a remuneration calculated at 10 per cent of the profits. There was a distinct deterioration in the character and quality of the managing agency viewed as a profit-making apparatus and this deterioration was of an enduring kind. The reduced remuneration having been separately provided, the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 must be regarded as having been paid as compensation for that injury to or deterioration of the managing agency.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid and received not to make up the difference between the higher remuneration and the reduced remuneration but was in reality paid and received as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous terms as to remuneration as it was in terms expressed to be. In other words, so far as the managed company was concerned, it was paid for securing immunity from the liability to pay higher remuneration to the assessee firm for the rest of the term of the managing agency and, therefore, a capital expenditure and so far as the assessee firm was concerned, it was received as compensation for the deterioration or injury to the managing agency by reason of the release of its rights to get higher remuneration and, therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax.

FACT: ‘ITF’ was managing agent of a company. Under an agreement ‘ITF’ transferred the managing agency of company to the assessee firm. The assessee firm took over the management of the company in pursuance of the general power of attorney executed by the ‘ITF’ in its favour. Thereafter due to some disputes, the ‘ITF’ asked the assessee firm to resign from the office of managing agency. The matter was ultimately referred to arbitrators who awarded compensation to the assessee for loss of the managing agency commission. The ITO held that the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was compensation for the loss of commission which the assessee-firm would have otherwise earned, but for the breach of the terms of the agreement and brought to tax the amount of the compensation for the assessment year 1963-64 on the basis that it was a revenue receipt. The appeals of the assessee were dismissed by the AAC and the Tribunal. On the question of the assessee-firm's accounting being of mercantile system and, therefore, it should be held that the amount received by the assessee-firm should be attributable to respective years on accrual basis, the Tribunal held that the amount received could not be apportioned in the manner in which the assessee-firm sought.

On reference :

HELD: There is difference between compensation or damages paid or received for non-performance of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business and compensation or damages paid for discontinuance of the business itself. The former only is treated as income, but not so with regard to the latter. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the firm itself was formed solely for the purpose of managing the company by entering into the agreement in question with the I.T.F. and there was no other business for it. If that was so, when on account of the loss of the managing agency the assessee-firm lost its business itself, the compensation received by it for that loss would be capital in nature. It is also generally held by the courts that lump sum amounts received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreements are capital in nature.

In the possible case, it was not possible to say that the agreement entered into between the assessee-firm and the I.T.F. under which the assessee-firm acquired the managing agency of the company was a contract, entered into in the ordinary course of business or a trading contract. It followed from the above discussion that the amount of compensation awarded to the assessee-firm was capital receipt and not a revenue receipt liable to tax. Though the amount awarded to the assessee-firm was capital in nature, none the less it was to be treated as "profits and gains of business" as provided under section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act and section 28(ii ) of the 1961 Act.

On reference : HELD: As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.
