HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1956-57 - Assessee was one of two managing directors of private limited company namely 'T' Ltd. - He held nine shares and his son one share in 'T' Ltd whereas remaining ten shares were held by 'P', his wife and cousin - 'T' Ltd. was managing agent of public limited company i.e., 'A' Ltd. - Assessee held 1674 shares in said public limited company - Subsequently, assessee sold his shares in 'T' Ltd. as well as in 'A' Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin - Whether profits earned on sale of aforesaid shares were assessable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, no

FACT: The assessee was one of the two managing directors of a private limited company T. Ltd. The other managing director was one 'P'. Out of the total of 20 shares of Rs. 100 each, the assessee held nine shares and his son one share, the remaining shares being held by 'P', his wife and cousin. This company was the managing agent of a public limited company A Ltd. Both these companies had been incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The public limited company had issued 11,986 shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each, out of which the assessee held, 1,674 shares. The assessee and his son transferred ten shares in T. Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin or their nominees for Rs. 3,50,000 as also 4,165 shares in the A Ltd.

By the transfer two sets of shares the assessee made a profit of Rs. 3,14,100 in respect of nine shares and another sum of Rs. 72,515 in respect of 1,674 shares. These two amounts were brought to tax for the assessment year 1956-57 treating them as income and liable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act. Both the ITO as well as the AAC repelled the assessee's contention that the receipts were in the nature of capital assets by sale of the shares. The AAC accepted the view that the amounts in excess of the book value of the shares transferred by the assesses were in the nature of inducement to him or compensation for giving up the management.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was neither a manager nor a managing agent of an Indian company within the meaning of section 2(9A) of the Indian Companies Act and that the provisions of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act were, therefore, not applicable to the two amounts.

The Tribunal also considered the further question whether the two amounts could be regarded as compensation for loss of management rights in A. Ltd. and came to the conclusion that there was no material to hold that the profit represented such compensation.

On reference:

HELD: Having regard to the definitions of managing agent and manger in section 2(9A) and 2(9) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the assessee by himself could not by any means be regarded as a managing agent. He by himself never entered into an agreement with either of the companies by which he was entitled to be a managing agent. Nor it could be said that as one of the two managing directors he was entitled to the management of the whole affairs of either of the companies. It was only the corporation of which the assessee along with 'P' was the managing director that was entitled to manage the whole affairs of the 'A' Ltd. That was one of the lines of reasoning on which the Tribunal held that clauses (a) and (b) of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act would be inapplicable to the amounts. That view was to be accepted. Thus, the assessee by himself was neither a managing agent nor a manager as the terms were defined in the Indian Companies Act, 1913.

Clause (c) of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act will be inapplicable because, as the Tribunal rightly held, that contemplates a company other than an Indian company.

For clause (d) to apply, the assessee must be holding an agency relating to the business of "any other person". It is impossible to say that the assessee in instant case by himself held such an agency. The managing agency was vested in the corporation and not in any one of the directors.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipts - Assessment year 1944-45 - By an agreement assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent of a company - During relevant accounting year managed company received offer from another company, company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as managing agents - Said offer was accepted by managed company and it asked assessee to retire - Assessee received certain amount by way of compensation towards termination of managing agency - Majority of shareholders of company ‘J’ were members of assessee-firm - Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was not casual receipt and it did arise out of business of assessee and, therefore, was not exempted under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

HELD: The instant case was not one of a change of opinion by the successor as on the findings of the Tribunal the predecessor being unaware of the nature of the receipt had no occasion to form any opinion and the case was simply one of omission or may even be one of negligence and where the successor became aware of the omission or negligence. The case of a change of opinion simpliciter occurs only where without reference to the papers on the record or books or information from any outside source the same person who formed the opinion originally, changes that opinion subsequently by process of contemplation or by mere thinking about it a second time. It followed that action under section 34 of the 1922 Act was validly taken.

The Tribunal was also justified in holding that the receipt was a revenue receipt liable to tax.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

Iqbal Ahmad and R.S. Pathak for the Applicant.

Gopal Behari for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was managing agent of a company receiving commission at rate of 20 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Subsequently, by a resolution managed company resolved that as per agreement between parties assessee, in consideration of managed company paying a lump sum amount as compensation for releasing it from obligation to pay commission at rate of 20 percent, should accept as remuneration for rest of period of managing agency agreement 10 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Whether lump sum amount in question was received by assessee as compensation for deterioration or injury to managing agency by reason of release of its rights to get higher remuneration and therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee appellant which was a registered firm was appointed the managing agent of a company.

Some of the shareholders and directors of the managed company felt that the scale of remuneration paid at the rate of 20 percent to the assessee firm under the existing agreement was extraordinarily excessive and unusual and should be modified. Accordingly negotiations were started for a reduction of the remuneration and, after some discussion, the assessee firm and the managed company arrived at certain agreed modifications which were eventually recorded in a special resolution passed at the extraordinary general meeting of the managed company held on 22-10-1946.

It was resolved that the managing agents, in consideration of the company paying Rs. 7,50,000 as compensation, for releasing the company from the onerous term as to remuneration contained in the present managing agency agreement should accept as remuneration for the remaining term of their managing agency ten per cent. of the net annual profits of the company as defined in section 87C, sub-section (3) of the Indian Companies Act 1913 in lieu of the higher remuneration to which they were entitled under the provisions of the existing managing agency agreement.

The agreed modifications were thereafter embodied in a supplementary agreement made between the assessee firm and the managed company on 24-3-1948. The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 was paid by the managed company and received by the assessee in the calender year 1947 which was the accounting year for the assessment year 1948-49. The ITO treated the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 as a revenue receipt in the hands of the assessee firm and taxed it as such. On appeal, that decision was confirmed by the AAC and thereafter, on further appeal, was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the High Court also held that the sum in question was a revenue receipt liable to tax.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: There could be no doubt that by paying the sum of Rs. 7,50,000 the managed company had secured for itself a release from the obligation to pay a higher remuneration to the assessee for the rest of the period of managing agency covered by the principal agreement. Prima facie, that release from liability to pay a higher remuneration for over 17 years must be an advantage gained by the managed company for the benefit of its business and the immunity thus obtained by the managed company might well be regarded as the acquisition of an asset of enduring value by means of a capital outlay which would be a capital expenditure.

In the resolution adopted by the managed company as well as in the recitals set out in the supplementary agreement that sum had been stated to be a payment "as compensation for releasing the company from the onerous term as to remuneration contained" in the principal agreement. It was true that the language used in the document was not decisive and the question had to be determined by a consideration of all the attending circumstances; nevertheless, the language could not be ignored altogether but must be taken into consideration along with other relevant circumstances.

The sum of Rs. 7,50,000 had undoubtedly not been paid as compensation for the termination or cancellation of an ordinary business contract which was a part of the stock-in-trade of the assessee and could not, therefore, be regarded as income. Nor could this amount be said to have been paid as compensation for the cancellation or cessation of the managing agency of the assessee firm, for the managing agency continued.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1954-55 - 'M' and his nominees who controlled assessee-company, a dealer in shares, acquired control of 'E' along with its managing agency which was later assigned to 'C' company - Pursuant to M's offer, 'J' purchased certain ordinary and preference shares of 'E' Mills and also simultaneously obtained resignation of managing agents and directors of 'E' Mills and got his own nominees appointed as directors, as per M's offer - Out of sum received, M paid a part of it to 'C' company as consideration for resignation of its office and distributed balance to respective shareholders including assessee-company whose shares had also been sold to 'J' - ITO assessed profit on sale of assessee's shares as its business income - AAC accepted assessee's claim that said amount represented a capital gain and did not form part of assessee's business income - Tribunal restored ITO's order, and observed that amount allocated to assessee by 'M' represented exclusively price of shares and did not include any consideration for procuring of resignation of directors, for obtaining appointment of directors of J's choice and for resignation of existing managing agents of 'S' Mills - Whether it is possible for a dealer in shares to convert a part of its stock-in-trade into investment, but, there was nothing in books of assessee or in its resolutions to show that it had changed its attitude towards shares of 'E' from year 1948 - Held, yes - Whether subsequent to acquisition of managing agency until it was relinquished in 1953, there was nothing on record of proceedings to show that at any time managing agency had felt its existence either precarious or in need of support, and therefore profit made by on sale of shares was its business income - Held, yes - Whether circumstances of case indicated that 'M' was, by reason of his influence and power, in a position to command obedience of his wishes from his nominees and associates concerned and part taken by assessee in transaction with 'J' was merely a passive part, viz., keeping at disposal of 'M' its holding in 'E' shares which it had held in its business as a dealer in shares - Held, yes - Whether what assessee parted with was shares which it held and what it received was payment for those shares, and therefore entire sum received by assessee from 'M' was price of shares disposed by 'M' and, consequently, whole of excess over cost price of shares was profit of appellant - Held, yes - Whether therefore, no part of amount received by assessee from 'M' could be regarded as consideration for any other valuable right excepting price of shares sold by it - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee is a private limited company controlled by 'M' and his nominees. It was a dealer in shares, both in forward and ready market. Obtained control of the E and also acquired the managing agency of the E for a consideration. M assigned the managing agency to a private company known as C, whose shareholders were M his nominees and the assessee. The dealings in shares of the assessee included dealings in shares of E also and the profit and loss in the dealings of E was taken by the assessee to its revenue account.

During the years from 1948 onwards there was a slump in the price of the shares of the 'E'.

On 25-9-1953, M wrote a letter to making an offer of sale of ordinary shares and preference shares of the E. He stated in that letter that the shares offered stood in the names of himself, his family members and his allied concerns. The offer for sale was accompanied by a further offer that, if the offer for sale was accepted, M would obtain the resignation of the instant directors of the E and would also get appointed as directors persons of the choice of and that he would obtain the resignation of the present managing agents of the E viz., accepted the offer and paid the sum out of which M paid Rs. 10 lakhs to Chidambaram Mulraj and Co. Ltd., which relinquished the managing agency at his instance. The balance was distributed to the respective shareholders including the assessee whose shares had been sold to.

For the assessment year 1954-55, the ITO treated the profit from the sale of the shares as the assessee's income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the AAC held that the said amount represented a capital gain and did not form part of the business income. On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal restored the ITO's order.

On reference, the High Court held that the said amount was the assessee's income, and that the amount allocated by 'M' out of the money received from 'J', represented exclusively the price of the shares.

On appeal to Supreme Court:

HEADNOTE: Section 2(13) read with section 14 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(4)read with and section 6 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Adventure in nature of trade - Assessment year 1929-30 - Assessees were engaged in business as merchants and agents of various companies - Assessee agency with two of companies was terminated - During the assessment year under consideration, assessee received from one of companies whose agency had been terminated a sum as full compensation for cessation of agency and certain sum from another as compensation for loss of office as agent to company - Income-tax authorities took above mentioned receipts as profits and gains and after allowing certain deductions included balance in total income - Whether sums in question which revenue sought to charge could only be taxable if they were result of carrying on agencies of companies in year in which they were received by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since sums were received not for carrying on business but as some sort of solatium for compulsory cessation, sums in question were not income, profits or gains within meaning of Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees were engaged in business as merchants and agents of various companies having branch officer in different parts of India. Assessees’ agency with two of the Companies was terminated in the end of previous assessment year. During the assessment year under consideration i.e. 1929-30, assessee received from one of the companies whose agency had been terminated a sum as full compensation for cessation of the agency. However another company also panel certain sum as compensation for the loss of officer as agent to the Company. The quotations were accepted on both sides as correctly expressing the nature of the transactions. While computing the assessable income of assessee, ITO took abovementioned receipts as profits and gains from business and also allowed certain deductions thereform in respect of compensation paid to various employees. Consequently the balances were included in the total income. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner and Commissioner confirmed the assessment. On further appeal, High Court held that sums in question were not incomes, profits or gains with in meaning of Act at all. In one part of its judgment the High Court seemed to hold that "compensation for loss of these agencies is a receipt in respect of a capital asset in the nature of goodwill. In another part of the judgment the payment seemed to be regarded as in the nature of compensation in lieu of notice.

On revenue’s appeal to the Privy Council :

HELD: The object of the Indian Act is to tax "income" a term which it does not define. It is expanded, no doubt, into "income profits and gains," but the expansion is more a matter of words than of substance. Income, in this Act connects a periodical monetary return "coming in" with some sort of regularity, or expected regularity, from definite sources. The source is not necessarily one which is expected to be continuously productive, but it must be one whose object is the production of a definite return excluding anything in the nature of a mere windfall. Thus income has been likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree, or the crop of a field. It is essentially the produce of something, which is often loosely spoken of as "capital". But capital, though possible the source in the case of income from securities, is in most cases hardly more than an element in the process of production. The sources from which the taxable income under the Act are to be derived are enumerated in section 6, which runs as follows: —"Save as otherwise provided by this Act, the following heads of income, profits and gains, shall be chargeable to income-tax in the manner hereinafter appearing, namely: — (i) Salaries, (ii ) Interest on securities, (iii ) Property, (iv) Business, (v) Professional earnings, (vi) Other sources." The claim of the taxing authorities is that the sum in question is chargeable under head (iv ) business. The words used in section 2(4) are no doubt wide, but underlying each of them is the fundamental idea of the continuous exercise of an activity. Under section 10 the tax is to be payable by an assessee under the head business "in respect of the profits or gains of any business carried on by him." The words italicised are an essential constituent of that which is to produce the taxable income: it is to be the profit earned by a process of production. And this is borne out by the provision for allowances which follows. They include rent paid for the premises where the business is carried on; the cost of current repairs in respect of such premises; interest on money borrowed for carrying on the business, etc.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1955-56 - Whether compensation paid for terminat ion of a managing agency business is a payment in relation to said business; as such said receipt was obviously related to that business and was not or income from a new and independent source and, therefore, previous year relevant to that receipt would be same as previous year for managing agency business itself - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a private limited company. In 1944, the assessee purchased the managing agency of certain company for Rs. 6 lakhs and thereafter entered into a separate managing agency agreement with the managed company for a period of seventeen years. The assessee's only source of income was this managing agency in the relevant year. M, one of the shareholders of the assessee, and his group also held among themselves 25,000 ordinary and 10,000 preference shares of that company. M entered into an agreement for sale of these shares with one 'K' for a consideration of Rs. 45 lakhs; one of the terms of the agreement was that M would have the managing agency of the assessee terminated. In implementation of this agreement, M wrote to the assessee on 21-10-1953, asking it to give up the managing agency in lieu of Rs. 10 lakhs as compensation. The assessee accepted M's offer and tendered its resignation of its office as managing agents. The assessee credited the amount of compensation in its capital reserve account. In the assessment year 1955-56, the ITO assessed the entire amount of Rs. 10 lakhs in the hands of the assessee under section 10(5A).

On appeal, the AAC held that section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act created a new source of income for which the previous year was not the previous year for the managing agency business which ended on 30-6-1954, that the compensation of Rs. 10 lakhs which the assessee received in October, 1953, fell in the financial year 1953-54, which would be the previous year for this income for which the assessment year was 1954-55, which was before sub-section (5A) of section 10 of the 1922 Act was enacted, and the fact that the assessee had entered the amount in its books for the year that ended on 30-6-1954, Could not be taken as an exercise of option by the assessee accepting the said year as the previous year in respect of the receipt. On second appeal, the Tribunal was of opinion that section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act only regarded the compensation received by the managing agent as profits and gains of a business and does not create a fresh source therefore, and as the amount in question in this case was received in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1955-56, it was taxable in the assessment year 1955-56.

On reference, the High Court overruled the contention of the assessee that the amount in question was income from a new source for which the previous year was 1953-54.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:—

HELD: Sub-section (5A) of section 10 of the 1922 Act came into force on 1-4-1955; therefore, the amount in question, if received by the assessee during the previous year for the assessment year 1955-56 would be taxable under that sub-section. By a legal fiction introduced by sub-section (5A) any amount received by a managing agent as compensation for the termination of his managing agency agreement which would otherwise have been a capital receipt is to be deemed as profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent.

The fiction introduced by sub-section (5A) regards the capital receipt as income and does not extend to treating the termination of managing agency itself as a business. The amount received by the assessee was a payment for the termination of the managing agency business and, as such, the receipt was obviously related to that business. It was of course true that the amount was not earned in carrying on the business of managing agency, but it was clear that the source of the receipt was the managing agency business itself. It could not, therefore, be said that the receipt was income from a new and independent source. The High Court was right in holding that in enacting sub-section (5A) the legislature was concerned only with providing a head under which the receipt which has been deemed to be income could be brought to tax and was not concerned with creating a new source for that deemed income.

of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375. As regards the point that compensation was for past service of the firm, from a perusal of paragraph 2 of the agreement, it was clear that the promotion of the company by the partners of the firm was consideration for the appointment of the firm and for its tenure. It was a duly executed consideration. The period of 99 years was a fixed period. The firm was to continue for the whole of that period, unless it resigned the managing agency. It was not removable while the period of 99 years was still running. It could be removed only after the expiry of that period, and then also, only by a 3/4th majority of the shareholders of the company. It is clear that the situation in which the managing agency firm might resign or be removed prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years was not envisaged in the agreement at all. It followed that services rendered by the partners of the managing agency firm in promoting the company could not under the agreement for the basis of any compensation to be awarded to the firm for termination of the agreement either by its resignation or by its removal prior to the expiry of the period of 99 years. The compensation paid could not be consideration for past services.

It was paragraph 3 only of the agreement, which made provision for the premature termination of the managing agency. That paragraph contemplated termination only in one contingency, that of the company being wound up. If the company itself was wound up, the managing agency would be discontinued. In that event only, compensation as provided in paragraph 3(a) was payable. Thus it was clear that the compensation paid on the termination of the managing agency was not compensation for past services and was quite independent of that agreement. At the Tribunal stage this argument stood overruled when the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the payment was not collusive but was genuine and bona fide and further when it held that services were actually rendered by the firm in pursuance of the managing agency agreement after the company came into existence. In the face of the finding that services were actually rendered by the firm, which is a finding of fact, the argument that if any service was at all rendered, it was only the past service for promoting the company, stood overruled.

The result was that the compensation paid was receipt of a capital nature.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee-firm was carrying on various business activities such as financing, money lending, selling agency etc. - It entered into an agreement with another firm and formed a new firm - This new firm was appointed as managing agent of a cotton mill - Subsequently, partners of assessee-firm retired from new firm after receiving compensation from remaining partners of new firm - Said amount of compensation was invested by assessee-firm in its other business activities and, thus, trading structure of assessee-firm was not affected - Whether, in aforesaid circumstances, amount of compensation received by assessee-firm could be regarded as its revenue receipt assessable under section 10 of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm (Bagla Group), besides carrying on business of financing, money-lending, selling agency, etc., was also selling agents of a cotton mills in which another firm (Jaipuria Group) were enjoying some quota rights. The previous year of the assessee-firm relevant to the assessment year 1948-49 ended in October, 1947. On 29-4-1996, a new firm (BJ) came into existence which consisted of six partners-three from the assessee-firm and three from Jaipuria Group. These partners did not enter into a deed of partnership. This partnership (BJ) was appointed as managing agents of the cotton mills. Subsequently, three of the partners belonging to the assessee-firm went out of the partnership on 6-10-1946 and, for doing so they were paid Rs. 35,01,000 which included the profits earned by the new firm (BJ) till the date of retirements of the above three partners. In the course of assessment for the assessment year 1948-49, ITO brought to tax the sum of Rs. 35,01,000 as income. On appeal, the AAC affirmed the ITO's order. He further held that the assessee's case fell within the scope of section 12B of 1922 Act. The Tribunal held that the receipt in question could not be brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act. On reference, the High Court held that receipt in question was liable to tax under section 10 of 1922 Act, but it was not taxable under section 12B of 1922 Act.

On cross appeals to Supreme Court :

HELD: There was no dispute that the portion of the compensation which represented past profits was a revenue receipt. The only question was whether the remaining portion was a revenue receipt or capital receipt. The remaining portion purported to be compensation given to the three partners for giving up: (i) the managing agency rights, (ii) the selling agency rights, and (iii) the goodwill. The managing agency rights vested with new firm (BJ). Similar was the case of the goodwill assuming that any goodwill had been built up by that time. 'BJ' continued to be in existence. It had not parted with managing agency rights nor its goodwill taken away. What had happened was that the partners representing the assessee firm in 'BJ' had surrendered their rights in partnership to the remaining partners and obtained certain payments for such surrender. This was not a case of parting with any agency rights. This was really a case of cancellation of a contract which had been entered into in the ordinary course of business. Such contracts are liable, in the ordinary course of business, to be altered or terminated on terms and any payment received in settlement of the rights as a result of the termination of the contract really represents the profits which the assessee would have made had the contract been performed. In the instant case, no deed of partnership had been entered into. Therefore, the same was terminable at will. Any of the partners of the firm could have brought the partnership to an end. Consequently, the possibility of termination of a partnership was inherent in the very course of business. Further the assessee-firm had various business activities; one of which was to join 'BJ' to carry on certain business activities. The assessee's representatives by entering into that agreement were merely carrying on a trading activity. Such being the case, it could not be held that the compensation paid for the termination of the contract was a capital receipt. It was not the case of the assessee that its only trading activity had come to an end. It had several activities. Just one of its trading had been put an end to. Hence, the amount received could not be considered as compensation for stopping its business.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i)  of the Income-tax Act 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee firm was agent of ‘HML’ - It assigned its agency rights to ‘P’ which agreed to pay part of its profits subject to minimum sum per annum - Subsequently, by another agreement, assessee transferred its rights under assignments to ‘O’ for lump sum consideration - Whether by second agreement assessee had parted with its profits making apparatus and, therefore, amount recived by it from ‘O’ was capital receipt - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was appointed as agent of ‘HML’ in 1955. In 1960, the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ according to which ‘P’ took over the business of the assessee and agreed to pay 31 per cent of its profits subject to a minimum of Rs. 25,000 per annum. Subsequently, by another agreement in 1962, the assessee transferred its rights under the agreement of 1960 for a consideration of Rs. 50,000 to 'O'. The ITO held the sum of Rs. 50,000 to be a revenue receipt of the assessee and taxed it as its income . The AAC maintained the addition in appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal deleted the sum of Rs. 50,000 from the income of the assessee, holding that it was a capital receipt.

On reference :

HELD: The agency agreement entered into by the assessee with ‘HML’ in the year 1955 was a capital asset; the whole of it was not destroyed, lost or parted when the assessee entered into an agreement with ‘P’ in the year 1960. It was merely an exploitation of the commercial assets in a different form. Till then, the recurring amount which the assessee was getting from ‘P’ was income. But by the arrangement arrived at on the basis of the second agreement, the whole of the profit-making apparatus of the assessee was parted with and lost. The question has presented some difficulty when the assessee gets some amount of compensation on termination of agency agreement from the principal itself. Sometimes, in a given case, such compensation, and especially with regard to the managing agency business, has been treated as revenue receipts. But, in the instant case, the type of agreement which the assessee entered into with ‘O’ even if it would have entered into with ‘P’ on payment of Rs. 50,000, would not have clothed the receipt with the chartered of a revenue receipt; still it would have been a capital receipt. This was clearly so, without presenting any difficulty, when the agreement was with another company. After having parted with all its rights of profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960, by a subsequent agreement executed in the year 1962, the assessee was left with no business activity in connection with the agency agreement with ‘HML’. The amount, therefore, received by it was not in lieu of compounded profit but surely in lieu of loss of profit-making apparatus.

What is received by way of price or compensation on disposing of circulating capital or stock-in-trade, namely, the trading asset, is ordinarily and generally revenue receipt. What, however, comes in the hands of the assessee on disposal of the capital assets referable to fixed capital is generally a capital receipt. What is capital asset in the hands of one may be a trading asset in the hands of another.

In the instant case the assessee was not parting with the benefits of a trading contract, rather it parted with its profit-making apparatus, namely, the agreement of the year 1960; by utilising that apparatus it was earning profit from the agency business, and the whole of it was lost when he decided to retire on the receipt of Rs. 50,000. It was a sum paid to the assessee, truly a compensation for parting with its business, and the agreement entered into deprived the assessee of the benefit of its agreement entered in 1960, with ‘P’ which constituted the framework or whole structure of the assessee's profit-making apparatus. For the reasons stated above, the receipt of Rs. 50,000 by the assessee was a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether share of a partner in partnership concern is property and, thus, a capital assest within meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Assessee and ‘G’ were partners in three partnership firms which were managing agents of three mills - Assessee’s share in one concern was transferred to ‘G’ in exchange for G’s share in other concerns and additional sum of Rs. 1,00,000 - Whether transaction in question involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets and had all elements of sale and, thus, sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was assessable to tax as capital gains - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

HELD: Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1949-50 and 1950-51 - Taking up managing agency along with secretaryship to plantation company and other trading rights was part of assessee's normal trading activities - Assessee dealt with, among other things, export of tea produced in India - Managing agencies, assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event assessee received compensation it was entitled to by agreement - Such agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for company but was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea - Assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding termination of such agreements - Whether termination of agreement with tea company could be said to have been brought about in ordinary course of business of assessee and money paid to assessee as a result of or in connection with termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in ordinary course of business of assessee and, therefore, it was a trading receipt - Held, yes

FACT: In the course of its varied business activities, the assessee-company took up the managing agencies of plantation companies, to which the assessee also acted as secretaries. Whenever a managing agency was terminated, as for example when the plantations were sold and the plantation company itself wound up its operations the assessee was paid compensation, the quantum of which was decided by agreement. In 1945-46, the assessee-company held such managing agencies for sixteen plantation companies. T, was one of such plantation companies, and the agreement between that company and the assessee was in 1937. In 1945, T sold its plantation, which was in India, and the company subsequently went into liquidation. In accordance with a resolution passed by T, assessee received certain amount on 30-6-1946. That amount was treated as a trading receipt to the Department for the purpose of assessment to income-tax, excess profits tax and business profits tax. When the assessee appealed to the Tribunal it purported to apply the principles laid down by this Court in CIT v. South Indian Pictures Ltd. [1951] 20 ITR 605 and upheld the claim of the assessee, that this sum constituted a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :

HELD: In the case the assessee, taking up managing agency along with secretary ship to the plantation company and other trading rights was part of the assessee's normal trading activities. The assessee dealt with, among other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other things, the export of tea produced in India, and obtaining managing agencies and other rights from the plantation companies certainly facilitated that trade in tea. The managing agencies, the assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event the assessee received the compensation it was entitled to by agreement. The agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for T. It was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to the assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea. The assessee was in a position to obtain such contracts with plantation companies because of its large experience in handling tea for export and also in managing plantations in India. Even confining to the managing agency the loss of one of several such managing agencies could have little effect on the structure of the assessee's business even in tea or on its profit earning apparatus as a whole. They endured virtually unimpaired by the termination of the managing agency for the T even as the business of the assessee remained unimpaired when other managing agencies were terminated in the past. The assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding the termination of such agreements. The termination of the agreement with the T could well be said to have been brought about in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and the money paid to the assessee as a result of or in connection with the termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee and that therefore, it was a trading receipt.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii), read with sections 45 and 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee received certain amount from a company which he claimed as professional goodwill - Assessing Officer held that said amount was received by assessee on account of relinquishment of his rights in management of a company and, therefore, was to be taxed under section 28(ii)(a) - Whether since Assessing Officer had not established that assessee was person who was managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of company, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed - Held, yes - Whether even, assuming that amount received by assessee was relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, cost of any such managerial right being indeterminate, provisions relating to computation of capital gain were not workable and, consequently, amount could not be taxed under section 45 also - Held, yes [Para 7.4] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : For invoking section 28(ii)(a) it has to be established whether amount due or received is against termination of any right which an assessee was enjoying by managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of an Indian company; where Assessing Officer did not record such finding, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed

FACT: The assessee received certain amount from company CARE. According to it, the amount was received as professional goodwill and was liable to be treated as capital receipt not liable to capital gain.

The Assessing Officer observed that the amount was received by the assessee on account of relinquishment of his rights in the management of a company in favour of CARE and not on account of relinquishment of any right relating to professional expertise or acumen as surgeon. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, brought the amount to tax holding that it was covered under the provision of section 28(ii)(a).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal:

HEADNOTE: II. Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether when assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to carrying on of business in agencies - Held, yes - Assessee-company had income from contracts and commission from various parties - It was also distributor of products of a foreign company for 22 years - A joint venture - company HTIPL was formed to manufacture and market products of said foreign company in India - Under an agreement, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets such as trained manpower, personal dealings, list of customers, etc., and in turn it had received certain amount by way of compensation, which was claimed by the assessee as consideration for ‘goodwill’, being capital receipt not taxable - Whether since assessee continued to do same line of business, i.e., distributorship of other companies with same name, fame, place and approach even after formation of joint venture, it could not be said that assessee had received compensation for sale of ‘goodwill’ - Held, yes - Whether what assessee had got in terms of compensation was a normal incidence of business arising due to its re-organisation and formation of a joint venture and, thus, what assessee had received was of revenue character and was taxable accordingly - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was a distributor of products of foreign company for last 22 years. A joint venture company HTIPL, consisting of the assessee and the foreign company, was formed to manufacture the products of foreign company in India and also to market products of the foreign company manufactured abroad. Under an agreement entered into between the assessee and company HTIPL, assessee agreed to transfer certain intangible assets like trained manpower personnel dealing with said products in India and detailed list of customers of said products and introduce HTIPL to all the customers both in public and private sectors for sale of said products. In view of transfer of above intangible assets, the assessee received certain compensation from HTIPL. The assessee treated that sum as a consideration for transfer of goodwill and offered same for taxation as long term capital gains. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had income from service contracts and commission from various parties; that it was a compensation received on termination of managing agency; that the assessee was carrying on several managing agencies and it gave up only one and continued with other; that the business structure of the assessee did not suffer and it was free to carry on the trade with other agencies; that the cancellation and compensation, therefore, was merely a normal incidence of business; and that the income of the assessee had increased in the subsequent years. The Assessing Officer, therefore, held that the amount received by the assessee was revenue receipt taxable in its hands. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had parted with a part of its apparatus to a joint venture and for the loss so suffered it had received compensation. He directed the Assessing Officer to tax the receipt as capital receipt.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: A careful consideration of the case laws indicated following principles :

1. When a payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of contract which does not affect the trading structure of the recipient’s business nor deprive the assessee from source of income, then termination of contract is only a normal incidence of business.

2. Where trading structure of the assessee is impaired or cancellation results in loss of sources of income, payment to compensate such loss of source is capital.

3. A source of income may be a capital structure of one assessee. But where the assessee is dealing in several such sources/assets, then it becomes a stock in trade. Loss of one such source/asset will be a loss of capital if the assessee is dealing only in one but will be revenue if it is dealing in many such sources/assets as stock in trade.

4. When assessee is dealing in several agencies, loss of one such agency will be incidental to the carrying on of the business in agencies. Where there is a modification in the terms of any one of such agencies, it will again be a normal incidence of business.

5. There is no immutable principle that compensation received on cancellation of an agency must always be regarded as capital.

6. Compensation paid for agreeing to refrain from carrying on business in the commodities in respect of the agency terminated for loss of goodwill, is prima facie of the nature of capital receipt.

7. Manner of payment of compensation is not material. Whether capital is repaid in instalments or is paid in lump sum, it will not affect the basic nature of receipt in the hands of the recipient.

8. When assessee is not disposed of any asset, then amount received cannot be regarded as compensation in respect of loss of an enduring asset.

ibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act. Where on a consideration of the circumstances, payment is made to compensate a person for cancellation of a contract which does not affect the trading structure of his business, nor deprive him of what in substance is his source of income, termination of the contract being a normal incident of the business, and such cancellation leaves him free to carry on his trade (freed from the contract terminated) the receipt is revenue : Where by the cancellation of an agency the trading structure of the assessee is impaired, or such cancellation results in loss of what may be regarded as the source of the assessee's income, the payment made to compensate for cancellation of the agency agreement is normally a capital receipt.

In the instant case, on a review of all the circumstances, there was no doubt that what the assessee was paid was to compensate him for loss of a capital asset. It matters little whether the assessee did continue after the determination of its agency with the company to conduct the remaining agencies. The transaction was not in the nature of a trading transaction, but was one in which the assessee parted with an asset of an enduring value. The court was therefore, unable to agree with the High Court that the amount received by the appellant was in the nature of a revenue receipt.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(3), read with sections 28 and 56, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii), read with sections 10 and 12, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] – Casual and non-recurring receipts – Assessment year 1926–27 – Assessee was carrying on business of managing agents of various companies – One of such companies was wound up voluntarily and it paid certain amount to assessee as compensation for their loss of office as managing agents of said company – Whether amount received by assessee was receipt arising from business and, therefore, exemption relied on by assessee under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act was of no use – Held, yes

FACT: The assessee carried on business as merchants and also as managing agents and agents of a many companies and firms. They were appointed as managing agents of company 'C' but there was nothing in the articles regarding their appointment for any fixed term of years. There was no contract actually executed between the company and the assessee for their services as managing agents of the company. It was not at the option of the company to very the remuneration from time to time and the assessees were at liberty to terminate their own appointment as managing agents at their option. On 16-01-1925 company 'C' was wound up voluntarily. Certain amount was paid to the assessee as compensation for their loss of office as managing agents of the company. The assessee claimed that sum as a receipt of casual non-recurring nature not arising from business or the exercise of a profession, vocation or occupation and so exempt under section 4(3)(vii)of the 1922 Act. The ITO considered the sum as a receipt from business and included it in their income for purposes of assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessment. On reference, the Commissioner also took the same view which was taken by the ITO.

HELD: Section 10 of the 1922 Act, indicates that tax is payable under the head of "business" in respect of the profits or gains of any business carried on by the assessee; and section 12 of the 1922 Act which deals with the residuary heading "other sources" expressed that the tax shall be payable in respect of "income, profits and gains of every kind and from every source to which the Act applies (if not included under any of the preceding heads)". If therefore, a payment comes under clause (vii) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, it is not covered by section 12 at all.

In the instant case, the assessee-company had several – managing agencies. The assessee was given the said sum of money because, without notice the them, in the middle of the year, one of their managing agencies was being brought to a close. In the circumstances, it was thought right to give the assessee this amount by way of compensation for their sudden dismissal. It was impossible to say that the receipt was not a receipt arising from business and that was the statutory test which had to be applied. It was not contended before the Commissioner that the instant case, if it did not come under section 10 of the 1922 Act, would not, apart from this exemption clause, be hit by section 12 of the 1922 Act. There was no doubt that the payment in the instant case was income within the meaning of section 12of the 1922 Act unless it was saved by section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act. In these circumstances, the Commissioner was right in deciding that the exemption relied on was of no use to the assessee and that income-tax was rightly assessed.

Note: The case was decided against the assessee.

Langford James and W.A.K. Page for the Applicant.

B.L. Mitter and S.M. Bose for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessee-firm was appointed as a managing agent in a company which was floated by it and its partners held majority shares in that company - Subsequently managed company in a resolution passed by its director removed assessee-firm from managing agency and appointed a newly floated company 'JKCE' in which partners of firm also had majority share as its new managing agent - For said termination, managerial company paid certain amount as compensation to assessee which revenue treated as revenue receipt of assessee - Tribunal found that said payment to assessee was collusive and partners of firm continued to run and enjoy benefit of managing agency as shareholders and directors of newly formed company by reason of their holding a majority of shares in that company - Tribunal also held that whole transaction was a hoax for purpose of evading income-tax - Whether, on facts, it could be held that managing agency business carried on by assessee was not destroyed or lost to individual partners who constituted it - Held, yes - Whether, there was therefore proper material before Appellate Tribunal in support of its finding that receipt by assessee-firm was a receipt in the course of its managing agency business and was a revenue receipt - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was constituted of four partners. The shareholding of the three brothers PS, LS and KS was 51 per cent constituting a majority of the shareholding in the partnership firm and remaining was held by one 'B'. The partners of the firm floated a company, namely, 'JK' in which said three brothers along with their wives held majority share. In consideration of the fact that the assessee-firm promoted the company "JK", the assessee was appointed the managing agent of the company.

In a meeting of the board of directors of the managed company letter of the financiers asking for re-payment of advances made by the financier to the company was discussed. Accordingly, it was decided to ask the assessee to arrange for advance of such sums of moneys as would be necessary to pay off the loan of the financiers, and also to equip the company with working capital. A resolution was, accordingly, passed at the meeting to that effect. A letter addressed to the assessee informing it of the resolution and asking it to make immediate arrangement for an amount which would not only reduce the account of JK, bankers, but must also provide the company with working capital. The assessee replied to this communication that under the terms of the managing agency agreement it was not obligatory upon it to make advances to the managed company. The assessee stated that it had been specially constituted to act as the managing agents of the managed company and had no capital of its own. It had no assets also on the security of which it could raise a sum which would be necessary to reduce the account of JK, bankers, but must also provide the company with working capital. The assessee replied to this communication that under the terms of the managing agency agreement it was not obligatory upon it to make advances to the managed company. The assessee stated that it had been specially constituted to act as the managing agents of the managed company and had no capital of its own. It had no assets also on the security of which it could raise a sum which would be necessary to reduce the amount of JK, bankers, to the limit required by the managed company and to equip the company with working capital. The letter of the assessee was considered by the managed company at the meeting of its board of directors and it was decided that 'JKCC' Ltd. was willing to make advance provided it was appointed the managing agent of the company. Therefore it was decided that assessee should be terminated from the management agency and the company should pay a fair compensation in consideration of the premature termination of the managing agency. Accordingly a compensation was paid to assessee-firm by managed company. The managing agency of the assessee was thereafter terminated and JKCC were appointed the managing agents.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was allowed, in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of the managed company as a consequence of its take over by the State Government. For the assessment year 1960-61, the ITO taxed the compensation amount, treated it as a capital receipt.

On appeal, the AAC while upholding the assessment, held that only the amount actually received during the previous year should be the amount of income taxable.

On Second Appeal, the Tribunal held that entire receipt to which the provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted, was a taxable income assessable during the year in question as the assessee itself having credited the entire sum to its profit and loss account in keeping with the system of its accounting, which was mercantile, no justification vested with the AAC to change it.

On reference :

HELD: Since a managing agency is a creature of contract and since its formation, operation and termination are all to be governed by the provisions of the Contract Act, in so far as they apply, there was no force in the contention that a managing agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other agency contract can be terminated only by act of parties and in no other manner. The words "termination………….of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A), contemplated termination of the agency agreement, in the several manners contemplated under the Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of the mutual rights and obligations of either party under the agency agreement.

Then again, the taking over of the electric supply business of the managed company by the State Government did not by itself, occasion termination of the managing agency. Even after the takeover, the managing agency of the assessee was continuing for about two years and had to be terminated by a resolution which was made retrospective with effect from the date of the take-over.

The business of the assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature. There was no material to show that the assessee was not carrying on such business, after the State Government had taken over the electric supply corporation. ‘Business’ could not be read in restricted sense, as meaning only that business to which the compensation related. In any case, section 10(5A) spoke of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent. Since such compensation of the business, the section provides that it shall be deemed to be the income even after the termination. Further, clause (a) of section 10(5A) speaks not only of compensation due or received on termination of managing agency but in connection with the termination of managing agency. This widens the circumstance of payment and compensation may be deemed to be profits and gains of business during the assessment year.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the compensation amount was taxable profit within the meaning of section 10(5A).

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee owned certain coal mines - Later, he formed a company along with family members and transferred entire management of coal mines to company - Company agreed to pay assessee a royalty and certain amount in respect of goodwill - Whether, in instant case, there was no transfer, sale or exchange of capital asset as all that was done was to give management of that asset to someone else - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee in effecting transfer of management of coal mines to company did not make any capital gain - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee owned coal mines. Later, he along with other family members incorporated a company. By an agreement, the assessee transferred the management of entire business of working his collieries and mines to the company for consideration of royalty. The company also agreed to take over all the business liability of the assessee by allotting shares of the equivalent net value. The ITO was of the opinion that by the transfer of the management of the mines to the company the assessee made a capital gain.

On appeal, the Appellate Commissioner upheld the order of ITO but reduced the amount of capital gain.

On further appeal, though the Tribunal held that the company would have been required to pay higher amount of royalty if it had not paid certain amount on account of goodwill. The Tribunal, thus, opined that the assessee had capitalised a part of his income. It accordingly, concluded that the amount paid to assessee was liable to be taxed at the rates appropriate to 'income' and not at the rates appropriate to capital gain.

On reference:

HELD: Firstly, in the instant case, it was certainly not the assessee's case before the Tribunal that the amount received towards goodwill was his income, nor did it appear to have been the case for taxing authority. The Tribunal apparently on its own motion came to that conclusion on the facts before it.

Following the decision in New India Life Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1957] 31 ITR 844 it could be said that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to do so.

As regards question whether capital gain arose in instant case, one has merely to read the definition of 'capital gain' to realise that transfer in question could not conceivably be a capital gain, because there was no transfer, sale or exchange of a capital asset. All that was done was to give the management of that asset to someone else. Therefore, the assessee in effecting the transfer of the management of the Coal mines to the company did not make any capital gain.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt. As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

. In such a case, it is the board of directors collectively who can be said to be managing the business affairs of the company. Therefore, the assessee was not managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the company and the impugned amount cannot be related to the three rights referred to in the Addendum. [Para 7.1] Management right has now been included in the definition of 'property' and, therefore, is a 'capital asset' under section 2(14). This being so, taxability of any amount received against relinquishment of 'management right' has to be tested on the touchstone of provisions relating to computation of capital gain. The assessee argued that since management right is a capital asset, provisions relating to capital gain will apply and when such computation provisions are applied, they are unworkable. It is true that under the scheme of taxation of capital gain, it is not the entire sale consideration of an asset which is chargeable to tax but it is the 'profit or gain' arising on transfer thereof which is taxable. This observation is subject to the specific provisions of law which prescribe that in case of some category of capital assets, cost of acquisition is considered to be nil and, in those cases, full consideration accruing on transfer will become taxable. In the instant case, it is the stand of assessee that cost of acquisition of management right being indeterminate, no capital gain can be worked out and so the provisions are not workable. [Para 7.3]

Section 55(2) does not specify that cost of acquisition of 'management right' will be taken to be nil. In other words, there is no deemed cost of acquisition provided in the statute. No case has been made out by the Assessing Officer to show as to what was the cost of management right in the hands of assessee. Therefore, what has been brought to tax is the entire consideration for relinquishment of management right which runs contrary to the settled proposition of law, which was laid down by Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 5 Taxman 1/128 ITR 294. In this decision, the Supreme Court has laid down the proposition that machinery and charging provisions constitute an integrated code and where in the situation computation provision fails, it has to be assumed that such a transaction was not intended to be falling within the charging section and, therefore, the charge on account of capital gain must fail. [Para 7.3]

It is evident that the revenue has not established that the assessee was managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the company as no case has been made out by the revenue that the amount received by the assessee from CARE was on account of relinquishment of any managerial rights. Even assuming that the amount received by the assessee is relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, in view of ratio laid down by Supreme Court in the case of B.C. Srinivasa Setty (supra) the cost of any such managerial right being indeterminate, provisions relating to computation of capital gain are not workable and consequently, it has to be held that the charge under section 45 never intended to levy a tax on such a transaction. [Para 7.4]

In the above view, the amount received by the assessee is neither chargeable under section 28(ii)(a) nor under the head capital gain. [Para 7.5]

Such being the case, it could not be held that the compensation paid for the termination of the contract was a capital receipt. It was not the case of the assessee that its only trading activity had come to an end. It had several activities. Just one of its trading had been put an end to.
