Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

Section 28(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee, who was one of partners of managing agency firm and was director of managed company, received his share of compensation from managed company in terms of arbitration award for premature termination of managing agency agreement - Assessee claimed amount so received to be capital receipt and hence not liable to tax - Whether amount in question was capital receipt and not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee was managing agent of company F - It entered into agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company - 'M' also agreed to compensate assessee for loss of office - Subsequently, assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of company - Accordingly, assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation received by assessee to relinquish managing agency could not be regarded as revenue receipt and, thus, it was not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee company was managing agents of various companies including one 'G', in which assessee held a large block of shares - In 1951, board of directors of 'G' decided to terminate agency against payment of certain amount to assessee - Whether termination of managing agency in question had resulted in destruction of source of in come of assessee and, thus, amount received by assessee was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as – Assessment year 1952-53 – Assessee was acting as managing agents for 'N' - Subsequently, agreement was terminated when Government of State of Madras in exercise of powers conferred upon it by Electrical Undertakings Acquisition Act, 1949, compulsorily acquired undertaking of that company, and assessee was paid as compensation for premature termination of its agency - The ITO observed that assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end, assessee still continued as 'managing agents of other companies' and therefore receipt was to be considered as revenue - Whether such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of assessee, was a capital receipt, therefore, same was not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was managing agent of a company receiving commission at rate of 20 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Subsequently, by a resolution managed company resolved that as per agreement between parties assessee, in consideration of managed company paying a lump sum amount as compensation for releasing it from obligation to pay commission at rate of 20 percent, should accept as remuneration for rest of period of managing agency agreement 10 percent of net annual profits of managed company - Whether lump sum amount in question was received by assessee as compensation for deterioration or injury to managing agency by reason of release of its rights to get higher remuneration and therefore, a capital receipt not liable to tax - Held, yes

SECTION 45 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CAPITAL GAINS-CHARGEABLE 
AS-WHETHER ON FACTS GIVEN UNDER HEADING ‘COMPENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF MANAGING AGENCY’ SALE CONSIDERATION RECEIVED BY ASSESSEE- COMPANY FROM FIRM WAS LIABLE FOR CAPITAL GAINS TAX-HELD, NO

Section 28(ii)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1963-64 - Whether amount received by managing agents towards termination of their managing agency agreement are capital in nature - Held, yes - ‘ITF’ was managing agent of a company - Under an agreement, it transferred managing agency to assessee firm - Due to some disputes arose subsequently between assessee and ‘ITF’, assessee had to resign from office of managing agency and in arbitration proceedings, received damages towards compensation for loss of managing agency commission - Whether compensation received by assessee was capital receipt and not revenue receipt - Held, yes - Whether, however, said amount would be treated as ‘profits and gains of business’ under section 28(ii) of 1961 Act - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and compensation was awarded to assessee on basis of remuneration as having accrued to it during earlier five assessment years, compensation must be deemed to have accrued to assessee during said years - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 28(ii), read with  section 2(34) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A), read with section 2(11) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1955-56 - Assessee, who was managing agent of certain company and whose accounting year was calendar year, entered into agreement with a third person on 8-1-1955, whereby assessee agreed to sell or to procure for that person 2,500 shares of managed company and also agreed to resign its managing agency from that date for specified consideration to be paid by that third person to assessee - Assessing authority brought compensation amount to tax under section 10(5A) in assessment year in question - Whether sum received at or in connection with termination of managing agency was taxable under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether since previous year for managing agency business itself was calendar year 1955, same previous year had to be adopted for receipt of payment in question - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, payment received on 8-1-1955 was assessable in assessment year 1956-57 and not in assessment year in question - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation for termination of agency - Assessee was paid a sum as liquidated damages as well as interest thereon by the Nizam for latter's failure to abide by an earlier agreement under which Nizam had undertaken to buy shares in a company of which assessee was managing director and on account of Nizam's failure to buy shares assessee had to resign from managing directorship - Whether in view of fact that compensation received by assessee could not be apportioned towards loss of managing directorship said sum was not taxable under section 28(ii) - Held, on facts, yes

Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipts - Assessment year 1944-45 - By an agreement assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent of a company - During relevant accounting year managed company received offer from another company, company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as managing agents - Said offer was accepted by managed company and it asked assessee to retire - Assessee received certain amount by way of compensation towards termination of managing agency - Majority of shareholders of company ‘J’ were members of assessee-firm - Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was not casual receipt and it did arise out of business of assessee and, therefore, was not exempted under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

SECTION 28(ii)(c)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-COMPENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF MANAGING AGENCY-AN AGREEMENT WAS ENTERED INTO BETWEEN ASSESSEE-COMPANY AND FIRM UNDER WHICH ASSESSEE AGREED TO MANUFACTURE ‘BIDIES’ AS PER SPECIFICATIONS, SUCH AS SHAPE, SIZE AND STANDARD, OF FIRM-ASSESSEE WAS FREE TO MANUFACTURE BIDIES FOR ANY PERSON, FIRM OR COMPANY-IT WAS PROVIDED THAT ASSESSEE WAS TO PURCHASE RAW MATERIALS AT ITS OWN DISCRETION BUT WRAPPING PAPERS AND LABEL BEARING FIRM’S TRADE-MARK WERE TO BE SUPPLIED BY FIRM-THEREAFTER ANOTHER AGREEMENT WAS ENTERED UNDER WHICH EARLIER AGREEMENT WAS MUTUALLY TERMINATED AND IT WAS AGREED THAT ASSESSEE WAS TO SELL ITS RUNNING BUSINESS TO FIRM WITH ALL ASSETS AND LIABILITIES-FIRM HAD PAID CERTAIN CONSIDERATION AS ‘SLUMP PRICE’ TO ASSESSEE-WHETHER ASSESSEE WAS HOLDING ANY AGENCY AND CONSIDERATION SO RECEIVED ON SALE WAS TAXABLE UNDER SECTION 28(ii)(c)-HELD, NO

Section 2(13) read with section 14 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(4)read with and section 6 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Adventure in nature of trade - Assessment year 1929-30 - Assessees were engaged in business as merchants and agents of various companies - Assessee agency with two of companies was terminated - During the assessment year under consideration, assessee received from one of companies whose agency had been terminated a sum as full compensation for cessation of agency and certain sum from another as compensation for loss of office as agent to company - Income-tax authorities took above mentioned receipts as profits and gains and after allowing certain deductions included balance in total income - Whether sums in question which revenue sought to charge could only be taxable if they were result of carrying on agencies of companies in year in which they were received by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since sums were received not for carrying on business but as some sort of solatium for compulsory cessation, sums in question were not income, profits or gains within meaning of Act - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1954-55 - 'M' and his nominees who controlled assessee-company, a dealer in shares, acquired control of 'E' along with its managing agency which was later assigned to 'C' company - Pursuant to M's offer, 'J' purchased certain ordinary and preference shares of 'E' Mills and also simultaneously obtained resignation of managing agents and directors of 'E' Mills and got his own nominees appointed as directors, as per M's offer - Out of sum received, M paid a part of it to 'C' company as consideration for resignation of its office and distributed balance to respective shareholders including assessee-company whose shares had also been sold to 'J' - ITO assessed profit on sale of assessee's shares as its business income - AAC accepted assessee's claim that said amount represented a capital gain and did not form part of assessee's business income - Tribunal restored ITO's order, and observed that amount allocated to assessee by 'M' represented exclusively price of shares and did not include any consideration for procuring of resignation of directors, for obtaining appointment of directors of J's choice and for resignation of existing managing agents of 'S' Mills - Whether it is possible for a dealer in shares to convert a part of its stock-in-trade into investment, but, there was nothing in books of assessee or in its resolutions to show that it had changed its attitude towards shares of 'E' from year 1948 - Held, yes - Whether subsequent to acquisition of managing agency until it was relinquished in 1953, there was nothing on record of proceedings to show that at any time managing agency had felt its existence either precarious or in need of support, and therefore profit made by on sale of shares was its business income - Held, yes - Whether circumstances of case indicated that 'M' was, by reason of his influence and power, in a position to command obedience of his wishes from his nominees and associates concerned and part taken by assessee in transaction with 'J' was merely a passive part, viz., keeping at disposal of 'M' its holding in 'E' shares which it had held in its business as a dealer in shares - Held, yes - Whether what assessee parted with was shares which it held and what it received was payment for those shares, and therefore entire sum received by assessee from 'M' was price of shares disposed by 'M' and, consequently, whole of excess over cost price of shares was profit of appellant - Held, yes - Whether therefore, no part of amount received by assessee from 'M' could be regarded as consideration for any other valuable right excepting price of shares sold by it - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessee-firm was appointed as a managing agent in a company which was floated by it and its partners held majority shares in that company - Subsequently managed company in a resolution passed by its director removed assessee-firm from managing agency and appointed a newly floated company 'JKCE' in which partners of firm also had majority share as its new managing agent - For said termination, managerial company paid certain amount as compensation to assessee which revenue treated as revenue receipt of assessee - Tribunal found that said payment to assessee was collusive and partners of firm continued to run and enjoy benefit of managing agency as shareholders and directors of newly formed company by reason of their holding a majority of shares in that company - Tribunal also held that whole transaction was a hoax for purpose of evading income-tax - Whether, on facts, it could be held that managing agency business carried on by assessee was not destroyed or lost to individual partners who constituted it - Held, yes - Whether, there was therefore proper material before Appellate Tribunal in support of its finding that receipt by assessee-firm was a receipt in the course of its managing agency business and was a revenue receipt - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee owned certain coal mines - Later, he formed a company along with family members and transferred entire management of coal mines to company - Company agreed to pay assessee a royalty and certain amount in respect of goodwill - Whether, in instant case, there was no transfer, sale or exchange of capital asset as all that was done was to give management of that asset to someone else - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee in effecting transfer of management of coal mines to company did not make any capital gain - Held, yes

Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1944-45 - Assessee-company were managing agents of three companies - They transferred their managing agencies to other companies during relevant accounting year and received consideration which was taken to 'capital reserve account' - Transferee companies received from managed companies certain amounts as and by way of commission in relevant accounting year - Whether managing agency commission was not liable to be apportioned between assessee-company and respective transferee companies in proportion of services rendered as managing agents by each one of them and no income had accured to assessee-company on dates of respective transfers of managing agencies to transferees or at any time thereafter - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business Income - Compensation (Applicability of) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee company had joined hands with company DE to form a new venture in name and style of AMPL vide agreement - Assessee’s stake in said joint venture reached at 49 per cent - Balance 51 per cent equity in said joint venture remained with DE - Assessee and DE entered into an agreement wherein latter entity transferred its shareholding in AMPL to a wholly owned assessee’s subsidiary for US $ 1 and further agreed to pay it an amount of US $ 10 million as compensation for erosion in value of its investment in AMPL - Compensation received by assessee from DE was assessed under head business income under section 28(ii)(b) - It was noted that neither agreement clause between assessee and DE nor assessment order had proved assessee to be a managing agency in foregoing terms - Whether once assessee was not managing agency in foregoing terms, impugned compensation was not assessable under section 28(ii)(b) - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee company joined hands with a company to form a new venture and assessee and said company then entered into an agreement wherein latter entity transferred its shareholding in joint venture to a wholly owned assessee’s subsidiary and further agreed to pay it an amount as compensation for erosion in value of its investment in joint venture, since assessee was not managing agency in foregoing terms, impugned compensation was not assessable under section 28(ii)(b)

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business Income - Compensation (Applicability of) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee company had joined hands with company DE to form a new venture in name and style of AMPL vide agreement - Assessee’s stake in said joint venture reached at 49 per cent - Balance 51 per cent equity in said joint venture remained with DE - Assessee and DE entered into an agreement wherein latter entity transferred its shareholding in AMPL to a wholly owned assessee’s subsidiary for US $ 1 and further agreed to pay it an amount of US $ 10 million as compensation for erosion in value of its investment in AMPL - Compensation received by assessee from DE was assessed under head business income under section 28(ii)(b) - It was noted that neither agreement clause between assessee and DE nor assessment order had proved assessee to be a managing agency in foregoing terms - Whether once assessee was not managing agency in foregoing terms, impugned compensation was not assessable under section 28(ii)(b) - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 10(3), read with sections 28 and 56, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii), read with sections 10 and 12, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] – Casual and non-recurring receipts – Assessment year 1926–27 – Assessee was carrying on business of managing agents of various companies – One of such companies was wound up voluntarily and it paid certain amount to assessee as compensation for their loss of office as managing agents of said company – Whether amount received by assessee was receipt arising from business and, therefore, exemption relied on by assessee under section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act was of no use – Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1950-51 - Assessee-firm, who was a motor operator and also a dealer in motor-cars and trucks, was called upon by State Government to organise a corporation which had object of taking over entire road transport hitherto operated by private individuals and firms - In consideration of said work, assessee was promised managing agency of said proposed corporation - Subsequently, however, State Government decided to suspend this project and paid certain sum to assessee as compensation for loss and expenses sustained by him by reason of abandonment of project - ITO brought surplus over expenditure as business income of assessee - Whether since proposed corporation or profit making structure or managing agency were only an asset of a capital nature, compensation paid for loss of such capital asset was not and could not be taxable income - Held, yes

Section 28(ii), read with sections 45 and 55, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee received certain amount from a company which he claimed as professional goodwill - Assessing Officer held that said amount was received by assessee on account of relinquishment of his rights in management of a company and, therefore, was to be taxed under section 28(ii)(a) - Whether since Assessing Officer had not established that assessee was person who was managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of company, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed - Held, yes - Whether even, assuming that amount received by assessee was relatable to relinquishment of any managerial right, cost of any such managerial right being indeterminate, provisions relating to computation of capital gain were not workable and, consequently, amount could not be taxed under section 45 also - Held, yes [Para 7.4] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : For invoking section 28(ii)(a) it has to be established whether amount due or received is against termination of any right which an assessee was enjoying by managing whole or substantially whole of affairs of an Indian company; where Assessing Officer did not record such finding, invocation of section 28(ii)(a) failed

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1949-50 and 1950-51 - Taking up managing agency along with secretaryship to plantation company and other trading rights was part of assessee's normal trading activities - Assessee dealt with, among other things, export of tea produced in India - Managing agencies, assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event assessee received compensation it was entitled to by agreement - Such agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for company but was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea - Assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding termination of such agreements - Whether termination of agreement with tea company could be said to have been brought about in ordinary course of business of assessee and money paid to assessee as a result of or in connection with termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in ordinary course of business of assessee and, therefore, it was a trading receipt - Held, yes

Section 10(5A)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding to section 28(ii)(a) of the Income-tax Act 1961]-Business income-Compensation for termination of management agency agreement-Whether compensation paid by the managed company to the managing agent is taxable in the hands of managing agents under section 10(5A)(a) despite finding of tribunal in managed company's assessment for relevant period that termination of managing agency agreement by managed company was not bona fide-Held, on facts, yes

Section 86 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 14(2)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Exemption - Share income, as member of AOP/BOI - Assessment year 1957-58 - Assessee advanced certain amount to one 'R' to acquire share in a firm which was managing agents of a mill - Loan was repaid by 'R' - Thereafter, assessee and 'R' entered into an agreement under which assessee was to get 3 annas share from 'R' out of his 14 annas share in managing agency remuneration earned by aforesaid firm - Whether amount received by assessee from 'R' did not represent managing agency remuneration payable by mills to managing agents - Held, yes - Whether amount received by assessee was a mere receipt of income by assessee under a valid contract entered into by it with 'R' - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, in view of aforesaid, Tribunal was right in holding that terms of document did not create either a partnership in law or an AOP - Held, yes

Section 28(i)  of the Income-tax Act 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee firm was agent of ‘HML’ - It assigned its agency rights to ‘P’ which agreed to pay part of its profits subject to minimum sum per annum - Subsequently, by another agreement, assessee transferred its rights under assignments to ‘O’ for lump sum consideration - Whether by second agreement assessee had parted with its profits making apparatus and, therefore, amount recived by it from ‘O’ was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act - Business income - Compensation for termination of agency - Whether provisions of section 28(ii)(d) are attracted in such a case where not only the management is taken over but all assets and business are also taken and compensation given for the same - Held, no

Section 4 of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee A, was promoter and who proprietor of managing director of company and all its shares were held by him and two others - He was entitled to receive in addition to monthly remuneration 1/10th share of surplus profits of company in terms of articles of association - A under an agreement with one G, agreed to transfer all his shares to G and that he would cease to render services to company as mentioned in article of association and would also forgo his right to receive share of profits of company in consideration of payment of Rs. 1 lac - Whether article of association not merely created obligation as part of assessee to serve and to receive remuneration for services rendered but also created a right of lasting and enduring nature in favour of assessee and, therefore, consideration received for releasing such right as condition of sale was capital receipt not taxable in hands of assessee - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1944-45 - Appellant company appointed a firm as its managing agent for 20 years at 2½ per cent commission - Though firm was not guilty of negligence, laches, fraud or inefficience, appellant terminated managing agency after two years and for this paid certain amount to said firm as compensation - Appellant, however, appointed another managing agent at 2 per cent commission - Whether disbursement of compensation to outgoing managing agent was of capital nature and was, therefore, not deductible expenditure - Held, yes

Section 12B(1) of the indian income-tax act, 1922 [corresponding to section 45 of the income-tax act, 1961]-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessment year 1962-63-Assessee retired from firm and as per terms of settlement received his sharb in value of firm's net assets representing difference between their book value and market value-Whether impugned receipt was not assessable as capital gains since the transaction did not involve any element of sale or extinguishment of rights-Held, on facts, yes

Section 10(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Casual and non-recurring receipt - Assessment year 1942-43 and 1944-45 - Assessee-company was incorporated with an object of carrying on business and trade of commission agents, insurance agents, commercial agents, etc. - Assessee invested certain amount with a newly incorporated sugar company with a condition that assessee was to be given managing agency in a company to be erected in future - That company, however, could not be erected - During relevant accounting years assessee sold shares acquired by it and made certain profit - Whether object of assessee in buying shares in sugar company was purely to obtain managing agency of new mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from inception no intention whatever on part of assessee to re-sell shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them - Held, yes - Whether therefore investment of money in purchase of shares was of a capital nature and profits arising out of sale of shares were of a capital nature and were not liable to tax - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1949-50 - Assessee-company had managing agency agreement with another company S Ltd. - Remuneration payable by assessee-company was monthly allowance of Rs. 3,000 plus 25 per cent of its annual net profit - Directors desired to terminate managing agency agreement and wrote to S Ltd. on 1-8-1948 about termination and waiver of right to 25 per cent commission earned during year ending 31-3-1948 in consideration of lumpsum of Rs. 1,25,000 - That was accepted by both parties, managing agency came to an end and S. Ltd. were credited with Rs. 1,25,000 in assessee’s books of account - Whether since payment in question was made wholly and exclusively for purpose of business and, moreover, it did not result in acquisition of any capital asset, it was allowable under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 28(i) sections 45 and 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Compensation (Termination of agency) - Assessment year 2001-02 - 'Sea Land-India' was clearing and forwarding agent of 'Sea Land-USA' - Assessee was sub-agent of 'Sea Land-India' - As business of 'Sea Land-USA' was taken over by 'AP mollar', 'Sea Land-USA' terminated agency agreement with 'Sea Land-India' and 'Sea land-India' terminated sub-agency agreement with assessee - 'AP mollar' appointed 'Maersk' and 'Maersk' purchased shipping sub-agency business of assessee - Assessee offered consideration received by it on transfer of same as capital gains and claimed exemption under section 54EC - Assessing Officer completed assessment - Commissioner sought to revise assessment order on ground that amount was received in connection with termination of agency as stipulated in section 28(ii)(c) and exemption under section 54EC could not be claimed - Whether assessee was a recipient of impugned amount for holding an agency in India for activities relating to business of 'Sea Land-India' and it was received only in connection with termination of agency, and, therefore, Commissioner was justified in invoking section 263 - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 11] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where consideration received by assessee was only towards termination of agency, income received by assessee was to be treated as business income and not as capital gain

Section 28(1), read with section 15 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1), read with section 7 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1940-41 and 1941-42 - Assessee-firm was constituted with a view to float a company and obtain its managing agency - Accordingly a company was floated and assessee was given managing agency with right to receive monthly allowance, commission on sale and on profits of company - During relevant assessment years assessee-firm received income for working as managing agents as well as for working as sole agents of company - Assessee’s claimed that amount so received should be treated as salary and assessed under section 7 was rejected by ITO - Whether mere appointment as a managing agent or working as such would not necessarily make person a servant of company - Held, yes - Whether in case of a firm, which can be constituted only for purpose of sharing profits of a business, work of managing agency must be held to be business of firm - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profits which assessee-firm earned from their business of working as managing agents of company must be held to be their profits or gains from business, profession or vocation assessable to tax under section 10 of 1922 Act and not as salary under section 7 of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charge of tax - Capital or revenue receipt - Pursuant to a board resolution, assessee-company purchased shares of two other companies in order to secure managing agency of said companies - Having realized that managing agency of one of said companies could not be secured and that assessee would also be involved in misfeasance or misconduct of erstwhile managing agent of another company, assessee sold shares in very short span - Whether extra rate sanctioned and extra rate per share actually offered by assessee for purchase of shares would clearly indicate an object other than mere object of making profit in any of business from shares - Held, yes - Whether intention of company was to buy shares only with a view to acquiring controlling interest in said companies and, thereby acquiring its managing agency which would undoubtly be a capital asset - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gain accrued as a result would be on capital account - Held, yes

I. Section 28(i), read with section 4 , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company had received certain sum as compensation on account of termination of its agency and distributorship by GE group - It claimed said receipt as capital receipt - Assessing Officer, however, treated said sum as its business receipt and brought same to tax under section 28 on ground that GE group had control and management of assessee and that assessee was non-exclusive agent and distributor of GE group - Whether since on date of termination of agreement GE group was holding 50 per cent shareholding of assessee while other 50 per cent of shares were held by 'F', it could not be presumed that GE group had control over management of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, since further entire trained staff and customer network were taken over by GE and there was a restrictive covenant not to indulge in or to be associated with a similar business compensation received on account of termination of agency and distributorship agreements was a capital receipt which was not taxable as income from business or profession- Held, yes

SECTION 4 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CAPITAL OR REVENUE RECEIPT-WHETHER, IN VIEW OF FACTS MENTIONED UNDER 'BUSINESS INCOME-COMPENSATION FOR TERMINATION OF AGENCY', COMPENSATION RECEIVED BY ASSESSEE WOULD CONSTITUTE TAXABLE REVENUE RECEIPT-HELD, NO

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1950-51 - Whether on facts under head 'Business expenditure - Allowability of' amount voluntarily given up by managing agents and received as such by assessee could not be treated as receipt or income in hands of assessee and, hence, was not liable to income-tax - Held, yes

Section 17(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Salaries - Profits in lieu of salary - Assessment year 1984-85 - After resigning as director of a company, assessee started his own consultancy work - An agreement was entered into by company with assessee by which he agreed not to engage with other concerns having similar activities for a period of five years so that company’s secrets and technical knowledge gained by him may not be passed on to others - As a result of this, he was given Rs. 11 lakhs which he claimed as capital receipt - Assessing Officer held that amount was paid to assessee for services rendered by him during his employment and that resignation was made use of as a ploy to help him in getting huge sum without tax - Amount paid to assessee was, therefore, assessed as assessee’s income as ‘profits in lieu of salary’ - Whether assessee’s case was covered by ratio of decision of Supreme Court in McDowel & Co. v. CTO [1985] 154 ITR 148/22 Taxman 11 - Held, no - Whether, in absence of any material in support of reasoning given by Assessing Officer for subterfuge taxation of said amount as a revenue receipt or as ‘profit in lieu of salary’ was unjustified - Held, yes

Section 28(ii)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee-company under an agreement with an English company was appointed as a sole agent in regard to management of estates of English company in India - During relevant assessment year, that agency was terminated and certain sum was paid by way of compensation to assessee - Whether compensation amount was taxable in view of provisions of section 28(ii)(e) - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable - Block Period 1-4-1990 to 14-7-2000 - Where assessee had received a sum for relinquishing secretaryship of an educational society, amount received by assessee could not be treated as capital receipt since in forgoing life membership or secretaryship, there was no capital asset which had been transferred by assessee [In favour of revenue]

Section 17 (3)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 7(1), Explanation 2 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Salaries - Profits in lieu of salary - Assessment years 1939-40 and 1940-41 - Assessee joined an insurance company as manager at invitation of interim board of directors - Assessee was to receive salary and commission - Interim board of directors of insurance company was subsequently succeeded by new board of directors - Disputes arose between assessee and new board of directors and by agreement between those parties assessee’s services were terminated by board and in consideration he received certain amount as compensation for loss of employment - Said agreement recited that assessee ‘resigned’ his position of manager - Whether use of word “resigned” in agreement by which assessee’s services were terminated was clearly a euphemism for termination of employment under pressure and meant that assessee accepted annulment of his employment in consideration of what was stated in agreement - Held, yes - Whether payment made to assessee in consideration of termination of his employment did not include any remuneration for past services and must, therefore, be held to be solely compensation for loss of employment - Held, yes - Whether those payments were, therefore, exempt from income-tax under Explanation 2 to section 7(1) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether if there was an agreement enuring for a period of years and by mutual consent agreement is cancelled and payment is made, such payment would be regarded as capital payment - Held, yes - Assessee was sole distributor of oil expellers of a C  Co. - Under terms of agency agreement he was prohibited from dealing in any other Indian or foreign firm - Agreement was to be in force for six years to be continued automatically after giving notice - That agency was terminated due to suits and counter suits between parties - Finally, they reached a compromise - One of terms of compromise was that C  Co. would supply four expellers free of price to assessee worth Rs. 40,000 - Whether amount was paid to assessee as compensation for cessation of agency business, which it had with C  Co. and, therefore amount was to be regarded as capital receipt which could not be treated as income for purpose of taxation - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1948-49 to 1950-51 - Assessee had acted as agents and distributors of explosives manufactured by principal company but without a written agreement - Subsequently, principal company terminated agency and paid Compensation to assessee - Assessee claimed exemption contending that said amount was compensation for termination of agency and for agreeing to refrain from carrying on in future substantive business in explosives - Whether circumstances that agency was determinable at will of principal company which maintained a large staff at their expense justified inference that upon cancellation of agency, assessee's business organization was not substantially impaired - Held, yes - Whether since cancellation of contract of agency did not affect profit-making structure of assessee, nor did it involve a loss of an enduring trading asset, rather it merely deprived assessee of a trading avenue, leaving it free to devote its energies after cancellation to carry on rest of business, compensation in question did not represent price paid for loss of a capital asset - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee's claim was to be disallowed - Held, yes

Section 15, read with section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 7, read with section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Salary - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1941-42 - Assessee was managing agent in a company and his remuneration was fixed at 15 per cent of net profits of company or a monthly pay whichever he liked - During relevant previous year, assessee elected to receive his remuneration at 15 per cent of net profits of company - ITO treated his remuneration as business profit - Tribunal found though assessee was called as managing agent, powers conferred upon him under articles were more in nature of powers given to servant and that those powers could be terminated and managing agency agreement itself put an end to, as was decided on by certain resolutions passed by board at time when managing agent was appointed - Thus, Tribunal held that amount received by assessee was salary and not business income - Whether on facts, order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1954-55 - Assessee's business consisted of operating certain scheduled air services in India and Pakistan - Business affairs of assessee were managed by ATL, managing agents of assessee, who was appointed for a period of 20 years at a certain remuneration and commission - Business of assessee was taken over by Indian Airlines Corporation with effect from 1-8-1953 under Air Corporation Act, over, 1953 - Prior to takeover, in accordance with recommendation of board of directors and shareholders of assessee, certain sum was paid to ATL for termination of managing agency and also to 'K' for termination of his services as managing director - Whether payment to managing agent was dictated by any idea of furthering business of assessee - Held, no - Whether sole motive behind payment to managing director could only be one of giving a gratuity for services rendered in past and further managing director did not have a contract of service for a particular period and he had no expectation of reasonable gratuity, payment made to him was not expenditure deductible under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, payments made to managing agents and managing director were not allowable under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

facts.text:
The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee was a managing agent of a company F. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company and to procure that principal company 'M' also agreed to compensate the assessee for loss of office after it submitted its resignation.

Subsequently, the assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of the company. Accordingly, the assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office. In the proceedings for the relevant assessment year the ITO, included this amount in the assessee's taxable income. On appeal the AAC modified the assessment holding that the sum received by the assessee as compensation for surrendering the managing agency, which was to enure for five years more, and which in normal course might have continued for another term of twenty years, was a capital receipt. On further appeals Tribunal confirmed the order of the AAC. On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

An incorporated limited liability company 'L' had a subscribed capital consisting of preference shares, ordinary shares and deferred shares. The assessee-company became the managing agents of said company under an agreement. Subsequently, the assessee acquired its ordinary shares and preference shares. On 10-10-1947, the assessee made a further acquisition of some deferred shares. Thereafter, the assessee agreed to make over its managing agency to 'K'. The terms included that 'K' should take over the deferred shares and also pay the assessee a further sum of certain amount as compensation for loss of future remuneration to the assessee as managing agent. The assessee sold during the relevant assessment year, the ordinary and preference shares which resulted in a loss. After adjusting this loss on the extra amount received on the sale of deferred shares, there was a net profit. The assessee did not return the amount as its income for the year on the ground that it was a capital receipt. The revenue disagreed and brought the amount to tax treating it as income. The Tribunal concurred with that view. It also declined to a make a reference.

On application under section 66(2):

The assessee-company had held two-third shares of company A and was also its managing agent. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold all these shares to company B at a profit of Rs. 3,14,519 and claimed that the surplus realised was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains. The ITO took the view that the assessee had acquired these shares to procure the managing agency and it had, in fact, carried on multifarious activities in various lines including banking, financing of various companies as well as managing agency. He, accordingly, held that the entire profit from the sale of these shares represented business profit. On appeal, the AAC held that a major portion of the sale proceeds was relatable to the assessee's right to the managing agency which passed along with the shares. He further held that in view of the numerous agencies which the assessee carried on, this transaction involving the giving up of the managing agency was of a revenue nature. Consequently, the AAC upheld the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the assessee had parted with an asset of enduring nature and observed that nothing had been received by the assessee as price for its foregoing managing agency rights. What it had legally received was the value of the shares though it could not be denied that it received a higher value because the shares carried with it the managing agency rights. Further, the Tribunal was of the view that it was concerned with the true and legal realisation resulting from the transaction which appeared to be that of the sale of shares and that the shares were not the assessee's stock-in- trade It, accordingly, held that the impugned profit was liable to be taxed as capital gains and not as revenue gains.

On reference:

The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

On reference :

The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was appointed as the managing agents of the K Mills Ltd. under a managing agency agreement entered into in 1935. One C entered into an agreement with the assessee on 8-1-1955, whereby the assessee agreed to sell or to procure for C 2,500 shares of K Mills before a specified date. Another term of this agreement was that the assessee should resign its managing agency of the K Mills Ltd. and that a consideration of Rs. 2,24,000 should be paid therefor to the assessee by C. It was common ground that the terms of the agreement were fulfilled and that the resignation of the assessee-firm was also accepted by the board of directors of the K Mills Ltd. In the return of the assessee for the calendar year relevant to the assessment year 1955-56, the above receipt of Rs. 2,24,000 was not returned as part of the income. The ITO applied section 10(5A) and called upon the assessee to show cause why the said amount should not be included in the total income of the relevant year ending on 31-3-1955. The assessee objected contending that there was no termination of the managing agency agreement by the managed company and that the payment having been made by a third party and not by the principals, the amount was not compensation within the meaning of the Act. A further objection advanced was that since the amount was received on 8-1-1955, and since the previous year of the assessee was the calendar year, this amount could not be brought to assessment in the assessment year 1955-56. These objections were overruled. On the first question, the departmental authorities and the Tribunal came to the conclusion that section 10(5A) applied and that the amount was taxable. On the second question, the ITO was of the view that the previous year for a business "which had no books of account which were not made up to profit and loss account for any particular period" should be the financial year. So that, since the amount was received in the financial year ending on the 31-3-1955, it was assessable in the assessment year 1955-56. The appeal to the Tribunal on this point also failed.

On reference :

In the course of its varied business activities, the assessee-company took up the managing agencies of plantation companies, to which the assessee also acted as secretaries. Whenever a managing agency was terminated, as for example when the plantations were sold and the plantation company itself wound up its operations the assessee was paid compensation, the quantum of which was decided by agreement. In 1945-46, the assessee-company held such managing agencies for sixteen plantation companies. T, was one of such plantation companies, and the agreement between that company and the assessee was in 1937. In 1945, T sold its plantation, which was in India, and the company subsequently went into liquidation. In accordance with a resolution passed by T, assessee received certain amount on 30-6-1946. That amount was treated as a trading receipt to the Department for the purpose of assessment to income-tax, excess profits tax and business profits tax. When the assessee appealed to the Tribunal it purported to apply the principles laid down by this Court in CIT v. South Indian Pictures Ltd. [1951] 20 ITR 605 and upheld the claim of the assessee, that this sum constituted a capital receipt not liable to tax.

On reference :

The assessee was one of the two managing directors of a private limited company T. Ltd. The other managing director was one 'P'. Out of the total of 20 shares of Rs. 100 each, the assessee held nine shares and his son one share, the remaining shares being held by 'P', his wife and cousin. This company was the managing agent of a public limited company A Ltd. Both these companies had been incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The public limited company had issued 11,986 shares of the face value of Rs. 100 each, out of which the assessee held, 1,674 shares. The assessee and his son transferred ten shares in T. Ltd. to 'P', his wife and cousin or their nominees for Rs. 3,50,000 as also 4,165 shares in the A Ltd.

By the transfer two sets of shares the assessee made a profit of Rs. 3,14,100 in respect of nine shares and another sum of Rs. 72,515 in respect of 1,674 shares. These two amounts were brought to tax for the assessment year 1956-57 treating them as income and liable to tax under section 10(5A) of 1922 Act. Both the ITO as well as the AAC repelled the assessee's contention that the receipts were in the nature of capital assets by sale of the shares. The AAC accepted the view that the amounts in excess of the book value of the shares transferred by the assesses were in the nature of inducement to him or compensation for giving up the management.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was neither a manager nor a managing agent of an Indian company within the meaning of section 2(9A) of the Indian Companies Act and that the provisions of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act were, therefore, not applicable to the two amounts.

The Tribunal also considered the further question whether the two amounts could be regarded as compensation for loss of management rights in A. Ltd. and came to the conclusion that there was no material to hold that the profit represented such compensation.

On reference:

The assessee was a private limited company. In 1944, the assessee purchased the managing agency of certain company for Rs. 6 lakhs and thereafter entered into a separate managing agency agreement with the managed company for a period of seventeen years. The assessee's only source of income was this managing agency in the relevant year. M, one of the shareholders of the assessee, and his group also held among themselves 25,000 ordinary and 10,000 preference shares of that company. M entered into an agreement for sale of these shares with one 'K' for a consideration of Rs. 45 lakhs; one of the terms of the agreement was that M would have the managing agency of the assessee terminated. In implementation of this agreement, M wrote to the assessee on 21-10-1953, asking it to give up the managing agency in lieu of Rs. 10 lakhs as compensation. The assessee accepted M's offer and tendered its resignation of its office as managing agents. The assessee credited the amount of compensation in its capital reserve account. In the assessment year 1955-56, the ITO assessed the entire amount of Rs. 10 lakhs in the hands of the assessee under section 10(5A).

On appeal, the AAC held that section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act created a new source of income for which the previous year was not the previous year for the managing agency business which ended on 30-6-1954, that the compensation of Rs. 10 lakhs which the assessee received in October, 1953, fell in the financial year 1953-54, which would be the previous year for this income for which the assessment year was 1954-55, which was before sub-section (5A) of section 10 of the 1922 Act was enacted, and the fact that the assessee had entered the amount in its books for the year that ended on 30-6-1954, Could not be taken as an exercise of option by the assessee accepting the said year as the previous year in respect of the receipt. On second appeal, the Tribunal was of opinion that section 10(5A) of the 1922 Act only regarded the compensation received by the managing agent as profits and gains of a business and does not create a fresh source therefore, and as the amount in question in this case was received in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1955-56, it was taxable in the assessment year 1955-56.

On reference, the High Court overruled the contention of the assessee that the amount in question was income from a new source for which the previous year was 1953-54.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:—

The assessee company carried on business in hides and skins, minerals, tobacco and other commodities, and also acted as managing agents for the 'N' and for two other companies. 'T', 'M' and 'C' were directors of the company. The assessee was appointed by the Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and in accordance with the directions issued from time to time and agreed to pay to the assessee price of the tobacco purchased, charge at the rate of one anna per 1b. for tobacco not redried, and at the rate of two annas per 1b. for tobacco redried, and commission on all purchases. Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, inspecting tobacco at Guntur and at Madras Port, and for supervising shipment of tobacco, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of the net profit as remuneration. Under the contract with the Government of India, certain amount became due to the assessee as commission in the account year ending 31-3-1952. After providing for expenses, 30 per cent of the balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed in the assessment year 1952-53 as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act. On 28-12-1950 the managed company passed a resolution modifying the terms of the managing agency agreement in regard to the commission and added a proviso that for the years 1950 and 1951 if the directors of the company having regard to the result of the working were of the opinion that a lesser remuneration than that given in the agreement should be paid to the managing agents then the directors would have the right, in their absolute discretion, to fix such lesser remuneration payable either by way of lump sum or at a reduced percentage rate. The said modification had been agreed to by the managing agents. The managed company, on 8-4-1951, resolved that the managing agents should be paid Rs. 1,00,000 less than the commission calculated at the rates mentioned in the original agreement and on 31-12-1950, an entry to that effect was made in the books of the company. The income-tax authorities held that entire sum of commission which the assessee was entitled under the original agreement, was taxable income having accrued as commission during previous year and that Rs. 1,00,000 was mere voluntary surrender which could not affect the taxability of whole amount of commission accruing to managing agents. On appeal, the Tribunal held that as a result of the agreement between the managing agents and the managed company the right of the managing agents to claim full remuneration, had been taken away as from 1-1-1950, and it was not a voluntary relinquishment on the part of the managing agents and, therefore, the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 out of the commission due according to the original agreement was not income in the hands of the managing agents which was liable to taxation. On reference, the High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal.
