had been received by the assessee for covenants which had caused impairment to the income-earning apparatus of the assessee and for sterilisation and destruction of a capital asset as it was not to carry on a particular line of business, i.e., distribution of soft drinks for a particular period due to which it was deprived of a source of income. The covenants affected or impaired the trading structure itself of the assessee and thus, it was a capital receipt. [Para 21] Section 28(ii) specifically deals with compensation for general termination of agency or modification of terms and conditions relating thereto. These provisions were brought in only in the context of managing agency agreements. The assessee in its own right distributed products bottled by ‘S’ in pursuance of a distribution agreement, which definitely was not an agency agreement. The first appellate authority had observed that invoking of the provisions of section 28 by the Assessing Officer was not relevant as the assessee was not a management agent nor the agreement with ‘S’ was an agency agreement. Thus, the receipt in question would not fall within the net of section 28(ii) and was for restrictive covenant and the agreement had resulted in the entire business structure of the assessee in line of soft drinks distribution being impaired or destroyed. Therefore, what the assessee received was a compensation for loss of its source of business and not compensation for loss of income or profit and, thus, it was a capital receipt not exigible to tax. [Para 26]

The perception of the Assessing Officer that there was no requirement for ‘B’ to pay consideration for goodwill to the assessee-company as it was a mere transporter and not a distributor and dealer in soft drinks was not borne out by record or evidence. On the contrary, the statistics submitted by the assessee showed that it was marketing products of ‘S’ as distributor and there was substantial improvement in the business of the assessee. Further, the agreement of goodwill showed that ‘B’ acknowledged the fact that the assessee-company had goodwill and had agreed to pay for the same. The basis on which such goodwill was to be quantified was given in the agreement itself. The Assessing Officer could not simply state that he disbelieved the agreement, as in his perception there was no goodwill whatsoever, that too without any rhyme or reason. Hence, the observation made by the Assessing Officer that the agreement in question was a make-believe agreement was without an iota of evidence. Thus, the order of the appellate authority to tax amount of goodwill under capital gain was to be upheld. [Paras 27 and 29]

Section 50(2) refers to block of assets ceasing to exist as such by reason of transfer of the entire ‘block of assets’. The term ‘block of assets’ is defined in section 2(11) and comprises of certain tangible as well as intangible assets, but the primary requirement is that the rate of depreciation has to be prescribed, i.e., in other words, the asset should be a depreciable asset, e.g., ‘land’ does not fall within purview of ‘block of assets’ though it is a tangible asset. Thus, an amount received for a restrictive covenant cannot be said to have been received for transfer of an asset which forms ‘part of a block of assets’. The Assessing Officer had not stated as to how he considered the receipts as those which were received for transfer of ‘block of assets’ nor had he given any finding that in fact, after the transaction, there were no more assets left in the block. Without a factual finding that the block of assets ceased to exist, section 50(2) cannot be invoked. Even if it was taken as a capital asset, in view of the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Ambica Chemical Production v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal No. 238/V/2002, dated 26-5-2005] no tax was leviable in terms of section 45 on the amount received by the assessee. [Para 30]

Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was upheld. [Para 32]

The assessee-company was carrying on business as managing agents of two companies. The assessee was also a recognised share dealer and an investor in shares. For the assessment year 1957-58 the assessment of assessee included a sum of Rs. 43,190 as the profit on the sale of shares of a company. These shares, according to the assessee, were not acquired for the purpose of dealing in them but were received from its managed company in respect of managing agency commission. The assessment was confirmed on appeal by the AAC but on second appeal the Tribunal held that the difference between the price at which the shares were sold and the cost of the shares did not arise in the course of the assessee's business activity and, therefore, the profits were not taxable.

Another item included in the assessment was Rs. 31,355 which had been realised on the sale of the right to subscribe for the shares of a company.

The contention raised by the assessee before the ITO was that the sum of Rs. 31,455 was a receipt of a casual and non-recurring nature and as such was not taxable. In the alternative the assessee maintained that the realisation of Rs. 31,355 could be held not under the heading 'business' but as 'capital gains'. The assessee's contention was rejected by the ITO who included this amount in the taxable income as 'business income' and the AAC on appeal upheld the order of the ITO. The Tribunal held that the said sum was not income and, therefore, not taxable. The ITO served on 9-3-1962, a notice under section 34(1)(b) of 1922 Act alleging that he had reason to believe that the assessee's income for the assessment year 1957-58 had escaped assessment and had been under-assessed and, therefore, he proposed to reassess the said income.

of grant under the notified order was relatable to the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Saurashtra Grants (Resumption) Ordinance, 1949, which empowered the Government of the State of Saurashtra, inter alia, to resume the grant and to provide for incidental and consequential matters. In this background, it could never be said that the assessee had purchased income by surrendering his capital asset, viz., ‘jagir’ under the said grant. Such resumption had the effect of the capital asset of the assessee, which was an income producing estate, being lost to the assessee and in lieu of such capital loss, the reimbursement was being made by providing for payment of a determined amount only during the life-time of the assessee. This payment was clearly intended to compensate for the loss to the assessee, which was caused by virtue of his capital estate being taken over under the resumption order warranted by the said Ordinance. These annual instalments though described as cash annuity, were, when the substance of the transaction was looked at, not income, but were only intended to be payments towards the loss of the income-producing assets of the assessee and, therefore, they were capital receipts. It could be noted that these periodic payments described as cash annuity were required to be debited by the Government under the head ‘76. Other Misc. Compensation and Assignment - A-2 pension in lieu of Resumed Lands’. Thus, even the Government treated it as compensation, which was being paid to the assessee in lieu of the resumption of lands included in the Jagir granted to the assessee under the said grant. Further, it would be reasonable to assume that since the payments were required to be made under the resumption order, simultaneously on resumption of the grant they were in reality intended to compensate the assessee for the loss of his capital asset, i.e., the ‘jagir’. The true quality of the payment clearly showed that the payment though described as cash annuity was not annuity in the sense of purchase of income, but it was annual payment of compensation to the assessee for the loss of his income-producing asset. These payments were, therefore, clearly capital receipts in the hands of the assessee and could never be termed as income. Such capital receipts would not be taxable except as capital gains and any tax on such capital receipts would amount to taxing the capital, which is not the intention of the income-tax law.

Moreover, where a voluntary payment is made entirely without consideration and is not traceable to any source which a practical man may regard as a real source of income, but depends entirely on the whim of the donor, such payment cannot fall in the category of income. Therefore, even if the amount was paid under the resumption order voluntarily and without any consideration, and was not traceable to any real source of income depending entirely on the pleasure of the Government, such payment would not fall in the category of income.

Therefore, the Tribunal committed an error in holding that the cash annuity in the resumption of two villages was an income and not capital receipt in the hands of the assessee.

Moreover, where a voluntary payment is made entirely without consideration and is not traceable to any source which a practical man may regard as a real source of income, but depends entirely on the whim of the donor, such payment cannot fall in the category of income. Therefore, even if the amount was paid under the resumption order voluntarily and without any consideration, and was not traceable to any real source of income depending entirely on the pleasure of the Government, such payment would not fall in the category of income.

Therefore, the Tribunal committed an error in holding that the cash annuity in the resumption of two villages was an income and not capital receipt in the hands of the assessee.

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a firm. The said firm by agreement dated 7-9-1946 sold shares in a company together with the managing agency right of said company which it was holding to another firm for an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share, though the market value at the time was Rs. 46 per share. The department held that for purposes of computation of capital gains of assessee partner, the sale price of each share should be taken at Rs. 65 while the assessee contended that the market value of Rs 46 should be taken into account. The Tribunal upheld the decision of the department.

On reference:

HELD: The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

FACT: The assessee-company appointed ‘C’ as its managing agents in 1938 for a period of thirty years on a monthly remuneration besides ten per cent commission on net yearly profits of the company. Subsequently, in August 1941, Company ’J’ was appointed as its managing agents of the assessee instead of ‘C’. On 19-11-1952, the board of directors decided to terminate the managing agency agreement of ‘C’ and a resolution was passed to this effect by the extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders. The managing agents wrote back that the resolution constituted a breach of the contract of the managing agency and lodged a claim for compensation. The dispute was settled against certain payment which was approved in the extra ordinary general meeting of the assessee. For the assessment year 1952-53, the assessee claimed deduction of aforesaid amount as business expenditure. The ITO held that whole affairs was so hastily planned as to give an odour "of the pre-planned camouflage" and that the sum paid to the managing agents was a sort of solatium not admissible as a revenue business expenditure. However, on appeal, the AAC allowed the assessee’s claim. The order of AAC was confirmed by the Tribunal.

On reference:

HELD: The concepts of capital and revenue expenditure are not defined anywhere in the statute, but there is no dearth of guidelines indicated by eminent judges in reported decisions both in England and in India.

In the instant case the assessee was not forced with any immediate or present danger to be averted, neither any financial problem confronted the board of directors for terminating the managing agency agreement nor was any economic difficulty to be surmounted by adopting this course. Plainly, the directors compounded a consolidated claim of the managing agents whose services were terminated apparently without any cause and the amount was paid for this purpose which, undoubtedly, resulted in an enduring benefit, from the economic point of view, for the assessee. Considering that the agreement which was being terminated was assignable and no managing agents were appointed to succeed in place of company ‘J’, there was brought into existence a clear advantage of an enduring nature, an advantage indistinguishable from a material or fixed asset for the assessee.

In this view of the matter, the assessee’s contention must fail and it was held that the payment of made to ‘C’ was not a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act, in the hands of the assessee.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

The third mill was, however, not erected and the agreement about acquiring the managing agency fell through. The managing director died in December 1940, and the assessee decided to sell all the shares in 1941. The excess amount realized on sale of these shares was taxed by the ITO, as revenue receipts, the first in the assessment year 1942-43 and the second in 1944-45. The assessee-company's contention that the excess was in the nature of capital appreciation was not accepted. This order was confirmed by the AAC and the Tribunal.

On reference the High Court answered the question in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: The exact nature of the business which the assessee was doing was admittedly not clear from the record but it was not denied that the memorandum of association of the assessee did not authorise it to purchase and/or sell shares as dealers nor was it denied that beyond this isolated transaction of purchase and sale the assessee did not deal in shares. It seemed that the object of the assessee in buying shares was purely to obtain the managing agency of the third mill which no doubt would have been an asset of an enduring nature and would have brought them profits but there was from the inception no intention whatever on the part of the assessee to re-sell the shares either at a profit or otherwise deal in them. Naturally when the third mill was not erected and the object of securing the managing agency became impossible of fulfilment, the assessee withdrew the shares and sold them at a profit. After conceding that the taking up of the shares by the assessee in the sugar company was an essential part of the arrangement arrived at, the only reasonable conclusion to which the High Court should have come was that the investment of the money in the purchase of shares was of a capital nature and the profits arising out of the sale of the shares in the circumstances of this case were accretions to capital and were not liable to tax.

Accordingly, the decision of the High Court was to be reversed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

As held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chari and Chari Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 400/[1965] 3 SCR 692 (SC), that ordinarily compensation for loss of office or agency is regarded as a capital receipt, but this rule is subject to an exception that payment received even for termination of an agency agreement would be revenue and not capital in the case where the agency was one of many which the assessee held and its termination did not impair the profit-making structure of the assessee, but was within the framework of the business, it being a necessary incident of the business that existing agencies may be terminated and fresh agencies may be taken. But it is for the income-tax department to clearly establish that the case fell within the exception to the ordinary rule. In the instant case, according to the findings of the Tribunal, the termination of the agency in question had resulted in the destruction of a source of income of the assessee company. The Tribunal had arrived at the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee company represented the source from which it received its income by way of commission.

In the determination of the question whether a receipt is capital or income, it is not possible to lay down any single test as infallible or any single criterion as decisive. The question must ultimately depend on the facts of the particular case, and the authorities bearing on the question are valuable only as indicating the matters that have to be taken into account in reaching a decision. That, however, is not to say that the question is one of fact, for these questions between capital and income, trading profit or non-trading profit, are questions which, though they may depend to a very great extent on the particular facts of each case, do involve a conclusion of law to be drawn from those facts.

Applying the tests laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Kettlewell Bullen & Co. v. CIT [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC), as found by the Tribunal, the receipt must be considered as a capital receipt.

Note: The case was decided against the revenue.

The primary significance of the word "compensation" is "equivalence" and the secondary or more common meaning is "something given or obtained as an equivalent". The large number of ways in which this expression "compensation" has been interpreted has one common factor running through them all, that is, that compensation is regarded as an equivalent or recompense, that which makes good the lack of variation of something else. Flowing from this concept, the enlargement of the meaning of this expression takes in that which compensates for loss or privation, amends, remunerates or recompenses. Therefore the contention of the assessee that, unless and until the amount received by the assessee could be regarded as compensation, in the light of a recompense for a right which the managed company wilfully deprived the assessee of, it could not come within the scope of section 10(5A) , could not be accepted. Even apart from this argument raised upon the precise significance of the expression "compensation", the relevant section takes in both compensation or other payments. While it may be true that compensation in the special sense will certainly come within the scope of the provision, any other payment which was received by the managing agent "at or in connection with the termination" of his managing agency agreement is also within the mischief of the section. It is not necessary that the agency agreement should have been terminated by the managed company. If the payment is received at or in connection with the termination, that would be sufficient for the purpose of bringing it to tax under the Act. It could not be denied that it was so received. Therefore, the sum of Rs. 2,24,000 was rightly held taxable.

As to the question whether the receipt could be brought to tax in the assessment for the assessment year 1955-56, from the statement of the case of the Tribunal, it was clear that originally the previous year adopted by the assessee was the period ending on the 15th of March and from 1938-39 assessment till 1940-41, a change was allowed in the accounting year which ended on the 31st of July. Once again in 1941-42, there was a change in the previous year and this time it was the year ending with the 31st of December. It was clear that the previous year of the assessee was the calendar year. The disputed receipt was on 8-1-1955, that is, the calendar year 1955, relevant to the assessment year 1956-57.

The main part of section 10(5A) refers to any compensation or other payment received by a managing agent at or in connection with the termination of the managing agency agreement. If the managing agency was the business carried on by the assessee and its termination resulted in this receipt, it was not clear why this receipt should not be related to that source, viz., the managing agency itself. It was true that it could not be stated to be income, profits or gains of a business carried on, because it was not the carrying on of the business of the managing agency that gave rise to this receipt. But, undoubtedly, the source of this receipt was the managing agency business.

By the fiction embodied in section 10(5A) it is brought to tax as a revenue receipt and in addition is impressed with the character of the profits and gains of a business carried on by the managing agent, there was no obstacle to holding that this receipt must necessarily be correlated to the source from which it was deprived, which was the managing agency business; and if that was so, the previous year relevant to this receipt could not be a previous year different from the one relevant to the managing agency business itself. The source of this receipt was the managing agency itself, though it arose on the termination of the managing agency agreement, and it is the source that is important for determining the previous year. That during the calendar year 1955 the assessee was carrying on the business of managing agency up to 8-1-1955, was beyond question. During part of the year the managing agency itself was carried on and the profits and gains of that business would be assessable to tax in the assessment year 1956-57; and since this sum of Rs. 2,24,000, was derived from that very source, the same previous year as for the business must be adopted for this receipt as well.

In view of the above, the sum of Rs. 2,24,000 was rightly, includible in the taxable income of the assessee, but that it could not be brought to assessment in the assessment year 1955-56.

Note : The case was decided partly against assessee and partly in his favour.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

There was no evidence to come to conclusion, that one of the lines of the business of the assessee-company was to promote companies and to sell out after the companies had been formed. Nor was it one of the regular lines of business of the assessee-company to acquire licences or permits and sell them. Nor even was it a regular line of business of the assessee-company to acquire managing agencies and sell them.

The licence obtained by the partnership, of which the assessee-company was a member, was a valuable asset and a capital asset in its hands. That capital asset was sold for a sum out of which the assessee received, its share of the receipt. It was capital receipt in its hands, and, therefore, the Assistant Commissioner was right in taking in view that being a capital receipt it fell within the scope of section 12B of 1922 Act. It was not assessable to tax as a trading receipt. Therefore, the claim of the assessee, that it was entitled to the benefit of section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act, was erroneous. It was in connection with the business activities of the assessee that the assessee received the sum. That it was a capital receipt in its hand did not make it any the less income from business, and it certainly could not be treated as something of a casual receipt or windfall.

Therefore, the amount in question was assessable to tax as capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act.

The assessee held large number of shares in a company, in his own name as also in the name of some members of his family. The assessee was also the chairman of the Board of Directors of the company. Under an agreement the assessee transferred the shares held by him and his family to an individual and also delegated to him such power or powers as were vested in him for the purpose of carrying on business of the company. The consideration received by the assessee for the entire transaction exceeded the face value of the aforementioned shares, and the ITO treated the entire difference as capital gains on the sale of the shares and brought it to tax under section 12B of the 1922 Act, overruling the assessee's objection that the amount of such difference could not be treated and taxed as capital gains in its entirety because the same had accrued from two sources, namely, from the value of the transfer of the shares and from the transfer of the office of the managing director. On appeal, the AAC and the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO. The Tribunal held that the price received by the assessee was the price for the sale of the shares and not the price for delegating the power of the office of managing director because even if it was assumed that the assessee delegated the power to the purchaser of shares he was not the competent authority under the Indian Companies Act, to delegate such power.

On reference:

The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

It was not the case of the Department and it had never been their case that the capital asset in respect of which capital gain was made by the assessee and which was sought to be taxed was the shares and the managing agency. The whole of the reference was based upon the fact that the only capital asset concerned with was the shares and not the managing agency. Therefore, one must separate the managing agency from the shares in considering what was the value to be put upon the shares. The parties had put upon the shares a value which was much higher than the market value. Admittedly, it was an artificial value and it was artificial because the value put upon the shares was not the value of the shares alone but it was the composite consideration paid by the purchasers for obtaining the shares and also acquiring the managing agency. Under the circumstances, for the purposes of section 12B(2) the sale price of the shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. 65 per share.

Note : The case was decided in favour of assessee.

Section 10 of the 1922 Act, indicates that tax is payable under the head of "business" in respect of the profits or gains of any business carried on by the assessee; and section 12 of the 1922 Act which deals with the residuary heading "other sources" expressed that the tax shall be payable in respect of "income, profits and gains of every kind and from every source to which the Act applies (if not included under any of the preceding heads)". If therefore, a payment comes under clause (vii) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, it is not covered by section 12 at all.

In the instant case, the assessee-company had several – managing agencies. The assessee was given the said sum of money because, without notice the them, in the middle of the year, one of their managing agencies was being brought to a close. In the circumstances, it was thought right to give the assessee this amount by way of compensation for their sudden dismissal. It was impossible to say that the receipt was not a receipt arising from business and that was the statutory test which had to be applied. It was not contended before the Commissioner that the instant case, if it did not come under section 10 of the 1922 Act, would not, apart from this exemption clause, be hit by section 12 of the 1922 Act. There was no doubt that the payment in the instant case was income within the meaning of section 12of the 1922 Act unless it was saved by section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act. In these circumstances, the Commissioner was right in deciding that the exemption relied on was of no use to the assessee and that income-tax was rightly assessed.

The provision of section 28(ii )(a) is meant for termination of managing agency or modification of terms or modes of appointment of employees or persons managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the Indian company. Once the person has already resigned from the managing directorship, the agreement entered into after a month of the event cannot be viewed as modification of the terms of appointment. [Para 6.1]

It is true that an item which is treated as capital in nature in the hands of the payer need not be capital but can be treated as revenue in the hands of the recipient. But in the instant case the very same payment under the same non-competition agreement entered into between the two parties had been treated as non-compete fee in the hands of the payer, but treated as payment received for modification of terms of appointment in the hands of the assessee (recipient). This was a peculiar stand that the very same department had taken while interpreting the very same document between the very same two parties in a different way while dealing with the assessments of the parties. In other words, the revenue could not blow hot and cold on the same situation. [Para 6.2]

The minutes of the meeting of the directors and the terms of the subsequent agreement for non-competition were all to be considered in the light of the above. If done so, it was to be treated as fees received for non-competition only and it could by no stretch of imagination be treated as payment received for modification of the terms and conditions of employment. Moreover, competition need not always be from outside only. On the other hand it could also be from within. The managing director of one company is not generally prohibited from being a director in some other company and render services as director of that other company. In the instant case, the assessee, was contemplating such association and only to restrict him from that this agreement was entered into by the company. So, there was no harm in the assessee continuing in the company without being a managing director. So, for that reason it need not be treated as taxable under section 28(ii)(a ). [Para 6.3]

Clause (va ) of section 28 along with proviso and Explanation was introduced only prospectively and not retrospectively. Hence, upto 1-4-2003 the amounts referred to in the clause (va) received by any assessee were not taxable under section 28(va). Thus, non-compete fee received by him was capital in nature not subject to income-tax. [Para 6.4]

Therefore, the amount received by the assessee was the outcome of the non-competition agreement in view of the restrictive covenant put on him for a period of five years and such amount received by the assessee for restrictive covenant was not to be subjected to income tax. In the result, the assessee’s appeal was to be allowed. [Para 6.5]

From the finding of the Tribunal, the following inferences seemed to be derivable : (1) That the receipt was compensation. (2) The compensation was for loss of anticipated profits. (3) The profits were to accrue by the operation of the Hind Roadways Corporation. (4) The loss was suffered by the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation at the instance of the Government.

On this premises which was clearly implied in the finding of the Tribunal, it appeared to be plain that the compensation was not for loss of profit of any business of the assessee but was to accrue out of a profit-making structure, viz., the corporation, of which the assessee was to be appointed the managing agent. With the abandonment of the scheme of the corporation, the prospect of the assessee becoming the managing agent of the corporation also vanished. Compensation was paid to him in lieu of the benefit which he might have derived by becoming the managing agent of the corporation. The corporation or the profit-making structure or the managing agency were only an asset of a capital nature. Compensation paid for the loss of a capital asset is not and cannot be taxable income. It followed that on the finding recorded by the Tribunal, the conclusion in law which it arrived at, namely, that "the amount was clearly taxable" was entirely erroneous.

The agency and distributorship agreements were entered into on 1-5-1991 and 31-10-1995, respectively, and were terminated vide agreements dated 1-7-1996 with retrospective effect from 31-10-1995 and 3-12-1995, respectively. As on the date of the termination of the agreement the GE group was holding 50 per cent shareholding of the company, while the other 50 per cent of the shares were held by 'F' Company, and, hence, it could not be presumed that the GE group had the control over the management of the assessee-company. [Para 14]

A perusal of the agency as well as distributorship agreements showed that the assessee was the non-exclusive agent and distributor of the GE group, but was not an agent simplicitor. It was not merely an intermediary between the principal and its customers but was expected to employ staff; promote the sale and also to maintain warehousing facility. Thus, it was carrying on the business of GE by creating its own infrastructure and for the said purpose it had made huge financial commitments; the assessee was not entitled to act on its own behalf and for itself in respect of the goods entrusted to it. Thus, there was a relationship of agency with GE and not on principal-to-principal basis, as contended by the assessee. As regards the assessee's contentions that since it had to make huge financial commitments, it was acting as a principal, it was found that all the expenses incurred by the agent in connection with the fulfilment of its obligations [like travel, correspondence, telephone, telecopy and the like] had been taken into account while fixing the rate of commission at 6 per cent on all the sales of the products initiated by the agent. Thus, it could not be said that the assessee was acting as the principal agent of GE. [Para 15]

Thus, it could be seen that the amount received for termination of agency was a taxable receipt. However, the nature of the receipt is to be seen before bringing it to tax under section 28(ii)(c ). If the receipt is on termination of the agreements of agency and distributorship simplicitor, the compensation received is for the loss of revenue and, hence, a revenue receipt. In such a case, the agent/distributor can carry on business of a similar nature with any other principal. But if there is a restrictive covenant to deal with similar business, then all the agreements have to be considered in unison and not in isolation. By the restrictive covenant the assessee is not only losing the revenue but is also losing the revenue-generating source. As held by the Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. Ambadi Enterprises Ltd. [2004] 267 ITR 702/139 Taxman 96, one test for ascertaining as to whether what had received was a capital receipt or a revenue receipt is to find out whether the assessee had snapped its link with the profit making apparatus that had been transferred. [Para 16]

In the instant case also, the entire trained staff and the customer network were taken over by the GE and there was a restrictive covenant not to indulge in or to be associated with a similar business. In view of the same, the compensation received on account of termination of the agency and distributorship agreements and for entering into the non-compete agreement was a capital receipt which was not taxable as income from business or profession. [Para 17]

The Tribunal found that the materials on record showed that there were two groups involved in the substantial ownership of the company. The assessee, who was the managing director, went out of the picture along with his group. The resolution dated 23-10-1967 clearly referred to the premature retirement of the assessee and the transfer of his shares while referring to the payment of Rs. 95,000. A finding was recorded by the Tribunal that the assessee and his group sold their shareholdings (majority interest) in the company at the time of the assessee’s retirement. Section 28(ii)(a ) deals with a case where any compensation or other payment, due to or received by any person, by whatever name called, managing the whole or substantially the whole of the affairs of the Indian company, at or in connection with the termination of his management or the modification of the terms and conditions relating thereto. Such income shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head ‘Profits and gains of business or profession’.

As the factual position noticed by the AAC and the Tribunal would show, the assessee and his group sold their shareholding (majority interest) in the company at the time of assessee’s retirement. The resolution dated 23-10-1967 also referred to the premature retirement of the assessee. The payment was not extricably linked with the services rendered by the assessee as an employee-director of the company, as observed by the Assessing Officer. On the contrary, the AAC recorded that there was some controversy between the two groups of shareholders and it was decided that in the interest of the company, one group of shareholders should part with the other group in the company. Accordingly, the group headed by the assessee together with other directors representing that group resigned. As a matter of fact, the decision of the Delhi High Court in the case of Ishwar Dass v. CIT [1980] 123 ITR 379/ 3 Taxman 476 helped the case of the assessee. In that case the effect of section 28(ii)( a) was not considered because such a plea was raised for the first time before the High Court while reference was being heard. Nevertheless, the High Court observed that there was force in the contention raised by the assessee about the applicability of section 28(ii)(a ). Not only that, the Court observed that, if law permitted, the assessee might prefer the claim under section 28 before any authority in accordance with law. While in civil actions, the expression ‘compensation’ may have peculiar significance, the expression as used in the Act does not appear to be susceptible to only that meaning and no other. The primary significance of the word ‘compensation’ is ‘equivalence’ and the secondary or more common meaning is ‘something given or obtained as an equivalent’. The large number of ways in which the expression ‘compensation’ has been interpreted has one common factor running through them all, that is, that compensation is regarded as an equivalent or recompense, that which makes good the lack of variation of something else. Flowing from this concept, the enlargement of the meaning of this expression takes in that which compensates for loss or provision, amends, remunerates or recompenses.

The Tribunal was, therefore, correct in law in holding that the amount of Rs. 95,000 received by the assessee during the year was to be assessed only under section 28(ii) and that thereby the assessee was entitled to the deduction under section 80S.

It was true that the real nature of the receipt in the instant case had got to be determined with reference to the facts and circumstances of the case and particularly the contents of article 29 of the articles of association and the agreement between the assessee and G. The assessee was a promoter and one of the three directors of the company IP, and he was also its managing director. As managing director he was receiving certain monthly salary and in addition it was agreed to under article 29 that he would get for the duration of the life of the company a 1/10th share of the surplus profits in consideration of the services rendered by him in promoting the company and to be rendered in future by way of obtaining films for exhibition for the company. Under the said article the assessee had a right, on his rendering such services as were specified therein, to obtain a 1/10th share in the profits of the company. The effect of the said article was not merely to create an obligation on the assessee to serve. From the said article sprang up rights as well as liabilities on either side. There was a right in the assessee to be entitled to profits on the rendering of services. There was undoubtedly an obligation to serve, but a contract of service, though it always involve an obligation on the party entering into service to serve, is not concerned only with the matter of obligation but involves a right to the service and the remuneration which the rendering of services is to bring. There was, therefore, not only an obligation to serve but also, considered from the opposite point of view, a right to the service in favour of the assessee. There was, on the other hand, an obligation on the company on services rendered by the assessee, which he was entitled to render, to give him a share of profit as specified in the said article.

If the assessee were not to render the services, which he was expected to render under the article, the company might have been able to resist making the payment to him as stipulated. But that did not mean that if the assessee was willing to render services the company could prevent him from so doing and absolve itself of the obligation to pay him a share in the profits. It was clear from the terms of this article, that the company had agreed to continue A to go on rendering services to it and had promised to remunerate him by paying a tenth of its surplus profits all throughout its life. Under these terms A had a right to the rendering of services and to be entitled to the remuneration as stipulated. That a right of a lasting and enduring nature was created in favour of A under the said article was clear from the subsequent agreement. If there was no right to service created under the article, there was no reason whatsoever why a payment of Rs. 1 lakh should have been offered for releasing that right. It was impossible to regard this payment of Rs. 1 lakh as remuneration for services, because no services were to be rendered. The payment was being made as a matter of fact for ceasing to render services and giving up the right to serve and receive payment. It was impossible, therefore, to regard the payment made in the instant case as a capitalised payment for remuneration. It was a payment for forgoing the right, which the assessee had under article 29 of the articles of association and which entitled him to have a 1/10th share of the profits of the company for the entire duration of the life of the company on the rendering of services. It is well settled that, although remuneration for services rendered is undoubtedly an income received, a compensation paid for the destruction of a contract of service or loss or termination of service is a payment of a capital nature. In the instant case the payment made to A was for the extinction of the contract of service, which he had under article 29 of the articles of association to serve the company for the duration of its life and receive remuneration at the rate of 1/10th of its surplus profits. Giving up the right under article 29 of the articles of association was an important and vital condition of the sale of the shares. It was not, therefore, that A was voluntarily agreeing to forgo his rights, but he was doing it as a part of the bargain for which he was being compensated by the payment that was being made to him.

It was, therefore, held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the amount of Rs. 1 lakh was not taxable as a revenue receipt.

When the remuneration or commission is expressed at so much per annum without anything more it would amount in law to a stipulation for the payment of remuneration per year and the servant would not be entitled to get any remuneration unless and until he has completely performed his contract and such performance would be a condition precedent to the recovery of any wages or salary for that definite period of service. That would be the position even if the remuneration was to accrue due and becomes vested at stated periods and unless the servant performed the condition and fulfilled his duty as a faithful servant down to that stipulated date or the stated period no salary would accrue due and become payable to him until at the end of such period of service. It is not the work done or the services rendered by the person but the income received or the income which has accrued to the person within the chargeable accounting period that is the subject-matter of taxation. That is the proper method of approach while considering the taxability or otherwise of income and no considerations of the work done for broken periods or contribution made towards the ultimate income derived from the source of income nor any equitable considerations can make any difference to the position which rests entirely on a strict interpretation of the provisions of section 4(1)(a ) of the 1922 Act.

Income may accrue to an assessee without the actual receipt of the same. If the assessee acquires a right to receive the income, the income can be said to have accrued to him though it may be received later on its being ascertained. The basic conception is that he must have acquired a right to receive the income. There must be a debt owed to him by somebody. There must be as is otherwise expressed debitum in praesenti, solvendum in futuro. Unless and until there is created in favour of the assessee a debt due by somebody it cannot be said that he has acquired a right to receive the income or that income has accrued to him.

In the instant case from the managing agency agreement it followed that the contract of service between the companies and the managing agents was entire and indivisible, that the remuneration or commission became due by the companies to the managing agents only on completion of a definite period of service and at stated periods, that it was a condition precedent to the recovery of any wages or salary in respect thereof that the service or duty should be completely performed, that such remuneration constituted a debt only at the end of each such period of service and that no remuneration or commission was payable to the managing agents for broken periods.

Sassoons had no doubt rendered services as managing agents of the companies for the broken periods. But unless and until they completed their performance, viz., the completion of the definite period of service of a year which was a condition precedent to their being entitled to receive by the remuneration or commission stipulated thereunder no debt payable by the companies was created in their favour and they had no right to receive any payment from the companies.

All that the transferees obtained under the deeds of assignment and transfer executed by the Sassoons in their favour was an income-bearing asset consisting of the office of the managing agents, the managing agency agreement and all the rights and benefits as such managing agents under the agreements and no part of the consideration paid by the transferees to the Sassoons could be allocated as a receipt of income by reason of their contribution towards the earning of the commission in the shape of services rendered by them as managing agents of the companies for the broken periods. What the transferees obtained under the deeds of assignment and transfer was the expectancy of earning a commission in the event of the condition precedent by way of complete performance of the obligation of the managing agents under the managing agency being fulfilled and a debt arising in favour of the managing agents at the end of the stated periods of service contingent on the ascertainment of net profits as a result of the working of the company during the calendar year.

The Sassoons had therefore, not earned any commission for the broken periods nor had any income accrued to them in respect of the same, and what they transferred to the transferees under the respective deeds of assignment and transfer did not include any income which they had earned or had accured to them and which the transferees by virtue of the assignment in their favour were in a position to collection.

When a partner retires, what he receives is his share in the partnership assets after deducting the liabilities. It is not consideration for transfer of his interest in the partnership to continuing partners. In the transaction of a retirement of a partner, just as in the case of a dissolution of partnership, there is no element of transfer. The transaction is in law an adjustment of the rights of the partners and not relinquishment or even extinguishments of interest of the retiring partners. Therefore, on the retirement of the assessee from the partnership firm no transfer of any capital asset took place within the meaning of section 45. There was hence no question of any income being chargeable to tax as capital gains.

Note : The decision was in favour of assessee.

Sassoon & Company (Sasoons) were the managing agents of three companies. The Sassoons transferred their managing agencies of the said companies to other companies. The Sassoons executed in favour of the transferee companies formal deeds of assignment and transfer and received from them the net consideration of Rs. 75,77,693. This was taken by them to the "Capital Reserve Account". The accounts of the managing agency commission payable by the respective companies to the managing agents for the year 1943 were made up in the year 1944 and the transferee companies received from managed companies certain amounts as and by way of such commission.

For the assessment year 1944-45 the original income-tax assessment of the Sassoons were made on a total income of Rs. 46,48,483. This income however did not include any part of the managing agency commission received by the transferees. The entire amounts of the managing agency commission received by the transferees were assessed by the ITO for the assessment year 1945-46 as the income of the transferees. The Tribunal accepted the transferees' contention that the managing agency commission received by them should be apportioned on a proportionate basis and the transferees should be made liable to pay tax only on the commission earned by them during the period that they had worked as the managing agents of the respective companies.

The ITO discovered that the amounts of the managing agency commission earned by the Sassoons prior to the dates of the respective transfers were not brought to tax and therefore issued on 29-6-1946, notice under section 34 of 1922, Act upon the Sassoons on the ground that their income from the managing agency had escaped assessment, the amount proposed to be included was Rs. 28,51,934. According to ITO, such managing agency commission had accrued to the Sassoons for services rendered upto the dates of transfers so that on the dates on which the agencies were transferred the Sassoons were entitled to such remuneration from the managed companies. In spite of the objection of the Sassoons the ITO determined the said sum as their escaped incomes and assessed them accordingly. The AAC dismissed assessee's appeals. The Tribunal relied upon its order in the case of the transferees and confirmed the orders of the AAC. The Tribunal was of the opinion that the managing agency commission was earned for services rendered and therefore, it was taxed in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the managing agency and not in the hands of the person to whom it was assigned, and that therefore so far as the Sassoons were concerned the managing agency commission should be apportioned between them and their transferees. On references by the assessee and the Department, the decision of the High Court was against the contentions which had been urged both by the Sassoons and the Commissioner. The High Court adopted test of the services rendered by the Sassoons as well as the transferees during the whole of the year and considered the proportions of the services rendered by the Sassoons and the transferees as the managing agents of the companies as decisive of the portions of the managing agency commission earned respectively by each. The High Court held in substance that (1) the managing agency remuneration for the year in question accrued as the joint income of the both the assignor and the assignee and was apportionable between them, and (2) the assignee-companies received the assignor's share of the joint income by virtue of the assignments of the assignor's share and hence to that extent it was not their taxable income but continued to be the taxable income of the assignor. The income was held assessable to tax not on the basis of receipt but on the basis of accrual.

On appeal by the Revenue the Tribunal held that the extinguishment of the assessee's right in the flats allotted was actually extinguishment of a right in relation to a capital asset in view of the provisions of section 47 of the Act and fell within the definition of transfer and hence, resulted in capital gains chargeable under section 45 of the Act. Since right to purchase residential flats could only be a long-term capital asset, the assessee was eligible for relief under section 54 of the Act.

(supra) that when a thing is destroyed by fire or when a ship sinks into sea, the capital asset is no longer available for being owned, used or enjoyed by anyone including the assessee and with destruction of the asset, right of assessee in that asset would be destroyed and destruction of such rights in an asset consequent upon assets ceasing to exist is a situation which is not contemplated either in definition of 'transfer', or in charging section 45 of the Act.

In other words, if the asset is destroyed due to natural calamity the question of "transfer of asset" by "extinguishment of rights" does not arise.

■ The name given to a transaction by the parties concerned does not necessarily decide the nature of the transaction. In such a case the question always is what is the real character of the payment, not what the parties call.1

■ It is the quality of the payment that is decisive of the character of the payment and not the method of payment or its measure and makes it fall within capital or revenue.2

■ The fact that receipt is a periodic receipt or a single receipt is immaterial for the purpose of determining its nature; an income receipt is not necessarily recurring; nor a capital receipt necessarily single.3

■ The nature of the receipt is to be determined from a commercial point of view.4

■ The nature of the receipt is to be seen in the hands of the receiver and not in the hands of the payer.5

■ The nature and quality of the payment is to be seen and the motive of the payer is not material though motive may be enquired into. Whether the amount is large or is periodic in character, that does not determine its quality.6

■ The fact that a certain payment is measured by estimated annual yield or profit does not make the payment an income receipt.3

If the agreements, which constitute the source and profit-making apparatus, are terminated, the compensation received by the assessee is capital receipt provided; besides the agreements, there are no other capital assets producing the income.5

6.1-2 Contracts 'relating' to business

The amended section 28(ii)(e) covers any contract "relating" to the business. Hence, it would cover contracts relating to purchases, sales or services or any other aspect of a business including joint venture agreements, distribution, etc.

6.1-3 Contracts 'relating' to acquisition of capital assets

Since the amended section is very widely worded it would cover contracts relating to acquisition of capital assets and hence on a literal reading, the compensation or other payment at or in connection with termination of such contract would be taxable as business income under section 28(ii)(e). On the other hand, Courts have held that giving up the right to obtain conveyance of immovable property or to claim specific performance is a transfer, assessable as capital gains [CIT v. Smt. Laxmidevi Ratani [2005] 147 Taxman 642 (MP); CIT v. Vijay Flexible Container [1990] 48 Taxman 86 (Bom.); Asian PPG Industries Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 38 SOT 114 (Mum. - Trib.); Asstt. CIT v. United Motors (I) Ltd. [2009] 32 SOT 399 (Mum. - Trib.)]

Thus, it is possible that a receipt is taxable as capital gains as well as under section 28(ii)(e) on its literal reading, if such receipt is in connection with the termination of the contract. In such circumstances, it could be argued that the provision may be so construed as being applicable to cases other than those relating to transfer of a capital asset. See for instance a case such as Patel Brass Works v. CIT [2007] 163 Taxman 279 (Guj.). In CIT v. T. P. Sidhwa [1981] 6 Taxman 91 (Bom.), the Bombay High Court explained the Supreme Court judgment in Nalinikant Ambalal Mody v. CIT [1966] 61 ITR 428 and stated that "whether an income falls under one head or the other has to be decided according to the common notion of practical men, for the Act does not provide any guidance in the matter. In other words, the heads of income must be decided on the nature of the income by applying practical common notion and not by reference to the assessee's treatment of income". Now, under the common notion, gains of the type mentioned above should fall under capital gains and not profits and gains of business which is ordinarily not meant to cover capital receipts.

Further, the Explanatory Memorandum reads as follows:

"Under the existing provisions of the Act, certain types of compensation receipts are taxable as business income under section 28. However, the existing provisions of clause (ii) of section 28 is restrictive in its scope as far as taxation of compensation is concerned; a large segment of compensation receipts in connection with business and employment is out of the purview of taxation leading to base erosion and revenue loss."

Thus, the intent is to bring within the scope of the law cases that presently fall outside resulting in base erosion and revenue loss and not cases which are already covered under the head capital gains.

The Calcutta High Court in the case of Principal CIT v. ITC Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 88 (Calcutta) held that sum received for relinquishment of right to operate hotel under operating license agreement is revenue receipt.

In this case the assessee-licensee was running the hotel owned by the licensor along with the licensor's employees under an operating license granted by the licensor under an Operating licence agreement, and the licence was terminated by the licensor, and the assessee received the compensation by way of settlement of all disputes in relation to the agreement as per the Arbitrator's award as per consent terms.

The following substantial question was referred to the High Court—

"Whether receipt of money by the Assessee on account of relinquishment of its right to operate a hotel as a licensee would constitute capital receipt exposing the Assessee to capital gains tax or the same shall be treated as business receipt?"

The High Court held that "as it is a compensation received for loss of trading operation of running the hotel under the agreement and not for the loss of any asset of enduring value the amount received is a revenue receipt and not a capital receipt."

Paragraph 29 of this judgment is the highlight of this decision and the same is extracted below—

"Vide in Commissioner of Income Tax, UP, Lucknow v. Gangadhar Baijnath, Generalganj, Kanpur (1972) 4 SCC 28 (para 14) Hon'ble Supreme Court noted that one way of distinguishing capital from revenue receipts, is to take the classical economists' distinction between fixed capital and circulating capital receipts in respect of former is capital while the latter is not. Fixed capital is what is retained by the owner and turned to profit while circulating capital is parted with in order to yield profit. The ITC had not (made) any fixed capital investment to run the hotel under the "Operating Licence Agreement". On the other hand, from perusal of various clauses of the agreement it appears that the ITC has introduced some circulating capital to run the hotel. Therefore, from Classical Economists distinction point of view also, the receipts of Rs. 32.42 crore by the ITC from the ELEL being not for transfer or loss of any capital asset but at best in lieu of circulating capital introduced to operate the hotel, is "revenue receipt" arising from the trading contract i.e. "Operating Lisence Agreement". Mere use of the word "relinquishment" in the "Settlement Agreement" and in the "Consent Terms" without disclosing any rights in any capital asset or relinquishment any rights in any capital assets, is not decisive rather establishes that the receipt is not capital receipt."

CIT [2008] 302 ITR 255/171 Taxman 390 (Delhi) is an authority for the proposition that even when an assessee becomes entitled to an undefined and undivided share in a property, through an agreement, which he later relinquishes, the gain has to be assessed as income from capital gain, and not as income from other sources." It was finally submitted on behalf of the assessee that the Tribunal clearly fell into error by not appreciating the fact that the provisions of Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act were clearly not attracted in this case since the amount received by the assessee had no nexus or correlation with the cessation of his employment with TTPL and further that the Assessing Officer as well as the Tribunal had clearly misconstrued the scope and ambit of Section 17(3)(iii) of the Act.

The High Court took into consideration the arguments put forth on behalf of both sides and answered the principal question whether the Tribunal was justified in bifurcating the settlement consideration between salary and capital gains in the negative by noting that a bifurcation of the consideration amount between salary and capital gains was one which was never advocated by the respondents (Revenue). The High Court went on to observe that "it thus clearly appears to represent an exercise which the Tribunal undertook of its own volition."

The High Court allowed the appeal of the assessee by setting aside the order passed by the Tribunal on the following grounds—

(a)

TTPL had never doubted the fact that the assessee did possess share certificates of the 50,000 sweat equity shares which had been allotted to it. This aspect should also be viewed in light of the well settled position in law of a share certificate being prima facie evidence of valid title. The litigation before the CLB had ensued only because of a refusal on the part of TTPL to record the name of the assessee in the Register of Members. It was in the aforesaid context that the assessee had addressed a prayer for specific performance before the CLB.

(b)

From various clauses of the Settlement Agreement the consideration was concerned with an unconditional and irrevocable relinquishment of the right of the assessee to seek and enforce the registration of the shares held by him. It was the relinquishment of the aforesaid right which formed the basis for the assessee being compensated by TTPL.

(c)

As the assessee undertook not to take any steps to enforce any right, title or interest in the shares in question, the consideration thus would appear to be undeniably connected with the relinquishment of all claims which could have been raised by the assessee in respect of sweat equity.

(d)

The Tribunal lost sight of the difference between a 'perquisite' and 'profits in lieu of salary' and both of whom have been dealt with separately in Section 17 of the Act. This subtle difference was appreciated by the High Court by explaining that "Section 17 of the Act, while seeking to define the expression 'salary', includes perquisites' in terms of sub-section (2) and sweat equity being a constituent of perquisites by virtue of clause (vi) thereof. Sub-section (3) to Section 17, on the other hand, deals with 'profits in lieu of salary.'"

(e)

'Profits in lieu of salary', spoken of in Section 17(3), would deal with compensation received by an assessee from his employer or former employer in connection with the termination of his employment or on a modification of terms and conditions of service. However, the Tribunal had fundamentally erred in ignoring the indubitable position of the employment of the assessee having been brought to an end on 24th August, 2010 itself and thus before the action came to be even laid or instituted before the CLB.

(f)

In the petition, which was filed before the CLB, there was no relief which was sought with respect to the cessation of employment of the assessee or the validity of termination of employment and that the principal relief sought by the assessee in those proceedings was for the registration of the 50,000 sweat equity shares in his name and thus essentially of specific performance.

(g)

Clause (iii) of Section 17(3) should be construed bearing in mind the subjects covered in the preceding parts of that sub-section. Consequently, the lump sum amount spoken of in clause (iii) would also have to draw colour and meaning from compensation received in connection with termination of employment or modification of terms and conditions of service and which are the principal subjects of 'profits in lieu of salary'. In the instant case, as already stated above, termination of employment took place as early as 24th August, 2010 and

(h)

All that the Tribunal was called upon to examine was whether the settlement consideration was liable to be construed as capital gains or taxed as 'profits in lieu of salary'. Based on the facts of the case, the consideration could not have possibly or justifiably been placed in the category of 'profits in lieu of salary'.

Winding up - Even the realisation of an asset of a company, which took place before actual liquidation but manifesting intention to wind up, was held to be an act of realisation of asset and not carrying on business of the company [CIT v. National Mills Co. Ltd. [1958] 34 ITR 155 (Bom.)].

When the Liquidator of a company is engaged in merely realising the assets of the company, he cannot be said to be carrying on any business [Vijay Lakshmi Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1972] 86 ITR 402 (All.)]. Also see, Banyan & Berry v. CIT [1996] 84 Taxman 515 (Guj.).

Tax is not levied on gross receipts but on profits or gains - 'Gains' is really the equivalent of 'profits'. The profit of a trade or business is the surplus by which the receipts from the trade or business exceeded the expenditure necessary for the purpose of earning those receipts. The tax is upon income, profits or gains; it is not a tax on gross receipts [CIT v. Bokaro Steel Ltd. [1987] 34 Taxman 374 (Pat.)].

Assessable profits must be real profits - The assessable profits of a business must be real profits and they have to be ascertained on ordinary principles of trading and commercial accounting. Where the assessee is under a liability or is bound to make a certain payment from the gross profits, the profits and gains can only be the net amount after the said liability or amount is deducted from the gross profits or receipts [Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1971] 82 ITR 363 (SC)].

Tax is chargeable on aggregate basis - While profits or losses of each distinct business may be computed separately, but income-tax is chargeable on the aggregate of profits of all business carried on by assessee after adjusting profits of one or more business against losses, if any, of other business and not on separate income of every separate and distinct business [CIT v. Jethalal Zaverchand Patalia [1966] 61 ITR 357 (Guj.)].

'Compensation', meaning of - The primary significance of the word 'compensation' is 'equivalence' and the secondary or more common meaning is 'something given or obtained as an equivalent'. The large number of ways in which this expression 'compensation' has been interpreted has one common factor running through them all, that is, that compensation is regarded as an equivalent or recompense, that which makes good the lack of variation of something else. Flowing from this concept, the enlargement of the meaning of this expression takes in that which compensates for loss or provision, amends, remunerates or recompenses [CIT v. D. R. Sondhi [2001] 114 Taxman 259 (Delhi)].

8.3-2 Compensation

Section 56(2)(xi) applies to "compensation or other payment" received by a person.

The term "compensation" has not been defined in the provision.

Section 28(ii) uses the same expression, namely, any "compensation or other payment". For this purpose, the term "compensation" has been judicially explained as follows:

'(a)

It is true that compensation has the meaning that it is something paid to a person what has suffered a loss by another who has caused that loss, but that appears to be a secondary meaning. We have been referred to Salmond on Jurisprudence, where it is stated:

"It may be stated as a general rule, that the violation of a private right gives rise, in him whose right it is, to a sanctioning right to receive compensation for the injury so done to him. Such compensation must itself be divided into two kinds, which may be distinguished as Restitution and Penal Redress. In respect of the person injured, indeed, these two are the same in their nature and operation; but in respect of the wrongdoer, they are very different. In restitution the defendant is compelled to give up the pecuniary value of some benefit which he has wrongfully obtained at the expense of the plaintiff; as when he who has wrongfully taken or detained another's goods is made to pay him the pecuniary value of them, or when he who has wrongfully enriched himself at another's expense is compelled to account to him for all money so obtained."

It seems to us that the above passage is not applicable to cases like the present. It is no doubt true that if the managed company got rid of the services of the managing agent, in violation of the agreement of the managing agency, the managing agent would be entitled to obtain compensation in respect of the right he was deprived of. While in civil actions the expression "compensation" may have a peculiar significance, the expression as used in the Income-tax Act does not appear to us to be susceptible of only that meaning and no other. In Words and Phrases a variety of meaning is given. It is seen therefrom that the expressions "compensation", "damages" and "gratuity" are not synonymous. The primary significance of the word "compensation" is "equivalence" and the secondary or more common meaning is "something given or obtained as an equivalent". The large number of ways in which this expression "compensation" has been interpreted has one common factor running through them all, that is, that compensation is regarded as an equivalent or recompense, that which makes good the lack of variation of something else. Flowing from this concept, the enlargement of the meaning of this expression takes in that which compensates for loss or privation, amends, remunerates or recompenses. [R.V. Lakshmiah Naidu v. CIT [1963] 48 ITR 661 (Mad.)1]

(b)

"While in civil actions, the expression "compensation" may have peculiar significance, the expression as used in the Act does not appear to be susceptible of only that meaning and no other. The primary significance of the word "compensation" is "equivalence" and the secondary or more common meaning is "something given or obtained as an equivalent".
